نسخ بصيغة Markdown متقدّم آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-28. Beta header name and model support (Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5) can change as the feature approaches GA — reconfirm before shipping. Availability on Bedrock and Vertex is called out here; Microsoft Foundry parity was not stated when this page was written. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. For as long as Claude has had tool use, the tools array has been frozen for the life of a conversation — or, more precisely, frozen for the life of a cache entry. Change it and the prompt cache melts. That is because prompt caching hashes the request prefix in a fixed order: tools → system → messages. The tool list sits earlier than anything else you send. Add one tool, rename one description, and every cached turn after that point misses. On a long agentic session with hundreds of thousands of cached input tokens, that "small edit" can cost you real money and a fresh multi-second cold start. Mid-conversation tool changes are the tool-array counterpart to mid-conversation system messages. You still declare the full universe of tools in tools once, up front. But you now decide which subset is actually offered to the model on any given turn by appending tool_addition and tool_removal blocks inside a role: "system" message. The tools array itself never changes, so the cached prefix stays byte-identical. What you'll learn Why editing tools[] used to blow up the whole cache, not just the tool section How defer_loading, tool_addition and tool_removal split declaration from availability The exact placement rules for the system message that carries these blocks (they inherit the rules from mid-conversation system messages) How to reference MCP tools individually (mcp_tool_reference) or as a whole server (mcp_toolset_reference) When this beta beats the alternatives — sub-agents with their own tool_choice, per-turn resend, or an outer router ★ Insight ───────────────────────────────────── Two things make this feature quietly important. First, on Opus 5 the minimum cacheable prompt dropped from 1,024 to 512 tokens, so smaller sessions benefit from the cache — which means small sessions now also suffer when you invalidate it. Second, tools sitting before system in the hash means today, when you use mid-conversation-system-messages to sneak in a new instruction, you still pay full price the day you need to introduce a new tool. This beta closes the last hole. ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

A request's cache key is a rolling hash of the prefix, in this order: [ tools ][ system ][ messages…, up to the breakpoint ] A cache hit requires every byte before the breakpoint to match a recent request. So: What you change What still hits cache What you re-pay Append a new user turn at the end The whole prefix up to that turn Only the new turn Append a new mid-conversation system message Everything before it The new system message Edit the top-level system field Only tools system + every message Add one new tool to tools Nothing system + every message That last row is the one Mid-Conversation Tool Changes rewrites.
documents.s: The cache-hash problem in one picture

documents.t: 1. defer_loading: true — on a tool declaration in tools, this keeps the tool declared but withheld from the model. It is still hashed into the cache prefix (that is the whole point), but Claude never sees it as callable until you surface it. 2. tool_addition — a content block inside a role: "system" message. Surfaces a defer_loading tool from that turn onward. Also re-offers a tool that a previous tool_removal had withdrawn. 3. tool_removal — the mirror. Retracts a currently-offered tool from that turn onward. Every subsequent turn hits the cache, but the tool is no longer in Claude's choice set. Both tool_addition and tool_removal reference a tool via a tool field. Three reference shapes are legal: {"type": "tool_reference", "name": "get_forecast"} — a normal tool declared in tools. {"type": "mcp_tool_reference", "server_name": "linear", "name": "create_issue"} — a single MCP connector tool. {"type": "mcp_toolset_reference", "server_name": "linear"} — every tool exposed by an MCP server, in one block. Referencing a name that is not declared in tools returns a 400.

The beta requires the mid-conversation-tool-changes-2026-07-01 header and one of Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 4.8, or Opus 5. Below: declare both a "read" tool and a "write" tool up front, withhold delete_file, and surface it only after the user has confirmed a destructive intent. import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() TOOLS = [ { "name": "read_file", "description": "Read a file from disk.", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["path"], }, }, { # Declared but withheld. Hashed into the cache prefix so we can # surface it later without invalidating anything. "name": "delete_file", "description": "Permanently delete a file from disk.", "defer_loading": True, "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["path"], }, }, ] messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": "Read notes.md and summarize it."}, # ...several tool_use / tool_result turns... {"role": "user", "content": "OK, I confirm: delete notes.md."}, # Surface delete_file from this point onward. The cached prefix # (tools + all earlier turns) still matches byte-for-byte. { "role": "system", "content": [ { "type": "tool_addition", "tool": {"type": "tool_reference", "name": "delete_file"}, } ], }, ] response = client.beta.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024, betas=["mid-conversation-tool-changes-2026-07-01"], cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"}, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages, ) The next request will: Hash tools (unchanged) → cache hit. Hash every earlier turn (unchanged) → cache hit. Only the new user turn + system-role tool_addition block are new input. Contrast this with the "old way" — dropping delete_file into tools only at that moment. That single mutation would have invalidated the entire prefix.

Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Declare every tool the session might ever need in tools[] on the first request⌄ Include tools you plan to surface later, but set defer_loading: true on them. The point is to freeze the tool section of the cache prefix now. ←PreviousNext→ 2Turn on prompt caching explicitly⌄ Mid-conversation tool changes only save you money if the prefix is actually cached. Use cache_control: {type: ephemeral} at the top level, or an explicit breakpoint on the last stable block. Without a breakpoint, nothing is cached and there is nothing to preserve. ←PreviousNext→ 3Route your 'add tool' events through a system message⌄ When your application decides a new capability should become available — after login, after a plan is approved, after a mode switch — append a role: system message with tool_addition blocks. Place it right after the user turn or the tool_result turn, not between a tool_use and its tool_result. ←PreviousNext→ 4Retire tools with tool_removal, not by dropping them from tools[]⌄ Same reason: dropping them mutates the prefix. tool_removal is a system-role block that only appends. Common triggers: entering read-only mode, finishing a task phase, or after a rate limit locks a specific integration. ←PreviousNext→ 5Move the cache breakpoint past the system message on the next turn⌄ Once a mid-conversation system message is in the history it is itself cacheable. On the next request, either use automatic caching or move an explicit breakpoint past it, so the added/removed capability is baked into the cache from then on. ←PreviousNext→ 6Do not edit or delete a system block you already sent⌄ That is a prefix mutation and it invalidates everything after it. If you need to change your mind, append a new system message (tool_removal to withdraw what you just added, or a fresh tool_addition to re-offer it). ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Adopting it in an agentic loop

documents.t: Withhold destructive tools until the user confirms CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ system: <tool_addition tool={type: "tool_reference", name: "delete_project"}> Only append this after a user turn where the user explicitly confirmed destruction. Never place before a "clarify what you want to delete?" turn. Phase toolsets for a plan → execute → review loop CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Phase 1 (plan): tools[] visible = { read_repo, search_web } — everything else defer_loading: true. Phase 2 (execute): append system-role tool_addition for { edit_file, run_tests }. Phase 3 (review): append system-role tool_removal for { edit_file }, tool_addition for { post_review_comment }. The tools[] array never changes; only the offered set does. Cache is preserved across all three phases. Retire an MCP server after a rate limit CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ On 429 from the Linear MCP connector, append: system: <tool_removal tool={type: "mcp_toolset_reference", server_name: "linear"}> One block retires every tool that server exposed. Re-offer with a matching tool_addition once your backoff window expires. Sandbox: give a subagent a strict subset CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ When you dispatch a subagent, do NOT create a new conversation with a smaller tools[]. Instead reuse the same tools[] (cache hit!) and open the subagent turn with a system-role tool_removal for every capability that subagent should not touch. The parent conversation can restore them on return with a matching tool_addition.

The role: "system" message that carries tool_addition / tool_removal blocks is a regular mid-conversation system message and inherits its placement rules: Never first. A system message cannot be the first entry in messages; declare the initial toolset in the top-level system field and tools. Must follow a user turn or a server-tool assistant turn. A user message carrying tool_result blocks counts — that is exactly the slot for reacting to what a tool just returned. Must precede an assistant turn or be the last entry. Never between a tool_use and its matching tool_result. That is a 400. Consecutive system messages are legal and are treated as one section. You can mix tool_addition, tool_removal, and plain text blocks in the same content array.

Enable caching explicitly. A cache_control field somewhere is required; automatic caching at the top level is the simplest. Cache the stable prefix as usual — through the last block that does not change across requests. Because the appended system message comes after the cached prefix, it does not change the prefix hash. Once the system message is in the conversation, it becomes stable history and is cacheable on the next turn. Every tool in tools, including defer_loading: true tools, counts toward the minimum cacheable prompt length — 512 tokens on Opus 5, 1,024 on most other models. ★ Insight ───────────────────────────────────── This design pushes agent authors toward a specific discipline: declare the ambition of the session up front, and use runtime signals to modulate access. It is closer to how OS process capabilities are modeled (capabilities you have vs. capabilities you can currently exercise) than to how classic function-calling APIs are shaped. If you architect an agent around it, "what tools does this agent have?" becomes a question with two answers — the declared universe and the offered subset — and the cache stays warm. ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
documents.s: How this interacts with prompt caching

documents.t: It does not let you introduce a tool that was not in tools at all. Every tool the model may ever be offered must exist in tools from the first request. That is a feature, not a limitation — it is precisely what keeps the hash stable. It does not let you change a tool's input_schema or description mid-conversation. Either of those is a mutation of tools and triggers a cache miss. If a tool's schema needs to evolve, declare two tools with different names. It does not apply to Claude Sonnet 5 today. Sonnet 5 does not support mid-conversation system messages at all, so this beta cannot ride on top of it. Route Sonnet-tier turns through an outer router if you need dynamic toolsets there.

Provider Dynamic toolset without full prefix reprocess? Anthropic Claude Opus/Fable/Mythos Yes, via this beta. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 No — resend tools (cache miss) or route through an outer supervisor. OpenAI GPT-5/6 Practically no. Changing the tools array in the Responses/Chat Completions API is a prefix change; you rely on the automatic-caching prefix match to break at the tool list. Common workaround: parent/child agents where the child has a scoped tools array. Google Gemini 3 Similar to OpenAI. The tools config is part of the request; the pragmatic pattern is per-phase Function Declaration sets, accepting the cost of re-declaring. MCP servers in general Some hosts (Claude Code, Cursor) implement "on-demand tool loading" inside the host, but that is transport-level: the underlying model still receives a resent tools list until this beta lands provider-side. If you are building a cross-model harness, structure your code so the "dynamic tool" behavior is a capability you feature-detect per model rather than something you assume everywhere.
documents.s: How other providers handle the same problem

documents.t: You forgot the beta header. The request is accepted, tool_addition / tool_removal blocks are treated as unknown content in a system message, and behavior is undefined — often the block is quietly ignored and Claude never sees the new tool. You put the system message between tool_use and tool_result. 400 invalid_request_error. Move it to after the following user turn that carries the tool_result. You referenced a tool not declared in tools. 400. Declare it with defer_loading: true and try again. You edited the tool description "just to add clarification". Cache miss for the whole conversation. To evolve a tool mid-session, add a v2 tool under a new name and use tool_removal on v1 and tool_addition on v2. You are on Sonnet 5 wondering why it does not work. It does not, on Sonnet 5. Use a different tier or an outer router. لا توجد بطاقات بعد — أضف بعضها لبدء المذاكرة. 🃏 Check yourself 0/5

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متقدّم For most of 2026, tracing a Claude API call meant writing the span yourself: open a span, call messages.create, copy usage onto attributes, close the span. Agent observability is the page about doing that well — and it is still the page about what the names mean. This page is about the part that changed. The API and the SDK now emit those spans themselves, in beta, and they emit considerably more than you were writing by hand: a span per model request inside one API request, a span per server tool the API ran for you, a span per compaction, a span per Managed Agents turn. Things that happen on Anthropic's side of the wire, which hand-instrumentation structurally cannot see. There are two independent paths to turn this on, and the most expensive thing to misunderstand is that they overlap. Enable both without reading one paragraph of the docs and every Messages request shows up twice, with the same span name, and your token dashboards double. What you'll learn Choose between SDK tracing, API tracing, or both — and know exactly what each one can and cannot see Set up each path: a tracer provider in your code, a destination in the Console or via the Admin API Sum tokens correctly across overlapping spans — the one rule that stops double counting Pick a content mode deliberately, and know what overrides your choice (HIPAA/FERPA/K-12, zero data retention) Join API spans into your application's traces with traceparent — and avoid the sampled flag that deletes them Survive the delivery rules: at-least-once, best-effort, and automatic disabling after 24 hours of failures آخر تحقّق: 2026-10-19. OpenTelemetry export for the Claude API and SDK launched in beta on October 14, 2026. Anthropic states explicitly that span names, attributes, SDK options, and environment variables can change during the beta, and advises pinning your SDK version. Treat every name on this page as beta surface and re-check it before a migration. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
documents.s: First-Party OpenTelemetry Tracing: Two Paths, One Trace

documents.t: They are not two ways to do the same thing. They see different halves of the run. What you get SDK tracing API tracing Messages API and Sessions API requests yes yes Token usage yes yes Each model request inside one API request — yes Managed Agents turns — yes Server tools and MCP connector tools, run by the API — yes Your own client tools, run by the tool runner yes — Tools in a self-hosted sandbox yes — Other requests, such as file uploads yes — How you set it up code Console or Admin API Who can set it up any developer an admin Which clients it covers only clients using the SDK any client, including curl The split follows one line: the SDK sees what your process does, the API sees what Anthropic's side does. A server tool like web search runs inside the API request — your process never observes it, so only API tracing produces that span. Your own get_weather function runs in your process — only SDK tracing produces that one. Which is why "both" is the real answer for most production setups, and why the overlap rule below is not an edge case. Read that shape carefully, because it contains the trap. anthropic.messages.create appears four times for a two-request conversation: twice from the SDK (kind CLIENT) and twice from the API (kind SERVER), with each API span parented to its SDK span. They are not duplicates in the sense of a redelivery — they are two legitimate observations of the same request, from both ends.

SDK spans need no permissions and no Console access. The SDK uses whatever tracer provider your application already registered, so there is no Anthropic-specific exporter to wire up. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Upgrade the SDK⌄ Spans ship in the current Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby SDKs. On Java the minimum is `anthropic-java` 2.73.0. Pin the version — the beta note says a new SDK release may rename a span, an attribute, an option or an environment variable. ←PreviousNext→ 2Register a tracer provider before your first call⌄ This is the single most common reason people see no spans. The SDK reads the globally registered provider when it makes a call; register it at process start, not lazily. Start with a console exporter to confirm spans exist at all, then swap in OTLP. ←PreviousNext→ 3Call the SDK from inside one of your own spans⌄ Nothing nests automatically. If you want the SDK span (and the API span under it) to appear beneath your own `handle_request` span, open your span and call the SDK inside it. Without that, SDK spans are root spans and the trace tells you nothing about which feature or user triggered the call. ←PreviousNext→ 4Decide the content mode and conversation ID⌄ Default is metadata only. Set `traces.content_mode` to `content` (or `ANTHROPIC_OPEN_TELEMETRY_TRACES_CONTENT_MODE=content`) to include prompts and responses. Set `conversation_id` to group a multi-call conversation under one `gen_ai.conversation.id`. ←PreviousNext→ Minimum viable SDK tracing — console exporter first (Python) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from anthropic import Anthropic from opentelemetry import trace from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import ConsoleSpanExporter, SimpleSpanProcessor # Register BEFORE the first traced call. Swap ConsoleSpanExporter for an # OTLP exporter once you can see spans in the terminal. provider = TracerProvider() provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(ConsoleSpanExporter())) trace.set_tracer_provider(provider) # Record prompts and responses, and label this conversation. client = Anthropic(open_telemetry={"traces": {"content_mode": "content"}}) tracer = trace.get_tracer("my-service") with tracer.start_as_current_span("answer_question"): message = client.with_options( open_telemetry={**client.open_telemetry, "conversation_id": "conv_42"} ).messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, Claude"}], )

Option (Python spelling) Environment variable Default traces.content_mode ANTHROPIC_OPEN_TELEMETRY_TRACES_CONTENT_MODE metadata_only traces.max_content_bytes ANTHROPIC_OPEN_TELEMETRY_TRACES_MAX_CONTENT_BYTES 0.75 MB conversation_id — none tracer_provider — the registered global provider propagation ANTHROPIC_OPEN_TELEMETRY_PROPAGATION on open_telemetry (off switch) ANTHROPIC_OPEN_TELEMETRY on Two behaviors here will cost you an hour each if you meet them cold: Passing open_telemetry to the client overrides the environment variables as a whole, nested keys included. Any key you leave out of the object silently reverts to its table default even if its variable is set. Build the object from the existing one rather than from scratch. On TypeScript with @opentelemetry/instrumentation-undici — which @opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node pulls in — set propagation: false. A bug in that package adds a second traceparent header to each request, which makes the trace context invalid and breaks the join silently. آخر تحقّق: 2026-10-19. Option names, environment-variable names, the Java opentelemetry-api 1.57.0 floor, and the undici double-header warning are from the official SDK setup page. The per-language spellings differ (TypeScript/Java/PHP use camelCase, C# PascalCase, Go uses option.With…() functions); check the page for yours. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

API tracing needs no code change at all. You register a destination — your observability platform's OTLP endpoint plus credentials — and the API posts spans to it. What you need before you start: The admin role in the Console organization. The developer role can view destinations but not create or change them. An OTLP/HTTP endpoint accepting protobuf, over HTTPS, on port 443. This is the requirement that bites self-hosters: a standard OpenTelemetry Collector listens for OTLP/HTTP on port 4318, so you need a load balancer, reverse proxy, or a reconfigured receiver in front of it. There is no gRPC option and no non-443 port. Credentials for that endpoint, which go in request headers. The Console will not show the values again after you save. Create a telemetry destination with the Admin API (curl) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ curl --fail-with-body -sS "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/organizations/telemetry_destinations" \ -H "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_ADMIN_KEY" \ -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \ -H "anthropic-beta: telemetry-destinations-2026-08-11" \ -H "content-type: application/json" \ -d '{ "endpoint_url": "https://gateway.example.com/otlp", "headers": {"authorization": "Bearer YOUR_OBSERVABILITY_API_KEY"}, "traces": {"content_mode": "metadata_only"}, "workspaces": {"type": "all"} }' Note the endpoint URL shape: give the base OTLP URL and let the API append /v1/traces itself. A path prefix is allowed. If your platform receives traces somewhere else entirely, set the optional traces endpoint URL — but it must share the same host. Three settings deserve a deliberate decision rather than a default: Workspaces — all, selected, or all except. all includes workspaces created later, which is usually what you want and occasionally exactly what you don't. A destination only receives spans from the workspace where the request or session actually ran. Content mode — covered below. Maximum content size — only applies in full-content mode. Choosing a listed partner in the Console pre-fills a value that platform accepts; with Custom you are on your own. Then verify, in this order: send a test span from the destination's menu and confirm an anthropic.test span arrives; send a real request in the chosen workspace; check the Delivery column reads Healthy; filter your platform on service.name = claude-platform. Allow about a minute at each step — both destination changes and the health column lag by roughly that much. آخر تحقّق: 2026-10-19. The admin-role requirement, the OTLP/HTTP-protobuf-HTTPS-443 endpoint requirement, the telemetry-destinations-2026-08-11 beta header, the anthropic.test verification span, and the service.name value claude-platform are all from the official API setup page. Destinations can also be managed with the ant CLI. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

Every destination and every SDK client has one of two content modes. Metadata only (metadata_only) — the default. IDs, timing, status, token counts, and text you chose yourself: agent names, tool names and descriptions, MCP server names. Full content (content) — everything above plus model prompts and responses. In the span reference these attributes carry a Content badge: gen_ai.system_instructions, gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, gen_ai.tool.call.arguments, anthropic.tool_result.content. Full content is what makes traces usable for the thing teams actually want — reading a failed conversation, or building evals from real traffic. It is also what moves your prompts and your users' inputs into a second system, under that vendor's retention and access controls rather than yours. The same calculus as what your agent uploads: enabling it grants your observability provider roughly the clearance your application data has. Two overrides are worth committing to memory, because both produce confusing support tickets: A HIPAA, FERPA, or K-12 data-handling restriction with Anthropic forces destinations to metadata only, whatever the destination says. SDK spans are not affected — your own process can still emit content. So the symptom is "full content is on, the Console agrees, and the prompts only appear on the CLIENT spans." Zero data retention is compatible with full content. For Messages API requests the API holds exported content only in memory until delivery. Managed Agents is not ZDR-eligible in the first place, and its retention is unchanged by using OpenTelemetry.
documents.s: Content modes, and what overrides your choice

documents.t: Each span holds up to 0.75 MB of content by default — chosen to fit a 200k-token context window of English text while staying under the 1 MB request limit common to observability platforms and proxies. A full 1M-token window needs roughly 4 MB. When content exceeds the limit, the span is shortened and anthropic.content.truncated is set to true. The drop order is specified, and it matters for anyone building evals from traces: Request spans drop the system prompt first, then the earliest messages. Tool spans drop blocks from the end of the result. Images and documents appear only as their type — never as bytes. So a naive "replay every trace as an eval case" pipeline will quietly feed you system-prompt-less conversations unless you filter on anthropic.content.truncated. Make that filter the first line of the pipeline, not a later discovery.

This is the section to read twice. Token usage attributes appear on several spans per request, by design, because each span reports its own step. Summing everything you receive overcounts; summing the wrong level undercounts. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Pick exactly one source per request⌄ If a Messages request has both an SDK span and an API span, sum the API spans. Both are named `anthropic.messages.create`, so you cannot filter by name — tell them apart by span kind: the SDK span is CLIENT, its child API span is SERVER. Filtering on `service.name` = `claude-platform` works too. ←PreviousNext→ 2Within API spans for a Messages request, sum one level, not two⌄ Either the `anthropic.messages.create` spans or their `anthropic.model_request` children — never both. A request with three model requests reports its total on the parent and its parts on the children. ←PreviousNext→ 3Add compaction tokens, from one place only⌄ The `gen_ai.usage.*` totals exclude compaction. On SDK spans, add `anthropic.usage.compaction.input_tokens` and `anthropic.usage.compaction.output_tokens`. On API spans, add the `anthropic.compaction` child spans instead — and then do NOT also add the parent's `anthropic.usage.compaction.*` attributes, because they hold the same tokens. ←PreviousNext→ 4For Managed Agents, sum model requests and outcome evaluations⌄ Sum the `anthropic.model_request` spans plus the `anthropic.session.outcome_evaluation` spans. Turn spans are containers; the tokens live below them. An outcome evaluation is real spend that is easy to forget, because no model request of yours produced it. ←PreviousNext→ 5Deduplicate by trace ID and span ID⌄ Delivery is at-least-once, so the same span can arrive twice. If your platform does not dedupe, you must. This is a different problem from the CLIENT/SERVER overlap and needs its own fix. ←PreviousNext→ One more thing that is not a counting rule but will save you from a bad number: gen_ai.usage.input_tokens already includes cache reads and cache writes. Adding gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens to it double-counts the cheapest tokens you have. See prompt caching for what those tokens cost relative to each other. Traces are not a billing record Anthropic states plainly that exported spans are not guaranteed to be a complete record of usage. Delivery is best effort, so a span can be lost; and a caller can suppress a request's spans entirely by turning off the sampled flag in its traceparent. For per-key accounting — spotting a leaked key, reconciling an invoice — use the Usage API, which counts requests that produced no spans at all. Traces are for debugging and for cost attribution; they are not the ledger.
documents.s: The one rule: count each token once

documents.t: By default, API spans live in their own traces — technically correct and nearly useless, because you cannot tell which feature or user caused the call. The API reads the W3C traceparent header from each request. With the SDK, you get this for free as long as you called the SDK inside your own span and registered the W3C trace context propagator. (If your application standardized on B3 or another propagator, add W3C alongside it — the SDK writes headers with your propagator.) With any other client, inject the active span's context into the headers yourself before posting. Then there is the flag that surprises everyone: The sampled flag is an on/off switch for spans, not a hint If the sampled flag in the incoming traceparent is off, the API emits no span for that request and none of the spans under it. Head sampling in your application therefore decides whether Anthropic-side telemetry exists at all. A 1%-sampling service that enables API tracing gets 1% of model-request and server-tool spans — and will conclude the feature is broken. Either sample at the tail in your collector, or force the sampled flag on for the paths you need traced. The propagation goes one hop further than most people expect. When the Messages API calls your MCP server through the MCP connector, it passes a W3C traceparent in params._meta, so a server that reads it can attach its own spans under the API's. In a tools/call request that parent is the anthropic.mcp_tool_use span; in other messages it is anthropic.messages.create. An untraced request sends no traceparent at all. On the client side the picture is patchier: the Python mcp package from version 2.0 and the C# ModelContextProtocol package forward trace context in _meta; the TypeScript, Go, Java, Ruby, and PHP MCP SDKs do not do it on their own.
documents.s: Joining API spans into your own traces

documents.t: API-side export is a push from Anthropic's infrastructure to your endpoint, which means it has its own failure semantics — closer to a webhook than to an OTLP exporter in your process. Property Behavior Duplication At least once. Dedupe by trace ID + span ID. Loss Best effort. A lost span is never resent. Compression Each delivery's first request is gzipped with Content-Encoding: gzip. On a 400 or 415, the same spans are resent immediately, uncompressed. Retries Limited retries after a timeout, a connection/TLS/DNS failure, or a 408, 429, or 5xx. Other failures are not retried. Timeouts TLS handshake within 5 s, response headers within 5 s, 10 s total per delivery — including the uncompressed resend. User agent User-Agent: Claude-Platform. Useful for an allowlist rule. And three ways the API will disable a destination outright, stopping export until a human re-enables it: The endpoint returns a 3xx redirect. Redirects are not followed — point the destination at the final URL. The endpoint's hostname resolves to a non-public IP address. There is no tunnel to your VPC; expose a public collector or use a managed platform. Every delivery fails for 24 hours. That third one is the operational hazard. A rotated observability API key that nobody notices becomes a destination that is Failing for a day and then Disabled — and re-enabling is a manual click in the Console (with the workspace filter set to All), not an automatic recovery. If you alert on one thing from this page, alert on the Delivery state.
documents.s: Delivery rules, and how a destination dies

documents.t: Limit Value Destinations, including disabled ones 10 Workspaces selected for one destination 1,000 Request headers per destination 20 Header name length 128 bytes Header value length 4,096 bytes All header names and values together 16,384 bytes Endpoint URL length 2,048 characters آخر تحقّق: 2026-10-19. Delivery semantics, timeout values, the three auto-disable conditions, and the limits table are from the "Delivery and health" and "Limits" sections of the official API setup page. Beta surface — re-check before you build an SLO on these numbers. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

Sessions break the one-trace assumption, and the fix is a grouping key rather than a trace ID. A session's spans can land in several traces — a later request sent from a new root trace starts a new one — and with multiagent orchestration a session has several threads. So: One thread, as a transcript — group by gen_ai.conversation.id (the session thread ID), sort by start time. A whole session, all threads — group by anthropic.session.id, across traces. The span shapes are worth internalizing because they do not match the generic GenAI conventions you may already have dashboards for. anthropic.session.turn carries gen_ai.operation.name = invoke_agent and spans one thread's running state; a turn that a request started is a child of that request's span, while a turn that starts because another thread replied has no parent at all. In full-content mode the turn span holds the thread's content: gen_ai.system_instructions on a thread's first turn only, gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages. Advisor threads are deliberately thinner — gen_ai.agent.name is anthropic.advisor, and the instruction and input attributes are absent. Four cases produce no API tool span at all, and each has caused someone to think their tracing was broken: a tool your application runs (the SDK tool runner emits that span); a tool in a self-hosted sandbox (the SDK environment worker emits it, grouped under anthropic.environment.work); a multiagent or advisor tool; and a tool use denied under the auto permission policy or by a user.tool_confirmation event. Denied calls leave no tool span — if you are auditing what an agent tried to do, read the session events, not the trace.

Summing every anthropic.messages.create span you receive. Two legitimate observations per request, same name. Filter by span kind or service.name first. This is the mistake that produces a plausible, wrong, exactly-doubled cost number. Expecting spans at your usual sampling rate. A sampled-off traceparent suppresses the API spans completely. Head sampling in your service is head sampling of Anthropic's telemetry. Pointing a destination at a bare Collector. OTLP/HTTP on 4318 is not an HTTPS endpoint on 443. Put a proxy in front, or the destination never delivers. Treating full content as a logging flag. It relocates prompts and user input into your observability vendor. Decide it with whoever owns data handling, and know that a HIPAA/FERPA/K-12 restriction silently overrides it for API spans only. Building evals from traces without checking anthropic.content.truncated. Truncation drops the system prompt first. Your eval corpus will be missing exactly the part that determined behavior. Letting a Failing destination sit. 24 hours of failures disables it, and re-enabling is manual. Alert on the Delivery state, not on span volume — span volume looks fine right up until it is zero. Hard-coding these attribute names into forty panels. The spans follow the GenAI conventions at a specific commit (e57c543b, September 24, 2026) of a repository with no tagged release, and the beta note reserves the right to rename. The mapping-layer habit from agent observability applies here with extra force.

Any platform that accepts OTLP works. Anthropic documents integration guides with Arize AI, Braintrust, Databricks, Datadog, Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, Langfuse, LangSmith, New Relic, PostHog, Sentry, and Splunk; choosing a listed provider in the Console asks for that platform's own credentials and pre-fills a content size it accepts, instead of asking for a raw endpoint and headers. For Claude Code, the Agent SDK, and Cowork, this is a different system with different switches — CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY and friends, covered in agent observability. Enabling destinations here does nothing for them, and vice versa. Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways Two paths, two halves of the run: the SDK sees your process, the API sees Anthropic's side. Most production setups want both. Both paths emit anthropic.messages.create for the same request. Pick one source by span kind before you sum anything. Within API spans, sum one level — messages.create or model_request, never both — and add compaction from exactly one place. Spans are for debugging and attribution, not billing: delivery is best effort and a sampled-off traceparent erases a request entirely. Use the Usage API for the ledger. The sampled flag is an on/off switch, not a hint. A 1%-sampling service gets 1% of Anthropic-side spans. Full content relocates your prompts into your observability vendor. A HIPAA/FERPA/K-12 restriction overrides it for API spans only — a very confusing symptom if you do not know it. Check anthropic.content.truncated before building evals from traces: truncation drops the system prompt first. Alert on a destination's Delivery state. 24 hours of failures disables it, and recovery is a manual click.

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط Microsoft's playwright-mcp sits at ~35k GitHub stars and — per the community-maintained MCP registries — is currently the most-installed MCP server on the planet, ranked ahead of even the official GitHub MCP and Figma MCP servers. If you use Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf, or Claude Desktop and you have ever asked your agent to "check the site" or "grab data from that dashboard," this is the tool doing the actual work. Almost every guide to it stops at the two-line install. This page is the part that matters after: what the tool is actually doing under the hood, the modes people don't realize exist, and the sharp edges — token cost, security, browser-profile locking — that show up around week two. What you'll learn Understand why accessibility-snapshot mode (default) is not just faster than vision — it is a different automation paradigm the LLM treats deterministically Know the three profile modes — persistent, isolated, browser-extension — and when each is the right choice Turn on the opt-in capability packs (network, storage, devtools, vision, pdf, testing) with --caps and understand why they are off by default See the real token cost of Playwright MCP in a Claude Code session and know when Playwright-as-a-Skill wins instead Deploy Playwright MCP as a standalone HTTP/SSE server, in Docker, and safely for autonomous runs (secrets masking is a convenience, not a boundary)
documents.s: Playwright MCP: The Deep Practical Guide (2026)

documents.t: Playwright MCP is the reference implementation of "give an LLM a browser," and it made two design bets that turned out to be correct: Structured accessibility snapshots as the primary interface — not screenshots. The model gets a compact, deterministic tree of elements (roles, names, refs). No vision model required, no coordinate hallucination, tokens spent on structure instead of pixels. Playwright's real automation engine underneath — same waits, same auto-actionability checks, same locator system that has hardened over years of production QA. Nothing bespoke. Result: on a fresh install you get roughly 50+ tools across navigation, form filling, tabs, snapshots, screenshots, console access, network inspection, and a few opt-in categories. That is a lot of surface — which brings us straight to the first thing that surprises people.
documents.s: Why this server ate the ecosystem

documents.t: By default the MCP server runs in accessibility-snapshot mode. When your agent calls browser_snapshot, it does not get a screenshot — it gets a YAML-like tree: - Page URL: https://example.com/login - role: main - role: form - role: textbox, name: "Email", ref: e12 - role: textbox, name: "Password", ref: e13 - role: button, name: "Sign in", ref: e14 The agent then calls browser_click({ ref: "e14" }) — no CSS selectors it invented, no coordinates it guessed. ref is a handle the server minted from the underlying Playwright locator, so the click is as reliable as a hand-written page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click(). This is why people who come from Selenium/Puppeteer scripts written by an LLM think "browser use by AI is broken" — they were feeding the model raw HTML or screenshots. Snapshot mode does not have that failure mode, because the model never sees a selector it could get wrong. Pro tip If your agent is guessing CSS selectors, you are almost certainly using a different browser MCP — or you disabled snapshots. Snapshots are page-scoped. For iframes, use browser_snapshot inside the iframe explicitly; the tool exposes iframe navigation. Refs are ephemeral. They are only valid until the next page mutation — treat them like React fiber IDs.
documents.s: The mode you are actually running

documents.t: Only the boring, safe tools ship enabled. Powerful ones live behind the --caps flag and you turn them on per-server: { "mcpServers": { "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest", "--caps=network,storage,pdf"] } } } Cap What it unlocks Why it is off by default network Mock requests, set offline, route interception Can silently rewrite traffic; needs intent storage Read/write cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage Same-origin data theft is trivial once on devtools Tracing, video recording, element highlighting Very large artifacts, disk cost vision Pixel-coordinate mouse actions Bypasses the deterministic model — see below pdf Save current page as PDF Fine, just noise for most sessions testing Element/text/value verification, locator generation Test-authoring niche, adds ~a dozen tools config Read resolved server config back Debug-only The non-obvious one is vision. Turning it on gives the model browser_mouse_move_at_coordinates and friends. It also silently changes the failure profile of the whole session, because the agent will fall back to coordinate clicking when snapshots are inconvenient — and now you have a browser being driven by a language model doing pixel math. Enable it only when a canvas element or a broken-a11y widget forces your hand.

This is where the interesting design lives. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Persistent profile (default)⌄ The server launches Chromium against a per-workspace user-data directory (path derived from a hash of your working folder). Cookies, localStorage, saved passwords, and history persist across sessions. Great for authenticated dashboards. Sharp edge: only one instance can hold the profile at a time — a second Claude Code window against the same folder will error out. Point --user-data-dir at a shared location and you can share state across projects. ←PreviousNext→ 2Isolated mode (--isolated)⌄ Every session starts from a blank profile in memory and is destroyed on exit. This is the right choice for CI-like tasks and for anything you would not want to leave behind cookies for. Pair it with --storage-state <file.json> to preload cookies/localStorage — the classic pattern is 'log in once, save state, feed it to isolated runs forever.' ←PreviousNext→ 3Browser Extension mode (extension: true)⌄ You install the Playwright MCP Chrome/Edge extension and set { "extension": true } in the server config. Instead of launching a new browser, the server attaches to a tab already open in your everyday browser — with your real logins, your real session storage, your real ad blockers. This is a very different security model (see the last section), but for many personal-productivity flows it is the difference between a working agent and a demo. ←PreviousNext→

Standard local (Claude Desktop / Claude Code / Cursor) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ { "mcpServers": { "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest"] } } } Isolated + preloaded auth (CI-ish, reproducible) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ { "mcpServers": { "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "@playwright/mcp@latest", "--isolated", "--storage-state", "/Users/me/.auth/github.json", "--caps=network" ] } } } Attach to my real Chrome tab (browser extension) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ { "mcpServers": { "playwright": { "command": "npx", "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest", "--extension"] } } } Standalone HTTP server (share one browser across many agents) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # One-time on your workstation: npx @playwright/mcp@latest --port 8931 # Then every client points at it: { "mcpServers": { "playwright": { "url": "http://localhost:8931/mcp" } } } The HTTP mode is the one people miss. If you run four coding agents on the same machine, four separate npx installations of Playwright MCP each launch their own Chromium. One shared HTTP server keeps a single browser pool, which is both cheaper and easier to observe.
documents.s: Install: the four configs you actually want

documents.t: # One-shot (stdio): docker run -i --rm --init --pull=always mcr.microsoft.com/playwright/mcp # Long-lived HTTP server on port 8931: docker run -d -i --rm --init --pull=always \ --entrypoint node \ -p 8931:8931 \ mcr.microsoft.com/playwright/mcp \ /app/cli.js --headless --browser chromium --no-sandbox --port 8931 --host 0.0.0.0 Two things the docs bury: the Docker image is headless Chromium only (no Firefox, no WebKit, no headed mode), and --no-sandbox is required inside the container. If you need Firefox or a real GPU, run the server on the host.
documents.s: Docker: the only supported "headless server" recipe

documents.t: The other thing nobody warns you about: Playwright MCP is the heaviest single server you can attach to Claude Code, at roughly 3,500 tokens of tool-schema overhead per session — before you make a single call. That number lives in your context window for the whole conversation. Reported measurements from the community (link below) put a typical "test this site" task at: Approach Tokens for the task Sonnet cost (approx) Playwright MCP (default caps) ~114k ~$0.34 Playwright CLI + a Skill file ~27k ~$0.08 The Skill approach ships a small SKILL.md that documents Playwright's CLI and lets the agent shell out with bash. The tool schema stays out of the model's context until it is needed, and the skill file itself is read once. Recent Playwright MCP versions have narrowed this gap by no longer streaming full page state on every call, but the schema overhead is still the schema overhead. Rule of thumb: MCP for interactive/exploratory work where the model needs conversational back-and-forth with the DOM. Skill/CLI for repeatable jobs — screenshotting a list of URLs, running a test suite, or anything you would put in a cron. See the Claude Code page on MCP token cost for how to measure this in your own session.
documents.s: The token-cost fight: MCP vs Skill vs raw CLI

documents.t: Playwright MCP supports a secrets map in its config: { "secrets": { "OPENAI_API_KEY": "sk-real-key-here", "GITHUB_TOKEN": "ghp_real" } } When the server sees those exact strings inside a tool response, it substitutes the key name back in before forwarding the result to the model. This is genuinely useful — page content that echoes your API key will no longer leak it into the LLM transcript. But the project README is explicit and repeats it several times: "Playwright MCP is not a security boundary." Concretely: A page can render your secret in a title attribute or as base64 and the masker will not catch it. Anything the model asks the browser to do — including document.cookie reads via a form field trick — still executes with your real profile's authority. The extension mode attaches to your everyday Chrome. Every logged-in tab becomes reachable in principle. Treat an agent with Playwright MCP + persistent profile the same way you would treat a fresh employee with your admin cookies: fine for narrow, supervised tasks, catastrophic on --dangerously-skip-permissions. See Agentic browsers & same-origin trust and What your agent uploads for the wider threat model.
documents.s: Secrets masking is a convenience, not a boundary

documents.t: Recent releases (v0.0.79 line) are worth knowing about because they change defaults: --timeout-settle — the server now waits a configurable number of ms (default 500) after each action for triggered work to settle before returning. Raise it for slow SPAs, lower it for perf tests. WebP screenshots — browser_take_screenshot accepts type: "png" | "jpeg" | "webp" and infers from filename. WebP is roughly 30–50% smaller than PNG for the same quality, worth changing if you screenshot a lot. Codegen output for Python / Java / C# — the testing cap can now emit test skeletons in more than TypeScript. Download event detection — replaces the previous error-based inference; downloads now trigger a real event so agents can wait on them. Browser-extension CDP relay — hardened with header validation on the WebSocket upgrade. آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-06. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. المصادر: Playwright MCP releases: github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp/releases

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1The agent 'can't find' an obvious button.⌄ The snapshot is stale. Have the agent call browser_snapshot again after every navigation or form submit — refs from the previous snapshot are dead. If it still cannot find the element, the button may be inside an iframe or Shadow DOM; expand the snapshot scope. ←PreviousNext→ 2Second Claude Code window fails to launch Chromium.⌄ Persistent profiles are single-writer. Either use --isolated for one of the sessions, or run one shared standalone HTTP server with --port 8931 and point both clients at it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Everything is slow.⌄ Turn off caps you are not using — every unnecessary tool eats context tokens. Drop devtools and testing unless you need them. Consider the Skill/CLI approach if you are running batch jobs. ←PreviousNext→ 4Chromium download fails inside your CI.⌄ Use the Docker image (mcr.microsoft.com/playwright/mcp). It ships with Chromium preinstalled and fixes 90% of network-restricted-CI issues in one command. ←PreviousNext→ 5Your agent still writes coordinate clicks.⌄ You have vision cap enabled. Remove --caps=vision, or add an instruction to CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md that snapshot+ref is the only allowed interaction path. ←PreviousNext→
لا توجد بطاقات بعد — أضف بعضها لبدء المذاكرة. 🃏
Check yourself 0/5

You need shared login with an ongoing human browsing session. Consider a shared-login agent browser like the one covered in Browser agents that inherit your logins — Playwright MCP's extension mode gets close, but the UX around approvals and Spaces is different. You are testing production code paths and want the actual Playwright test runner. Use @playwright/test directly; the MCP is optimized for agentic exploration, not for CI test authoring. The workload is 100% headless scraping of static HTML. A plain fetch + parser is orders of magnitude cheaper. Save the browser for pages that actually need JavaScript execution. You cannot risk any browser state leakage. Use --isolated with a fresh --storage-state snapshot per run. Do not use the extension mode against your daily Chrome.
documents.s: When Playwright MCP is the wrong tool

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متقدّم What you'll learn Understand what actually happens when Claude calls your tool from inside a sandbox — and why your tool still runs on your own machine Enable it correctly with allowed_callers, and know why it is not a security boundary Know the real numbers: what it saves, on which workloads, and where it costs you Avoid the five failure modes that produce 400s and TimeoutErrors in production آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-14. Tool version strings, container timeouts and code-execution pricing move faster than most API surfaces. The mechanism below is stable; re-check the exact identifiers and per-hour price against the official docs before you ship. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

Classic tool use is a conversation. Claude asks for one tool call, you answer, the whole result lands in the context window, Claude reads it and asks for the next one. Twenty lookups means twenty inference passes and twenty raw payloads sitting in context forever. Most of that payload is waste. If you want to know which of twenty employees blew their expense budget, Claude does not need every line item — it needs the handful of names. But in classic tool use, the line items have to pass through the model to get filtered by it. Programmatic tool calling inverts that. Claude writes a Python script, the script calls your tools in a loop, filters the results, and only what the script prints comes back to the model. The raw data never enters the context window at all.

Here is the part almost every summary of this feature gets wrong: your tool does not run inside the sandbox. Anthropic's container has no access to your database. What really happens is that Claude's Python code pauses mid-execution, the API hands the call back to you, and the interpreter resumes once you answer: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Claude writes the script⌄ It runs inside the code-execution container. Your tools appear to that code as async Python functions — one per tool, each taking a single dict of arguments and returning a string. ←PreviousNext→ 2The script calls your tool, and execution freezes⌄ The API returns a normal tool_use block for query_database, exactly as in classic tool use — except it now carries a caller field pointing back at the code-execution run that made the call. ←PreviousNext→ 3You execute the tool, on your own infrastructure⌄ Same as always: run the query, send back a tool_result block. The container ID is REQUIRED on this follow-up request, not optional — the API rejects the request without it, because it needs to find the paused interpreter. ←PreviousNext→ 4The interpreter resumes where it stopped⌄ Your result becomes the return value of that await expression. The loop continues. Claude is not sampled in between — no inference pass, no tokens. ←PreviousNext→ 5Only stdout comes back⌄ When the script finishes, Claude receives a code_execution_tool_result containing stdout, stderr and a return_code. Everything the script fetched but did not print is simply gone. ←PreviousNext→ Because the functions are async, Claude can fan out with asyncio.gather and hit ten tools concurrently — something classic tool use can only approximate with parallel tool blocks. What Claude's generated code actually looks like CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import json rows = json.loads(await query_database({"sql": "<sql>"})) top = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["revenue"], reverse=True)[:5] print(f"Top 5 customers: {top}") Note the json.loads. The tool function returns a string — the literal text of the tool_result you send back. If your tool description does not say "returns a list of rows as JSON objects", Claude has no way to know it can deserialize the thing, and it will handle your data as an opaque blob. The output-format sentence in your tool description stops being documentation and becomes load-bearing code. That is the single highest-leverage line you will write when adopting this feature.

One field on the tool you want called from code, plus the code-execution tool in the request: Enabling programmatic calling on a tool CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ { "name": "query_database", "description": "Execute a SQL query against the sales database. Returns a list of rows as JSON objects.", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "sql": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["sql"] }, "allowed_callers": ["code_execution_20260120"] } allowed_callers takes three shapes: Value Meaning ["direct"] Classic tool use. This is the default when the field is omitted. ["code_execution_20260120"] Claude is guided to call it only from inside code. ["direct", "code_execution_20260120"] Either. The docs advise against this — pick one, so Claude gets an unambiguous signal. Every tool_use block in the response now carries a caller: either {"type": "direct"} or a code-execution caller whose tool_id matches the server_tool_use block that ran the script. That is how you attribute a call to the script that made it.

The docs are unusually blunt about this, and it is worth repeating because it is easy to assume the opposite: allowed_callers controls how the tool is presented to Claude. It is not a hard API-level block. Claude is strongly guided to respect it — but your client must still be prepared to receive a direct tool_use for any tool it defines, and you must not use this field as an authorization mechanism. Authorization belongs in your tool handler, where it always did.
documents.s: It is not a security boundary

documents.t: Anthropic's own reported figures, so you can judge whether the complexity is worth it: On complex research tasks, average usage fell from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens — a 37% reduction. On the GIA benchmarks, accuracy rose from 46.5% to 51.2%; on internal knowledge retrieval, 25.6% to 28.5%. Fewer tokens and better answers, because the model reasons over conclusions instead of drowning in raw payloads. On agentic search benchmarks (BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA), layering programmatic calling on top of basic search tools improved performance by an average of 11% while using 24% fewer input tokens. Latency: orchestrating 20+ tool calls in one code block eliminates 19+ inference passes. The shape of the win is the tell. It pays when you have 3+ dependent calls, a loop, a filter, or a fan-out. It pays nothing — and costs you a container — when Claude needs exactly one tool call and wants to read the whole answer anyway. Watch out Claude Haiku 4.5 accepts the newer tool types but does NOT support programmatic tool calling or the REPL state persistence that depends on it. The newer versions silently behave like code_execution_20250825 there. If you are routing to Haiku for cost, you are not getting this feature — and you will not get an error telling you so.

Programmatic tool calling is billed as code execution, and code execution is billed by container-hour, not by call: 1,550 free hours per month, per organization. Beyond that, $0.05 per hour, per container. Execution time has a minimum of 5 minutes — a two-second script still bills five minutes of container. If you attach files to the request, execution time is billed even if the tool is never invoked, because the files get preloaded onto a container regardless. It is free when the same request also uses web search or web fetch (web_search_20260209 / web_fetch_20260209 or later). Two consequences worth internalizing. First, the 5-minute floor means many short-lived containers is the expensive pattern; reusing one container across a session is the cheap one. Second, this feature is not eligible for Zero Data Retention — if ZDR is a contractual requirement for you, this is a hard stop, not a tuning knob.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1You put text in the reply. 400.⌄ When there are pending programmatic tool calls, your response message must contain ONLY tool_result blocks. Not text plus tool results. Not tool results followed by a polite sentence. Only tool_result blocks. ←PreviousNext→ 2You took too long. TimeoutError.⌄ A pending programmatic tool call times out after roughly four minutes and raises a TimeoutError inside Claude's running code (the docs' example stderr reads 'no response after 270s'). Claude sees it in stderr and usually retries. Put a timeout on your own tool execution so you fail fast rather than hanging the container. ←PreviousNext→ 3Your schema is recursive. 400 'Circular $ref detected'.⌄ An input_schema with a self-referencing $ref cannot be enabled for programmatic calling — even though the exact same schema is accepted for direct calling. Unroll the recursion to a fixed depth and describe deeper nesting in the innermost description, or keep that one tool direct-only. ←PreviousNext→ 4You forced it with tool_choice. 400.⌄ You cannot force programmatic calling of a specific tool. Naming a tool in tool_choice whose allowed_callers lacks 'direct' is an invalid_request_error. Also unsupported: strict: true (structured outputs) and disable_parallel_tool_use: true. ←PreviousNext→ 5The tool came from an MCP connector. It will not work.⌄ Tools provided by an MCP connector cannot be called programmatically. If you want an MCP-backed capability inside the sandbox, you have to expose it as a regular custom tool yourself. ←PreviousNext→

All three code-execution versions are generally available and need no beta header: Version What it adds code_execution_20250825 The baseline. Bash + Python + file ops. Supported on every current model. code_execution_20260120 Adds REPL state persistence and programmatic tool calling. This is the one you need. code_execution_20260521 Identical runtime to 20260120. The only difference is that the tool description tells Claude about the 90-second wall-clock limit per Python cell, so it can budget long-running cells. A cell that blows the limit returns a non-zero return_code with a detection_timeout status. That last row is a nice piece of API design to notice: a version bump whose entire payload is a better prompt for the model. Both strings are interchangeable inside allowed_callers, and responses always tag the caller as code_execution_20260120 regardless of which you declared. The container itself has no internet access — Claude cannot pip install at runtime, so you get the pre-installed library set (pandas, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, statsmodels, and friends) and nothing more. Containers are checkpointed after about five minutes of inactivity, restorable by ID, and expire 30 days after creation.

Reach for programmatic tool calling when the model is being used as a loop and a filter rather than as a reasoner: batch lookups across N entities, early termination once a condition is met, conditional tool selection based on an intermediate result, or crushing a 200 KB log dump down to the ten lines that matter. Reach for the Tool Search Tool instead when your problem is that definitions are eating your context before a single call is made — mark tools defer_loading: true and Claude loads them on demand. The two are complements, not alternatives: tool search finds the right tool, programmatic calling executes it cheaply. If your tool definitions exceed roughly 10K tokens, you probably need both. And if you are hitting this from the other end — an agent whose context is drowning in MCP tool results — start with MCP token cost and Context Engineering, because the cheapest tokens are still the ones you never send. Check yourself 0/5

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متقدّم آخر تحقّق: 2026-06-21. آليات التخزين المؤقت، وشروط الأهلية، وتسعير الرموز المخزّنة مقابل الجديدة تتغير — تحقق من ذلك في وثائق التخزين المؤقت للموجّهات الرسمية. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. إذا كان كثير من طلباتك يتشارك جزءًا كبيرًا غير متغير — موجّه نظام طويل، أو مستند ضخم، أو كتالوج أدوات — فإن التخزين المؤقت للموجّهات يتيح لـ API إعادة استخدام البادئة المعالَجة بدلاً من إعادة قراءتها في كل استدعاء. وهذا يخفض كلًا من التكلفة وزمن الاستجابة على الجزء المخزّن مؤقتًا. What you'll learn النموذج الذهني: نقطة فاصل للتخزين المؤقت بعد بادئة ثابتة، يُعاد استخدامها عبر الاستدعاءات كيفية تعليم نقطة الفاصل في Python وTypeScript باستخدام cache_control الثابت الوحيد الذي يصنع نجاحها أو يكسرها — يجب أن تكون البادئة مطابقة بايتًا ببايت كيفية قراءة حقول الاستخدام للتأكد من أنك تحصل فعلًا على إصابات للمخزن المؤقت أين يؤتي التخزين المؤقت ثماره أكثر، وكيفية إقرانه بالمعالجة الدُّفعية واختيار الحجم المناسب
تضع نقطة فاصل للتخزين المؤقت بعد البادئة الثابتة. في الاستدعاء الأول تُعالَج وتُخزَّن مؤقتًا؛ والاستدعاءات اللاحقة التي تتشارك البادئة نفسها تمامًا تصيب المخزن المؤقت وتدفع مقابلها أقل بكثير.

أضف cache_control إلى آخر كتلة ثابتة — هنا، موجّه نظام كبير. يأتي دور المستخدم بعدها ويتغير بحرية؛ وكل شيء حتى الكتلة المعلَّمة وبما فيها يُخزَّن مؤقتًا. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1حدِّد البادئة الثابتة⌄ اعثر على الجزء الكبير غير المتغير — موجّه نظام طويل، أو مستند ضخم، أو كتالوج أدوات يُعاد استخدامه عبر طلبات كثيرة. ←PreviousNext→ 2أرفِق cache_control بآخر كتلة فيها⌄ علّم آخر كتلة ثابتة بـ cache_control من نوع ephemeral، بحيث تُخزَّن البادئة حتى تلك الكتلة وبما فيها مؤقتًا. ←PreviousNext→ 3دع الجزء المتغير يتبع⌄ ضع دور المستخدم بعد الكتلة المعلَّمة — فهو يتغير بحرية في كل استدعاء ويُحاسَب عليه بالسعر الكامل. ←PreviousNext→ 4أكِّد الإصابة⌄ اقرأ cache_read_input_tokens من حقل usage في الاستجابة. القيمة الأكبر من الصفر تعني أنك حصلت على إصابة للمخزن المؤقت. ←PreviousNext→ Python TypeScript import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() message = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=1024, system=[ { "type": "text", "text": LARGE_STABLE_PROMPT, # long, unchanging — the cached prefix "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}, } ], messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the key points."}], # varies per call ) print(message.usage.cache_read_input_tokens) # > 0 means you got a hit import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk"; const client = new Anthropic(); const message = await client.messages.create({ model: "claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens: 1024, system: [ { type: "text", text: LARGE_STABLE_PROMPT, // long, unchanging — the cached prefix cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" }, }, ], messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Summarize the key points." }], // varies per call }); console.log(message.usage.cache_read_input_tokens); // > 0 means you got a hit يدفع الاستدعاء الأول علاوة كتابة صغيرة لملء المخزن المؤقت؛ وكل استدعاء لاحق بالبادئة نفسها يقرأها مرة أخرى بجزء بسيط من سعر الإدخال. يجب أن تكون البادئة طويلة بما يكفي لتكون مؤهلة — بضعة آلاف من الرموز، وذلك يعتمد على النموذج — وإلا فلن تُخزَّن مؤقتًا بصمت.

التخزين المؤقت دقيق على مستوى البادئة تتطلب إصابة المخزن المؤقت أن تكون البادئة المخزّنة مطابقة بايتًا ببايت. أكثر الأخطاء شيوعًا: مُبطِل صامت قرب أعلى الموجّه — طابع زمني، أو اسم مستخدم متغير، أو قائمة أدوات أُعيد ترتيبها — يغيّر البادئة ويُسقط معدل إصاباتك إلى صفر بهدوء. ضع كل ما هو ثابت أولًا، وكل ما هو متغير أخيرًا، وأبقِ البادئة ثابتة فعلًا.
documents.s: الثابت الذي يصنع نجاحها أو يكسرها

documents.t: لا تفترض — اقرأها من حقل usage في الاستجابة: cache_creation_input_tokens — الرموز المكتوبة إلى المخزن المؤقت في هذا الاستدعاء (الطلب الأول). cache_read_input_tokens — الرموز المخدومة من المخزن المؤقت (التوفير). input_tokens — الباقي غير المخزّن، ويُحاسَب عليه بالسعر الكامل. إذا بقي cache_read_input_tokens عند الصفر عبر طلبات متكررة يُفترض أن تتشارك بادئة، فإن مُبطِلًا صامتًا يعمل — قارن بايتات الموجّه المُصاغ بين استدعاءين للعثور عليه.

موجّهات النظام الطويلة المُعاد استخدامها عبر المستخدمين. RAG / الإجابة على الأسئلة من المستندات حيث يُستعلَم عن النص المصدري نفسه مرارًا. الوكلاء الذين لديهم كتالوج أدوات وتعليمات ثابتة عبر أدوار كثيرة. اقرن التخزين المؤقت مع المعالجة الدُّفعية لأحمال العمل غير المتصلة، ومع اختيار الحجم المناسب للنموذج (اختيار نموذج) لأكبر توفير مجمّع — انظر التكلفة وزمن الاستجابة. اختبر نفسك 0/3 Key takeaways ضع نقطة فاصل للتخزين المؤقت بعد البادئة الثابتة؛ الاستدعاء الأول يكتبها، والاستدعاءات اللاحقة تقرأها بثمن زهيد. تحتاج إصابة المخزن المؤقت إلى بادئة مطابقة بايتًا ببايت — أبقِ المحتوى الثابت أولًا والمحتوى المتغير أخيرًا. المُبطِلات الصامتة قرب أعلى الموجّه (الطوابع الزمنية، الأسماء، الأدوات المُعاد ترتيبها) تُسقط معدل الإصابات إلى صفر بهدوء. تحقق عبر الاستخدام: cache_read_input_tokens أكبر من الصفر يعني إصابة؛ والصفر عبر الطلبات المتكررة يعني أن هناك مُبطِلًا يعمل. يؤتي التخزين المؤقت ثماره أكثر مع موجّهات النظام المُعاد استخدامها، وRAG، والوكلاء؛ اقرنه بالمعالجة الدُّفعية واختيار الحجم المناسب للنموذج.
