documents.t: خمسة أعلام تشكّل موجّه النظام. أربعة منها تحدد نصه؛ والخامس يقرر هل تحتفظ المحادثة بالنص الذي بدأت به. العلم ما يفعله --system-prompt يستبدل الموجّه الافتراضي كاملًا بنصك --system-prompt-file يستبدله بمحتوى ملف --append-system-prompt يُلحق نصك بالموجّه الافتراضي --append-system-prompt-file يُلحق محتوى ملف بالموجّه الافتراضي --system-prompt-snapshot off يعيد بناء الموجّه عند كل طلب؛ on (الافتراضي) يعيد استخدام الموجّه المسجَّل الاختيار بين الإلحاق والاستبدال اختيار هوية. الإلحاق يُبقي إرشادات الأدوات الافتراضية في Claude Code وتعليمات السلامة وأعراف البرمجة، ويضع قواعدك فوقها — وهو مناسب لتعليمات كل تشغيل أو تنسيق المخرجات أو سياق المشروع. أما الاستبدال فيُسقط كل ذلك، بما فيه إرشادات الأدوات، ولذلك لا يصلح إلا حين لا تكون الواجهة مساعد برمجة حقًا: وكيل غير برمجي في خط معالجة لا يراقبه أحد. وإن استبدلت، فأنت المسؤول عن كل ما تظل المهمة تحتاجه. يمكنك الجمع بينهما. تمرير علم إلحاق مع علم استبدال يستبدل الافتراضي ثم يُلحق نصك. ومنذ v2.1.283 يمكنك أيضًا تمرير علم مع صيغته الملفية — --append-system-prompt و--append-system-prompt-file — فيستخدم Claude Code كليهما، ويأتي محتوى الملف أولًا أيًّا كان الترتيب الذي كتبتهما به. الفخ: المحادثة المستأنفة تعيد استخدام الموجّه الذي وُلدت به يبني Claude Code موجّه النظام مرة واحدة، عند أول طلب في المحادثة، ويسجّله في الجلسة. وإلى أن تُضغط المحادثة، يستخدم كل طلب لاحق ذلك الموجّه المسجَّل — بما في ذلك بعد --resume أو --continue. فتعدّل نص --append-system-prompt وتعيد تشغيل claude --continue ولا يتغير شيء. العلم ليس معطّلًا؛ المحادثة ما زالت تستخدم التسجيل. يسري النص الجديد حين تُضغط المحادثة، أو في محادثة جديدة كليًا. لتكرار صياغة النص عبر تشغيلات --continue، مرّر --system-prompt-snapshot off فيُعاد بناء الموجّه عند كل طلب. يتطلب الإصدار v2.1.257 أو أحدث. وثمة حيلة أخرى تستحق المعرفة في موجّه استبدال يمزج تعليمات ثابتة بسياق خاص بكل تشغيل. ضع بينهما سطرًا لا يحتوي إلا على __SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY__: يقسم Claude Code عند أول سطر كهذا ويزيله، فيبقى الجزء العلوي مخزّنًا مؤقتًا بينما يتغير الجزء السفلي. يتطلب الإصدار v2.1.275 أو أحدث. وسبب أهمية ذلك لفاتورتك هو موضوع التخزين المؤقت للموجّهات. وبالنسبة لأحمال العمل المبرمجة متعددة المستخدمين، ينقل --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections السياق الخاص بكل مستخدم، مثل موقع الذاكرة التلقائية، من موجّه النظام إلى أول رسالة مستخدم — فتتشارك المهمة نفسها على أجهزة مختلفة بادئة مخزّنة واحدة. ولا ينطبق إلا على الموجّه الافتراضي، ويُتجاهل حين تضبط --system-prompt أو --system-prompt-file.
documents.s: عائلة موجّه النظام، والفخ الكامن فيها

documents.t: يلجأ الناس إليها بالتبادل ثم يتساءلون لماذا لم يتحرك العَرَض. إنها تحل ثلاث مشكلات مختلفة. --bare --safe-mode --restricted المشكلة التي يحلها البدء بطيء جدًا لاستدعاء مبرمج إعداداتي معطوبة ولا أعرف أي جزء يجب ألا تلمس حزمة التقييم هذا الجهاز المشترك CLAUDE.md والمهارات والأوامر والوكلاء الفرعيون والإضافات وMCP والذاكرة التلقائية لا تُكتشف لا تُحمَّل لا يُحمَّل إلا الإعدادات المُدارة و--settings الأدوات المضمّنة Bash وقراءة الملفات وتحرير الملفات تعمل بشكل طبيعي تُزال الأدوات التي تشغّل الأوامر/الشيفرة وWebFetch ما لم تُسمَّ واحدة واحدة في --tools الوصول إلى الملفات عادي عادي محصور في مجلدات العمل bypassPermissions مسموح مسموح مرفوض السياسة المُدارة تنطبق ما تزال تنطبق، بما في ذلك خطافات السياسة وشريط الحالة تنطبق أثر جانبي يضبط CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE يضبط CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE يرفض إنشاء جلسات سحابية اقرأ الجدول كتدرّج في النية: --bare من أجل السرعة، و--safe-mode من أجل التشخيص، و--restricted من أجل الاحتواء. وتفصيل مفيد: المهارات في مجلد تمرره بـ--add-dir تُحمَّل رغم --bare، وهكذا تُبقي قدرة واحدة بعينها في تشغيل مجرَّد من كل شيء سواها. --safe-mode هو أول ما تلجأ إليه حين يسوء شيء ولا تعرف هل المشكلة في Claude Code أم في إعداداتك — بما في ذلك حين تحاول معرفة هل تخصيص ما هو ما يطلق الرجوع التلقائي بين النماذج. اقرنه بـclaude doctor الذي يطبع تشخيصات للتثبيت والإعدادات للقراءة فقط دون بدء أي جلسة. (أمر /doctor داخل الجلسة شيء مختلف: فهو يستطيع أيضًا تطبيق إصلاحات.) مزيد من تصحيح الأخطاء بدءًا من العَرَض في استكشاف أخطاء Claude Code. يتطلب --restricted الإصدار v2.1.248 أو أحدث.
documents.s: ثلاثة أعلام تُوقف أشياء، وليست متماثلة

documents.t: متى بدأت جلسات بـ--bg صارت الطرفية مستوى تحكم. لدورة الحياة كاملةً أمر، ولا شيء منها يتطلب فتح الواجهة التفاعلية. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1اعرف ما الذي يعمل — claude agents⌄ يفتح عرض الوكلاء لمراقبة الجلسات الخلفية المتوازية وتوزيعها. وللبرمجة النصية يطبع `--json` الجلسات النشطة كمصفوفة JSON، ويضيف `--json --all` الجلسات المكتملة. ويحصر `--cwd <path>` النتائج بالجلسات التي بدأت تحت ذلك المجلد. فتح العرض نفسه يحتاج طرفية تفاعلية؛ أما صيغة JSON فلا. ←PreviousNext→ 2انظر داخل واحدة — claude logs⌄ `claude logs <id|name>` يطبع المخرجات الأخيرة لجلسة خلفية. ومنذ v2.1.290 يمكنك تمرير جزء من اسم جلسة تعمل بدلًا من معرّفها — فغالبًا يكفي `claude logs auth`. ←PreviousNext→ 3تولَّ زمامها — claude attach⌄ `claude attach <id|name>` يجلب جلسة خلفية إلى هذه الطرفية. ومطابقة الاسم الجزئي تتطلب كذلك v2.1.290 أو أحدث. ←PreviousNext→ 4أعد تشغيلها — claude respawn⌄ `claude respawn <id>` يعيد تشغيل جلسة، عاملة أو متوقفة، مع بقاء محادثتها سليمة. و`--all` يعيد تشغيل كل الجلسات العاملة — وهو الخطوة المناسبة بعد ترقية الملف التنفيذي لـ Claude Code. ←PreviousNext→ 5أوقف ونظّف — claude stop وclaude rm⌄ `claude stop <id>` (وكذلك `claude kill`) يوقف جلسة. و`claude rm <id>` يزيلها من القائمة؛ ويبقى السجل على جهازك ويمكن الوصول إليه بـ`claude --resume`. وإن رُفضت الإزالة بسبب شجرة عمل الجلسة، فإن الرفض يطبع العلم الدقيق الذي ينبغي تمريره تاليًا — `--discard-unpushed` (v2.1.260+) أو `--force-remove-worktree` (v2.1.268+). ←PreviousNext→ 6حين يتعطل كل شيء — claude daemon⌄ تستضيف الجلسات الخلفية عملية مشرِف. يطبع `claude daemon status` حالتها وإصدارها ومجلد المقبس وعدد العاملين، ويخرج بالرمز 1 إن لم تكن تعمل. ويتتبع `claude daemon logs` الملف `~/.claude/daemon.log`. ويعيد `claude daemon stop --any --keep-workers` تشغيل المشرِف مع إبقاء الجلسات حية ليعيد المشرِف التالي الاتصال بها. ←PreviousNext→ أما المقابل لهذا من داخل الجلسة — كيف يُنقل العمل إلى الخلفية، وما الذي ينتقل معه — ففي المهام الخلفية و/loop والجدولة.

ستة التباسات يحسن استباقها --tools يقيّد الأدوات المضمّنة الموجودة. --allowedTools يحدد أي الاستدعاءات تتخطى طلب الإذن. --disallowedTools يرفض الاستدعاءات. هذه ثلاث مهام مختلفة، وتمرير الخطأ منها أشيع سبب لـ«لماذا ما زال يسألني». --tools لا يؤثر في أدوات MCP إطلاقًا. ولإزالتها أيضًا أضف --disallowedTools "mcp__*". الاسم المجرد في --disallowedTools يزيل الأداة من سياق Claude؛ أما القاعدة المحددة النطاق مثل Bash(rm *) فتُبقي الأداة متاحة وترفض الاستدعاءات المطابقة فقط. --dangerously-skip-permissions يبدأ في bypassPermissions. أما --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions فيضيف ذلك الوضع إلى دورة Shift+Tab فقط، فتبدأ في وضع الخطة وتبدّل لاحقًا. والثاني هو ما أردته فعلًا في الغالب. --add-dir يمنح الوصول إلى الملفات، لكن Claude Code لا يكتشف معظم إعدادات .claude/ من تلك المجلدات. إضافة مجلد ليست مثل تبنّي إعداداته. --desktop لا يقبل موجّهًا ولا أعلامًا أخرى سوى --verbose وأعلام --debug، لأن تطبيق سطح المكتب يبدأ الجلسة بنفسه. يتطلب الإصدار v2.1.285 أو أحدث. تفصيل صغير يريح: إن أخطأت في كتابة أمر فرعي اقترح Claude Code أقرب مطابقة وخرج دون بدء جلسة — فـclaude udpate يطبع Did you mean claude update? بدلًا من فتح محادثة لم ترد بدءها.
documents.s: أزواج الأعلام التي يخطئ الناس فيها

documents.t: Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways اختر نوع الجلسة أولًا — فالعلم الذي يحدده يقيّد كل علم آخر يمكنك تمريره. يحتاج التشغيل بلا إشراف إلى خمسة أعلام لا علمًا واحدًا: -p و--permission-prompts none و--max-turns و--max-budget-usd وتنسيق مخرجات منظَّم. عامل --max-budget-usd كقاطع دائرة لتشغيل واحد، لا كسقف للفاتورة. فهو تقدير من جهة العميل والمجاميع المستأنفة تفلت منه. تسجّل المحادثات موجّه نظامها عند أول طلب. فإن بدا تعديل الموجّه متجاهَلًا فهذا هو السبب — استخدم --system-prompt-snapshot off أثناء التكرار. --bare للسرعة، و--safe-mode للتشخيص، و--restricted للاحتواء. واختيار الخطأ منها يضيّع عصرًا كاملًا. --help ناقص بحكم التصميم. ومرجع CLI هو مصدر الحقيقة، وحدود الإصدارات مهمة — تحقق من claude -v قبل أن تلوم علمًا.

الوضع بلا واجهة وAgent SDK — ماذا تبني حين لا يكفي استدعاء -p لمرة واحدة settings.json: نظام الإعدادات — الموطن الدائم للأعلام التي تظل تعيد كتابتها استكشاف أخطاء Claude Code — تصحيح أخطاء ينطلق من العَرَض، بدءًا من --safe-mode شارك هذه الصفحة X LinkedIn Reddit Hacker News نسخ الرابط

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط What you'll learn Build the right mental model: five surfaces, one saved environment, a fresh throwaway VM per session Learn the table that trips up everyone: what carries over from your machine into a cloud session, and the five things that silently do not Pick a network access level — None, Trusted, Full, Custom — and know the four kinds of traffic that bypass your allowlist anyway Give a session an API key it can use but never read, with a network secret Choose correctly between a setup script and a SessionStart hook, and stay under the ~5-minute rule that decides whether your environment gets cached Plan around the real resource and time ceilings: 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 30 GB, a 2-minute default command timeout, and a VM that pauses when you walk away Run the full round trip: claude --cloud to send work out, claude -p --cloud to steer it, claude --teleport to pull it back آخر تحقّق: 2026-10-26. Verified against the official Configure cloud environments and Use Claude Code in the cloud pages. Cloud sessions are available on Pro, Max, and Team plans, and to Enterprise users with premium seats or Chat + Claude Code seats; if your organization uses custom roles, you also need a role carrying the cloud sessions permission. Resource ceilings are described by Anthropic as approximate and may change. Pre-installed tool versions move continuously — treat the toolchain table here as a shape, and confirm versions in a live session. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. A cloud session is a Claude Code session that runs on someone else's machine instead of yours — Anthropic's by default, or your own runners if your organization routes it there. You close the laptop; the work keeps going. There's no separate charge for the VM: a cloud session draws on the same plan usage limits as everything else you do with Claude. That part is easy to understand. The part that costs people an afternoon is subtler: a cloud session is not your laptop with a different hostname. It's a fresh Ubuntu box with your committed repository on it and nothing else of yours. Half the configuration you've spent months tuning lives in ~/.claude/ on your machine and does not make the trip. This page is mostly about that boundary.
documents.s: Cloud Sessions: the VM Claude Code runs in when it isn't your laptop

documents.t: You save a cloud environment — a named bundle of network policy, environment variables, and a setup script. Every surface that can start a cloud session picks one of your environments. When a session starts, Anthropic provisions an isolated VM (Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64, regardless of what you run locally), clones your repo from GitHub, runs your setup script, snapshots the filesystem so the next session skips that step, and launches Claude Code. All outbound traffic leaves through a proxy that enforces your access level. GitHub traffic takes a separate path where your real credential never enters the VM. When you stop typing, the VM pauses with its files intact; leave it long enough and it gets reclaimed, and reopening the session builds a new one.

The same saved environments apply wherever you start a cloud session: your browser at claude.ai/code, the Desktop app, the Claude mobile app, your terminal via claude --cloud, and cloud scheduled tasks. Configure the environment once and every surface inherits it. Two neighbors are not cloud sessions, and conflating them causes real confusion: Remote Control connects the web and mobile interfaces to a session running on your own machine. It uses your files and your network — there's no cloud environment involved. --remote-control is unrelated to --cloud, despite the similar names. --cloud creates a session on Anthropic's infrastructure; --remote-control exposes a local session to your phone. If you don't have an environment yet, onboarding creates one called Default: Trusted network access, no variables, no setup script. On Team and Enterprise, web onboarding may instead show you a create-your-first-environment form unless an Owner has enabled Quick setup; keeping the form's defaults produces the same thing.

This is the section to read twice. A cloud session starts from a fresh clone of your repository. The rule that explains every row below: if it's committed, it's there; if it only exists on your machine, it isn't. Your thing In a cloud session? Why Repo CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/ ✅ Yes Part of the clone Repo .claude/skills/, .claude/agents/, .claude/commands/ ✅ Yes Part of the clone Repo .claude/settings.json hooks and permission rules ✅ In a single-repository session Part of the clone Repo .mcp.json MCP servers ✅ In a single-repository session Found from the session's working directory Organization server-managed settings ✅ Yes (not in Claude Tag sessions) Fetched from Anthropic when the session starts Skills you enabled on claude.ai ✅ Yes Loaded from your account, not the repo Your user ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ❌ No Lives on your machine, not in the repo Your user ~/.claude/skills/, agents/, commands/ ❌ No Same reason. Commit them to the repo's .claude/ instead Plugins and marketplaces ❌ No A cloud session installs neither enabledPlugins nor the marketplaces under extraKnownMarketplaces — from the repo or from your user settings MCP servers added at local or user scope ❌ No Those write ~/.claude.json. Re-add with claude mcp add --scope project and commit the resulting .mcp.json MDM / managed settings files on your device ❌ No The session runs on an Anthropic-managed VM Transport variables like NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS or mTLS client certs in a repo env block ❌ Ignored The hosting environment owns the session's API connection; each ignored key is noted in the session's debug log Interactive auth like AWS SSO ❌ No Requires a browser login that can't run in a cloud session Two traps hide in that table: The plugin gap is the most expensive one. A repository that turns on a plugin in .claude/settings.json gets that plugin locally and nothing in the cloud. If a workflow depends on plugin-provided skills or commands, either commit the equivalents into .claude/ or accept that cloud sessions behave differently. See plugins and marketplaces for what lives where. "Single-repository session" is load-bearing. In an Anthropic-hosted environment, a session attached to several repositories loads hooks and permission rules from none of them, and a cloud thread inside a project loads only the repository root's CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, and non-path-specific .claude/rules/. If your setup depends on a SessionStart hook, a multi-repo session won't run it — provision with a setup script instead.
documents.s: What carries over from your machine — and what doesn't

documents.t: You don't have to push personal style rules into a shared repo. A setup script on one of your own environments can write the user-level memory file directly: Setup script: personal preferences without touching the repo CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ #!/bin/bash mkdir -p ~/.claude cat > ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md <<'EOF' Use conventional commit messages. Prefer small, reviewable diffs over one large change. EOF Claude Code loads that as user instructions. Confirm it worked by running /context in your next cloud session and looking for /root/.claude/CLAUDE.md under Memory files. Don't do this on a shared environment — it would apply to everyone in the organization.
documents.s: Getting your personal preferences in anyway

documents.t: Each environment carries exactly one network access level, which governs outbound connections from the session's network. Level What sessions can reach None Nothing through the session's network Trusted (default) An Anthropic-maintained allowlist: package registries, GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket, container registries, major cloud SDK endpoints Full Any domain Custom Your own list, one domain per line; a leading *. matches every subdomain. A checkbox decides whether the Trusted defaults are included too Changing the level on an Anthropic-hosted environment takes effect in existing sessions within about a minute. You don't need to start a new one. Now the part that matters for threat modeling. Four kinds of traffic take a path that never touches your allowlist, whatever level you pick — including None: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1GitHub, through its own proxy⌄ All GitHub operations in Anthropic-hosted environments route through a dedicated proxy that keeps your real credential outside the VM. Independent of the access level. ←PreviousNext→ 2MCP connectors you enable⌄ Connector traffic travels through Anthropic's servers rather than the session's network, so you never add a connector's host to Allowed domains. The flip side: an allowlist does not constrain what an enabled connector can reach. Turn off connectors you don't need. ←PreviousNext→ 3Hosts listed on your network secrets⌄ Sessions can reach a secret's hosts even when the access level otherwise wouldn't allow them. Adding a secret widens reachability as well as attaching a credential. ←PreviousNext→ 4api.anthropic.com⌄ Claude Code's own inference requests go out even at None. Anthropic says this plainly in its isolation notes: with network access disabled, Claude Code can still talk to the Anthropic API, which may allow data to exit the VM. None is not an air gap. ←PreviousNext→ If you were planning to use None as a containment boundary for untrusted code, read that fourth item again, then read hardening autonomous runs. Network level is a blast-radius reducer, not a sandbox guarantee. There is also no organization-level allowlist an admin can push onto every member's environment, and no server-managed setting that adds domains to one. The way to standardize a list across a team is an organization-shared environment created by an Owner, with Custom access and that list.
documents.s: Network access: four levels, and the four things that ignore them

documents.t: Worth its own heading because it breaks muscle memory. The GitHub proxy rejects GraphQL entirely with a 403, which means the gh subcommands built on GraphQL fail inside cloud sessions: gh pr ... and gh issue ... → 403, naming the REST fallback A GH_TOKEN of your own doesn't help — the restriction applies to every request through the proxy regardless of credentials APIs that exist only in GraphQL, such as Projects v2, are unreachable through the proxy The workaround is REST, which the built-in GitHub tools and gh api both speak: REST instead of the GraphQL-backed gh subcommands CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls --jq '.[] | "\(.number) \(.title)"' gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/issues/42/comments -f body="rerunning the flaky suite" The proxy enforces three more rules worth knowing: it rejects branch deletions and pushes of anything that isn't a branch (a tag, for instance); it serves API requests only for repositories attached to the session, returning a 403 containing is not enabled for this session otherwise — including for source archives fetched from codeload.github.com, even public ones; and it substitutes your real credential server-side, so when the proxy handles auth, GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN read as the literal placeholder proxy-injected inside the VM. gh works fine with that placeholder. A script of yours that reads GITHUB_TOKEN directly and expects a usable token does not. Check which GitHub auth case your session is in CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ echo $GH_TOKEN
documents.s: The GitHub proxy's sharp edge: no GraphQL

documents.t: Environment variables are the wrong place for credentials, and Anthropic's own UI says so: anyone who can use the environment can read its variables. A network secret is the right place. You store an API key on the environment, list the hosts it applies to, and Anthropic's agent proxy attaches it to matching requests after they leave the VM. The key itself never enters the session, doesn't appear in env, and isn't in any file. You can't read it back after saving either — to change a secret's value or hosts, delete it and add it again. Set-up notes that save a round trip: Plans: Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise. On Pro, Max, and Team you can add secrets to your own environments whatever your role; on Enterprise you need an organization admin role, otherwise ask an Owner to put the secret on a shared environment and run your sessions there. On Team without that role, the Add secret form is a shorter one-host variant with no *. wildcard. Default secret type is Bearer: the Authorization header with a Bearer prefix. For a header like X-Api-Key that carries the bare value, change the header name and clear the prefix. Hard blockers: self-hosted environments don't have network secrets at all, the API must accept connections from the internet (requests leave from Anthropic's network, not yours), and organizations using customer-managed encryption keys can't save secrets. Some requests never get a secret you add, by design: GitHub (the GitHub proxy already authenticates it), api.anthropic.com and the public package registries (registry.npmjs.org, jsr.io, npm.jsr.io, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org, index.crates.io, proxy.golang.org), anything your setup script does — it runs before Claude Code connects to the agent proxy — and Claude Code's own telemetry export. One quiet failure mode: if two secrets have hosts that overlap without matching exactly, neither gets a warning marker and the proxy sends only one of them. Keep host lists disjoint.
documents.s: Network secrets: a key the session uses but can't read

documents.t: Both run before you get useful work out of a session, and people reach for the wrong one constantly. The dividing line is simple: Setup script → provision the VM: toolchains and CLI tools that aren't pre-installed. Cloud only. SessionStart hook → project setup that should happen everywhere, cloud and local, like npm install. Setup script SessionStart hook Configured in The environment dialog (plus the admin Cloud environments page for shared environments) A settings file, typically the repo's .claude/settings.json When it runs Before Claude Code launches — skipped entirely when a cached environment exists After Claude Code launches, on every session including resumed ones Where it runs Cloud sessions only Local and cloud Gets cached Yes, if it finishes in roughly five minutes No — it pays its cost on every start and resume A setup script is Bash, runs as root on Ubuntu 24.04, and has four constraints to write around: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Exit zero or the session doesn't start⌄ A non-zero exit fails the session, not just the step. Append || true to anything non-critical so one flaky registry doesn't block your work. ←PreviousNext→ 2Finish in roughly five minutes, or lose caching⌄ Longer than that and Anthropic doesn't snapshot the environment — every session then pays full setup cost. Parallelize independent installs with & and wait; push a single huge download into a background SessionStart hook instead. ←PreviousNext→ 3Installs need network⌄ Package installs have to reach registries. Trusted covers npm, PyPI, RubyGems, and crates.io. At None, every install in your script fails. ←PreviousNext→ 4The environment's variables are not set yet⌄ The script runs before the session applies the environment's variables. Anything the script itself needs, set inside the script. ←PreviousNext→ Setup script: install a tool that isn't pre-installed CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ #!/bin/bash apt update && apt install -y shellcheck || true

When setup completes inside the ~5-minute budget, Anthropic snapshots the filesystem and starts later sessions from it, skipping the script. That's why a slow setup script is worth optimizing once: pulled Docker images, installed packages, and written files all survive. What the snapshot keeps and loses follows from it being a filesystem snapshot: ✅ Kept: packages you installed, Docker images you pulled, files you wrote ❌ Lost: anything that was merely running. A database the script started, a docker compose up stack, a dev server — all gone. Start those per session, by asking Claude or from a SessionStart hook. The cache rebuilds when you change the setup script or the allowed hosts, and when it expires after roughly seven days. It does not rebuild when a paused VM is restored — so editing your setup script doesn't reach a session that's merely idle. To apply a change immediately, start a new session.
documents.s: Environment caching, and when the cache is wrong

documents.t: Since hooks run in both places, scope them with the variable the VM sets. CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE is true in a cloud session and never true locally: scripts/install_pkgs.sh — cloud-only, and idempotent CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ #!/bin/bash if [ "$CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE" != "true" ]; then exit 0 fi cd "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" || exit 1 hashes=node_modules/.install_pkgs.sha256 if ! sha256sum --check --status "$hashes" 2>/dev/null; then # Delete the old hashes first, so a failed install runs again next time rm -f "$hashes" if npm install; then sha256sum scripts/install_pkgs.sh package.json package-lock.json > "$hashes" || rm -f "$hashes" fi fi exit 0 The hash check is the important half: a SessionStart hook runs on every start and every resume, so an unconditional npm install is latency you pay forever. If your install reads other inputs — a workspace package.json, an .npmrc, a postinstall script's own files — add them to the sha256sum line, or you'll keep stale packages after one of them changes.
documents.s: Installing dependencies only in the cloud

documents.t: Each Anthropic-hosted session gets a fresh VM with common toolchains pre-installed: Python with pip/poetry/uv/pytest/ruff/mypy/black; Node 20, 21, and 22 with npm/yarn/pnpm/bun; Ruby, PHP with Composer, OpenJDK with Maven and Gradle, Go, Rust, GCC/Clang/cmake/ninja; Docker and Compose; PostgreSQL and Redis; and the usual git, gh, jq, yq, ripgrep, tmux. Four practical notes on that: It's x86_64 Linux, not your Mac. When a dependency ships precompiled binaries — native Ruby gems, prebuilt Python wheels — you want the x86_64 Linux build. You don't get a shell. Claude runs every command for you, so phrase VM work as requests in your prompt. To see versions, ask Claude to run check-tools (a shell command on the VM, not a slash command); for tools it doesn't report, ask for psql --version and friends. Databases are installed but not running. Ask Claude to run service postgresql start or service redis-server start. Bun is installed but has known proxy-compatibility problems for package fetching, because all outbound traffic goes through the security proxy. Toolchains outside the list — the .NET SDK, for example — need a setup script, even though their registries are on the Trusted allowlist. Resource ceilings (approximate, and subject to change): 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM, 30 GB disk. A memory-hungry build or test suite can get stopped by the VM. Beyond that, the answers are Remote Control onto your own hardware, or a self-hosted environment on compute your organization operates. Time ceilings are the ones that surprise people mid-task: Limit Default How to change it Foreground command 2 minutes (Claude can request up to 10) BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS / BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS in the environment's variables, in milliseconds Command moved to background on timeout Up to 30 more minutes Raising BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS above 1800000 lengthens this too SessionStart command hook Cancelled after 600 seconds Set timeout (seconds) on the hook entry, or run it with async: true Setup script Not cached beyond roughly 5 minutes Parallelize, or move the long part to a background hook Idle session VM pauses after a few minutes, files saved Nothing to configure — your next message restores it A timed-out command isn't killed, by the way: Claude Code moves it to the background instead, unless it starts with sleep.
documents.s: What's in the box, and where the ceilings are

documents.t: After a few minutes of inactivity the VM pauses with its files saved, and your next message restores the same VM. Two consequences follow: Environment variables are re-read at creation and at every Claude Code start in the VM — which means on idle restore and on rebuild. So after you edit a variable, a running session keeps the old value until its VM next restores. To use a new value right away, ask Claude to set it inline (LOG_LEVEL=trace npm test) or start a new session. A paused VM can later be reclaimed. Reopening the session then provisions a fresh VM: your conversation history is restored, but background work isn't. Shell commands that were still running, subagents that were mid-flight, and session-scoped scheduled tasks or a waiting /loop do not carry over. Claude Code does tell Claude which commands and subagents stopped — and which subagents can be resumed rather than restarted — so "continue what got cut off" is a reasonable next prompt. Two environment variables behave specially. OTEL_* values are reserved for Claude Code's own telemetry export and are not passed to the commands Claude runs. And cloud sessions set CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE themselves, so compaction fires partway through the auto-compact window rather than when it fills — setting that key yourself has no effect. If you want to move the window, set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW instead. (Context management covers the window itself.)
documents.s: When the VM comes back — or doesn't

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Send work out with claude --cloud⌄ Creates a new cloud session for your current repository. The VM clones your current directory's GitHub remote at your current branch — not your local checkout. Push first. ←PreviousNext→ 2Steer it from anywhere with claude -p --cloud <session-id>⌄ Posts one message into a running session and exits. It sends no local state and authenticates with your account, so it works from any machine you're logged into — including a CI script. ←PreviousNext→ 3Pull it back with claude --teleport⌄ Fetches the session's branch, checks it out, and loads the full conversation into your terminal. From the CLI this handoff is one-way: you can pull a cloud session down, but you can't push an existing terminal session up. ←PreviousNext→ Start a cloud session from your terminal CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ claude --cloud "Fix the authentication bug in src/auth/login.ts" Each --cloud invocation is its own independent session, which makes fan-out trivial — and makes rate limits the thing to watch, since parallel sessions consume them proportionately: Fan out three independent tasks CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ claude --cloud "Fix the flaky test in auth.spec.ts" claude --cloud "Update the API documentation" claude --cloud "Refactor the logger to use structured output" The highest-leverage pattern here is plan locally, execute in the cloud. Thinking is cheap and interactive on your machine; execution is what you want to offload: Plan locally, then hand the plan to a cloud session CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ claude --permission-mode plan # collaborate on the approach, save the plan to the repo, commit, push claude --cloud "Execute the migration plan in docs/migration-plan.md" Steer a running session from any logged-in machine CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ claude -p "add a test for the empty-list case" --cloud <session-id> # machine-readable result: {ok, session_id, url} claude -p "status?" --cloud <session-id> --output-format json Pull a cloud session into your terminal CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ claude --teleport # interactive picker claude --teleport <session-id> # straight to one session Inside a running CLI session, /teleport (or /tp) opens the same picker without a restart; /tasks lists background sessions and t teleports into the selected one. Teleport checks four things before it resumes: clean git state (it offers to stash), the same repository (a fork won't do), the session's branch pushed to the remote, and the same claude.ai account. It also never waits for input — if git or ssh would prompt for a passphrase or an unknown-host confirmation, the fetch fails, so load your key into ssh-agent and run one manual git fetch first. A detail worth internalizing: the teleported session is a copy. Work you do locally afterward stays local and does not appear back in the cloud session on claude.ai or your phone. To keep steering from your phone after teleporting, start /remote-control in the local session. And --teleport is not --resume: --resume reopens a conversation from this machine's local history and doesn't list cloud sessions at all.
documents.s: The round trip: send it out, steer it, pull it back

documents.t: Every cloud session has a transcript URL, and the session can read its own ID from CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID. Commits Claude creates in a cloud session already carry a Claude-Session: git trailer and PR bodies include the link (set attribution.sessionUrl to false to suppress both). For anything else — a generated report, a Slack post — build the URL yourself. Note the prefix swap, which is the one thing people get wrong: Turn the session ID into a transcript URL CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ echo "https://claude.ai/code/${CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID/#cse_/session_}"
documents.s: Linking output back to the session

documents.t: --cloud clones your remote, not your working tree. The VM checks out your current branch from GitHub. Local commits you haven't pushed and uncommitted changes aren't there. If you see a line starting with Branch <name> is not on GitHub, the session still starts — just from a pushed ancestor or the default branch instead. Push and start again. No remote, or no GitHub App? Claude Code uploads your repo instead. From a repository with no git remote, or a github.com repository the Claude GitHub App isn't installed on, Claude Code bundles the local repository and uploads it — history across branches plus uncommitted changes to tracked files. Force it with CCR_FORCE_BUNDLE=1. Limits: a git repo with at least one commit, under 100 MB, and untracked files are excluded (so git add anything the session needs to see). Credential-file protection is platform-dependent. On macOS, Linux, and WSL, the bundle upload leaves out uncommitted changes to credential-shaped files — .env, Terraform *.tfvars, id_rsa, *.pem — and prints a Left on this machine: notice. On native Windows it does not: uncommitted changes to tracked files upload as they are, whatever the filename. Stash first. IP allowlisting kills every Anthropic-hosted cloud session. Cloud sessions call the Anthropic API from Anthropic's infrastructure, not your network. If your organization has IP allowlisting on, each one fails with an authentication error — and so do Code Review runs and cloud scheduled tasks on hosted environments. The fix is an Anthropic support exemption, or routing to a self-hosted environment, which calls the API from your own network. ZDR, HIPAA, and CMEK are hard blocks. Organizations with Zero Data Retention or the HIPAA configuration can't use /web-setup or other cloud session features; organizations using customer-managed encryption keys can't start cloud sessions at all. Cloud sessions need a claude.ai sign-in, not an API key. --cloud and --teleport are unavailable when Claude Code is configured for Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or another third-party provider — the error names your provider. An LLM gateway configured only through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL doesn't trip that check, but you still need claude auth login. Your organization's allow_remote_sessions policy must also be on. Archive environments; you can't delete them. Anthropic-hosted environments have no delete option — only Archive, which affects new sessions, not running ones. Delete any network secrets you no longer want before archiving: they stay attached in sessions that are still running. If the archived environment was your saved CLI default, new CLI sessions fall back to another environment in your list. Some slash commands behave differently. Commands that open a terminal picker take an argument instead — /model sonnet, /effort, /rename. Terminal-only commands like /plugin and /resume aren't available. /config in the browser opens your settings rather than setting a value; to change a setting for a cloud session, set an environment variable or commit the key to the repo's .claude/settings.json. Agent teams are off by default and need CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in the environment's variables.

On Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner can create organization-shared environments from the Cloud environments admin page. They appear in every member's selector under an Organization heading, below that member's Personal environments, and open read-only for everyone — Owners included — from the selector; edits happen on the admin page. An Owner can also share one of their own personal environments from its Who can use it row, which keeps the environment's ID, so sessions and scheduled tasks already pointing at it are unaffected. Two things to get right when you do this: Put credentials in network secrets, not variables. Every member's sessions can read a shared environment's variables. Set the organization default separately, in the Claude Code admin settings. Members who haven't chosen an environment get it. Claude Tag channel sessions, where Claude acts as the organization rather than as a member, can only use organization-level environments — shared or self-hosted — so a channel that needs a non-default toolchain needs a shared environment with a setup script that installs it. From the CLI, /remote-env picks your default environment for claude --cloud and saves it to remote.defaultEnvironmentId in your user settings, so it applies in every project on your machine until you change it — unless a higher-precedence settings layer, like a repo's project settings, sets the same key. /remote-env only sets the default: it doesn't start a session and can't create or edit environments. Check your understanding 0/5 Key takeaways A cloud session is a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 VM with your COMMITTED repository on it. Anything that lives only in ~/.claude/ — user memory, skills, agents, commands, local-scope MCP servers — does not make the trip. Plugins never do, from either the repo or your user settings. One saved cloud environment (network policy + variables + setup script) serves all five surfaces: browser, Desktop, mobile, claude --cloud, and scheduled tasks. Four network levels: None, Trusted (default), Full, Custom. Four kinds of traffic bypass all of them — api.anthropic.com, the GitHub proxy, MCP connectors, and network-secret hosts. None is not an air gap. Credentials belong in network secrets, never environment variables: the agent proxy attaches the key after the request leaves the VM, so the session can use it but never read it. Variables are readable by anyone who can use the environment. Setup script = provision the VM, cloud only, cached if it finishes in ~5 minutes. SessionStart hook = project setup, runs everywhere, never cached. Scope a hook to the cloud with CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE=true. The cache is a filesystem snapshot: installed packages and pulled images survive, running processes don't. Start databases and compose stacks per session. Ceilings to plan around: ~4 vCPU / 16 GB / 30 GB, a 2-minute default command timeout (30 more minutes once backgrounded), and a VM that pauses when idle and can be reclaimed — losing in-flight commands and subagents, though not your history. claude --cloud clones your GitHub remote, not your working tree. Push first. The CLI handoff is one-way: --teleport pulls a session down as a local copy, and nothing pushes a terminal session up.

Run these same sessions on hardware you own → Self-Hosted Environments The three ways work outlives a prompt, compared → Background Tasks, Loops, and Scheduled Runs One conversation that coordinates many cloud sessions → Projects and Coordinator Threads Put a cloud session on a clock → Cowork Scheduled Tasks شارك هذه الصفحة X LinkedIn Reddit Hacker News نسخ الرابط

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط A Claude Code project accumulates context debt the way a laptop accumulates browser tabs. Every skill you installed adds a line to a listing Claude re-reads on every turn. Every subagent adds a description. Every CLAUDE.md paragraph you wrote in March loads in September whether the task needs it or not. And every npm test dumps up to 30,000 characters into the conversation. None of it is visible until the session starts forgetting instructions or the bill stops matching the work. Context management covers the two commands you use in the moment, /clear and /compact. This page is the audit you run once per project: six places where Claude Code spends context before you type anything or between your turns, the setting that governs each, and the number it defaults to. Everything here is in the official docs as of September 2026, and most of the knobs are newer than the folklore about them. What you'll learn Measure before you cut: read /context, /usage attribution, and /doctor's listing estimate so you fix the biggest line item first Prune the skill listing with /skill-doctor (v2.1.252+) and the four skillOverrides states, and know the 1%-of-window budget the listing is capped at Cap what a shell command or background task returns inline (30,000 and 32,000 characters by default) with bashOutputMaxChars and taskOutputMaxChars Stop paying for CLAUDE.md in every subagent with omitClaudeMd (v2.1.271+) and keep subagent descriptions under the 15,000-token warning line Set the auto-compact window on purpose (/autocompact, autoCompactWindow) and understand the 25,000-token budget that decides which invoked skills survive compaction Cap effort fleet-wide with maxEffortLevel when thinking tokens, not context, are the real bill آخر تحقّق: 2026-09-15. Setting names, defaults, ranges, and minimum versions from the Claude Code settings reference (autoCompactWindow, bashOutputMaxChars, taskOutputMaxChars, maxEffortLevel, skillListingBudgetFraction, skillOverrides, disableBundledSkills). /skill-doctor behavior, the 1% listing budget, the 1,536-character description cap, and the 25,000-token re-attach budget from the skills docs. Bash inline limits from the tools reference. omitClaudeMd, the 15,000-token description warning, and what a subagent loads from the subagents docs. CLAUDE.md and cost guidance from Manage costs. Model context sizes are not repeated here; see Models and pricing. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
documents.s: Context Budget Audit: /skill-doctor, Output Caps and the Six Numbers That Fill Your Window

documents.t: Two facts make this diagram actionable. Everything in the left box is paid on every request, because Claude Code sends the full conversation each turn and only the cache-read discount softens it. And the right box is where a single verbose command can add more than the whole left box in one step. The audit below works left to right.
documents.s: What is in the window before you type

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 9 1Measure: /context, /usage, /doctor⌄ Run /context for a live breakdown by category with optimization suggestions, including which CLAUDE.md and auto-memory files loaded. On a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan, /usage attributes recent usage to skills, subagents, plugins, and individual MCP servers as percentages, and flags behaviors (long context, cache misses) that account for 10% or more. /doctor estimates the skill listing's context cost and its biggest contributors. Write the three biggest line items down before changing anything. ←PreviousNext→ 2Prune the skill listing with /skill-doctor⌄ Every skill in the listing costs context on every turn whether or not Claude uses it. /skill-doctor (v2.1.252+) shows each skill's context cost and invocation frequency, flags skills never invoked, and tells you where to turn them off; it also lists plugins you have not used recently. Start with the highest-cost unused ones. Interactive sessions open the report in the /plugin manager's Stats tab; with -p it prints as text. It does not cover bundled or enterprise skills, needs feature-flag fetching, and refuses over Remote Control. ←PreviousNext→ 3Collapse, do not delete, with skillOverrides⌄ Four states per skill: on (name and description listed), name-only (listed without description, still invocable), user-invocable-only (hidden from Claude, still in the / menu), off. The /skills menu writes this for you: highlight a skill, press Space to cycle, Esc to save to .claude/settings.local.json. Plugin skills are managed through /plugin instead. Setting disableBundledSkills: true removes Claude Code's own bundled skills and workflows in one line. ←PreviousNext→ 4Know the listing budget and the description cap⌄ The listing is capped at 1% of the model's context window (skillListingBudgetFraction, default 0.01). When it overflows, Claude Code keeps every name but drops descriptions starting with the least-used skills, which strips the keywords Claude needs to auto-select them. Each skill's description plus when_to_use is also cut at 1,536 characters (skillListingMaxDescChars). Put the key use case in the first sentence. ←PreviousNext→ 5Shrink what loads at startup⌄ Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and move workflow-specific instructions (PR review, migrations) into skills, which load only when invoked. Auto memory loads only its first 200 lines or 25 KB, so a bloated MEMORY.md silently truncates. Subagent descriptions are read every turn: when the combined descriptions of your custom subagents pass 15,000 tokens, Claude Code warns at startup. Move detail into each subagent's system prompt, which loads only when it runs. ←PreviousNext→ 6Cap tool output inline⌄ A successful Bash or PowerShell command returns up to roughly 30,000 characters inline by default; past that Claude gets a short preview plus a file path and reads the file on demand. A failing command returns up to 10,000 characters as a head-and-tail excerpt. bashOutputMaxChars (v2.1.261+, clamped to 4,000–128,000) sets the inline ceiling and read-back window together and makes Claude Code ignore BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH. taskOutputMaxChars does the same for background tasks read with TaskOutput (default 32,000, same range). Lower them on projects with chatty build tools; raise them only when Claude keeps opening the saved file anyway. ←PreviousNext→ 7Stop paying for CLAUDE.md in every subagent⌄ A non-fork subagent loads every level of your CLAUDE.md hierarchy plus a git-status snapshot, on top of its own prompt. The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip both. For custom subagents that get everything from the delegation prompt, set omitClaudeMd: true in the frontmatter (v2.1.271+): user, project, and local CLAUDE.md files are skipped; managed policy files still load. Ignored when the agent runs as the main session agent. For large shared instructions in headless runs, pass --append-subagent-system-prompt-file (v2.1.261+) instead of stuffing them into every description. ←PreviousNext→ 8Set the auto-compact window on purpose⌄ autoCompactWindow is a token count from 100,000 to 1,000,000, capped at your model's window; unset means Claude Code picks a window tuned for the model. /autocompact 500k writes it to user settings; --autocompact overrides for one session; CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW overrides both. CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE (1–100) can only lower the trigger point. After compaction, invoked skills are re-attached at up to 5,000 tokens each within a 25,000-token total, most recent first, so older skills can be dropped entirely. If a skill must survive, re-invoke it after /compact. ←PreviousNext→ 9Cap effort when thinking is the bill, not context⌄ Thinking tokens are billed as output. maxEffortLevel (v2.1.267+) caps the effort any session can use: one of low, medium, high, xhigh, or max (max = no cap). It applies before every request on every provider, the lowest cap across scopes wins, and a cap below xhigh disables ultracode. Per-model caps go in modelSettings. Deploy through managed settings to enforce for an organization. ←PreviousNext→

Project-local context caps (.claude/settings.local.json) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ { "bashOutputMaxChars": 12000, "taskOutputMaxChars": 12000, "skillOverrides": { "legacy-migration-notes": "name-only", "deploy-prod": "user-invocable-only", "old-design-system": "off" }, "autoCompactWindow": 500000, "maxEffortLevel": "high" } Read it top to bottom as decisions, not defaults. The two output caps assume a chatty test runner; drop them back toward the 30,000 / 32,000 defaults if Claude starts opening the saved output file on every run. The three overrides keep the skills reachable without paying for their descriptions. The compaction window is an explicit choice for a 1M-context model where you would rather compact at half than at the model-tuned point. The effort cap is the one line here that changes output quality, so set it last and only after /usage shows thinking tokens dominating. Subagent that does not load CLAUDE.md (.claude/agents/repo-auditor.md) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ --- name: repo-auditor description: Audits a repository for dead code and unused exports. Use for read-only sweeps. tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash model: sonnet omitClaudeMd: true --- You are a read-only auditor. Everything you need is in the delegation prompt. Report findings as a table of path, symbol, and evidence. Do not edit files. Run the skill report in a headless session CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ claude -p "/skill-doctor"
documents.s: A settings block you can paste

documents.t: Watch out Deleting skills instead of collapsing them. name-only keeps a skill invocable at near-zero listing cost; off removes it from the / menu too. Most 'unused' skills should become name-only, not disappear. Raising bashOutputMaxChars to the 128,000 ceiling because one build log overflowed. That makes every future command up to 4× more expensive inline. Filter the log with a PreToolUse hook (grep for FAIL, head -100) instead; the costs docs show the exact hook. Setting autoCompactWindow above the model's context. Claude Code caps it at the window silently, so the setting looks applied and does nothing. Assuming a subagent is cheap because its context is separate. Its startup still includes every CLAUDE.md level and a git snapshot unless it is Explore, Plan, or sets omitClaudeMd. Reading /skill-doctor over Remote Control from a phone. It returns 'Skill usage reports are not available on this connection.' Run it in the terminal where the session lives. Expecting an invoked skill to survive /compact. Only the most recent invocations fit in the 25,000-token re-attach budget, at 5,000 tokens each. Re-invoke the ones you still need.

Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways Measure first: /context for the live breakdown, /usage for attribution by skill, subagent, plugin, and MCP server, /doctor for the listing estimate. The skill listing is a per-turn tax capped at 1% of the window. /skill-doctor tells you what to collapse; name-only keeps a skill usable at near-zero cost. Tool output is the fastest way to blow a window: ~30,000 characters inline per successful command, 32,000 per background task. Cap with bashOutputMaxChars / taskOutputMaxChars, or filter with a hook. Subagents are not free at startup: every CLAUDE.md level plus git status, unless Explore, Plan, or omitClaudeMd. Keep custom descriptions under 15,000 tokens combined. Compaction keeps only the most recent invoked skills (5,000 each, 25,000 total). Set autoCompactWindow deliberately, and re-invoke what must survive. When thinking tokens dominate the bill, maxEffortLevel caps effort fleet-wide; lowest scope wins and it holds on every provider.

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط What you'll learn التمييز بين /clear و /compact واختيار الأمر الصحيح فورًا فهم الضغط التلقائي ولماذا يبقى المسح الاستباقي أفضل منه تطبيق أربع تقنيات لإبقاء الجلسات الطويلة حادة التعرّف على أعراض امتلاء نافذة السياق وإصلاحها بسرعة آخر تحقّق: 2026-06-20. أسماء الأوامر مثل /compact و/clear وسلوك الضغط التلقائي يمكن أن تتغير — تأكد من ذلك في الوثائق الرسمية. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
لكل جلسة نافذة سياق محدودة. ومع امتلائها، يُضغَط المحتوى الأقدم ويمكن أن يبدأ Claude في "الانحراف". إدارة السياق بتعمّد هي ما يبقي الجلسات الطويلة حادة.
أمران يغطيان تقريبًا كل موقف. الحيلة هي مطابقة الأمر مع نيّتك. قرّر بسؤال واحد: هل هذه مهمة جديدة أم المهمة نفسها؟

عندما يقترب السياق من الحد، يمكن لـ Claude Code أن يضغط تلقائيًا ليستمر العمل دون توقف تام. إنه شبكة أمان — لكن استخدام /clear بشكل استباقي بين المهام يعطي نتائج أفضل من الاعتماد عليه. Pro tip تعامل مع الضغط التلقائي كشبكة احتياطية، لا كاستراتيجية. المسح بين المهام غير المترابطة يبقي السياق أنظف من ترك النافذة تمتلئ حتى يتدخل الضغط التلقائي.

إلى جانب الأمرين، أربع عادات تبقي سياقك رشيقًا منذ البداية. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1مهمة واحدة لكل جلسة⌄ لا تدع فترة بعد ظهر من العمل غير المترابط تتراكم في سياق واحد. ←PreviousNext→ 2فوّض القراءة الثقيلة إلى الوكلاء الفرعيين⌄ سلّم القراءات الكبيرة إلى الوكلاء الفرعيين — فهم يحرقون سياقهم هم ويعيدون الخلاصة فقط. راجع /docs/claude-code/subagents. ←PreviousNext→ 3أشِر، لا تلصق⌄ وجّه Claude إلى الملفات عبر @path بدلًا من لصق كتل كبيرة، وأبقِ CLAUDE.md رشيقًا (راجع /docs/claude-code/claude-md). ←PreviousNext→ 4راقب الميزانية⌄ شريط حالة يعرض استخدام السياق يخبرك متى تضغط. راجع /docs/claude-code/statusline. ←PreviousNext→ تتطابق هذه مع الوثائق الحية: الوكلاء الفرعيون، وCLAUDE.md، وشريط الحالة. العَرَض ← الحل إذا بدأ Claude ينسى تعليمة سابقة أو يكرر نفسه، فالنافذة على الأرجح ممتلئة. /compact (المهمة نفسها) أو /clear (مهمة جديدة) يصلحانه فورًا عادةً. المزيد في استكشاف الأخطاء وإصلاحها. Key takeaways /clear يمسح المحادثة لبداية جديدة — استخدمه للمهام غير المترابطة /compact يلخّص الجلسة لتحرير مساحة — استخدمه لمواصلة المهمة نفسها عندما تمتلئ النافذة الضغط التلقائي شبكة أمان؛ المسح الاستباقي بـ /clear بين المهام يعطي نتائج أفضل أبقِ السياق رشيقًا: مهمة واحدة لكل جلسة، وفوّض القراءة الثقيلة إلى الوكلاء الفرعيين، وأشِر إلى الملفات بدلًا من اللصق، وراقب الميزانية عبر شريط الحالة النسيان أو التكرار يعني نافذة ممتلئة — /compact (المهمة نفسها) أو /clear (مهمة جديدة) يصلحه اختبر نفسك 0/4

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-27. /design is a research preview (shipped week 34, Aug 17–21, 2026). Version gates, plan availability, and behavior can move — confirm in the Claude Code whats-new digest before relying on any specific detail. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. Anthropic dropped a slash command into Claude Code that skips coding on purpose. /design publishes a canvas of editable UI artboards from a plain-English brief; you pick one, tweak it, and only then does Claude turn it into real code. It is the first Claude Code feature where the deliverable is not code — the design phase is the artifact. What you'll learn Understand what an artboard is and why it changes the coding-first flow Run /design correctly on the first try (version, plan, prompt shape) Know the three phases: draft → pick+edit → implement Avoid the three known traps: token cost, style drift from your repo, and the free-tier wall Pair /design with the Concise output style that shipped the same week

/design is a skill — not a plain slash command. When you invoke it, Claude Code hands off to Claude Design's artboard workflow and prints a link to a published canvas. An artboard is a working screen you can act on: change the color, move a block, widen a gap. It is rendered on the artifacts runtime, so it lives in your Claude account, not as files in your repo. That distinction matters. The output of /design is a URL, not a diff. Nothing lands in git status until you tell Claude to implement. What you'll learn Availability: Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise. Not free. Requires Claude Code v2.1.233 or later. Ships in both the CLI and Claude Code Desktop. Status: research preview — expect the invocation shape, output format, and included artboard count to shift.

Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Draft — describe the screen, not the layout⌄ Run /design with a brief that says what the screen is for. Claude publishes several artboard variants side by side, each editable. You get a link; open it in a browser. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick and edit — iterate on the canvas⌄ Choose the variant closest to what you want. Edit inline (colors, spacing, layout) or keep iterating in the same Claude Code thread with prompts like 'make the hero bolder' — the thread keeps context so you don't restate the brief. ←PreviousNext→ 3Implement — hand off to code⌄ Tell Claude which artboard to implement. It writes the code into your repo, using the artboard as ground truth for layout and copy. ←PreviousNext→

/design rewards briefs that describe purpose and audience, not pixel targets. Two patterns: /design — feature brief CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ /design a few options for the sign-in screen. Users are engineers on mobile. Optimize for one-hand thumb reach; SSO is the primary path, email/password secondary. Show a state for a locked-out account. /design — redesign an existing surface CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ /design redesign our composer based on what people actually use it for: drafting long messages, attaching files, and switching model. The current version buries the model picker; make it a first-class control. Two things that quietly do a lot of work in those briefs: Naming the user and constraint ("engineers on mobile", "one-hand thumb reach") pulls Claude off the statistical-average layout it defaults to. Naming a failure state ("locked-out account") forces the artboard to cover empty/error/edge cases, not just the happy path.

1. It is token-hungry. Multiple full-fidelity artboards per invocation eats budget faster than a normal chat turn. Research-preview users report this consistently. Save /design for real decisions, not throwaway sketches. 2. It does not match your codebase. Claude Design generates from a generic aesthetic, not from your existing components. If you want the artboard to feel like the rest of your app, front-load a DESIGN.md at the repo root (fonts, spacing scale, color tokens, existing components) and reference it in the brief — the same trick that keeps /design's implementation phase from re-inventing your button primitives. Reference DESIGN.md before /design CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Before you draft anything, read DESIGN.md and list the type scale, spacing scale, and named color tokens you'll use. Then /design a settings screen that respects those tokens. 3. Free-tier wall. /design is gated behind paid plans (Pro and up). If your team pays for Claude Code seats but a contractor is on free, /design silently isn't there for them.

Anthropic shipped the built-in Concise output style the same week (v2.1.237). It makes Claude lead with results and skip preamble — a good pair for /design, because the handoff turn ("implement option 2") does not need narration: ~/.claude/settings.json { "outputStyle": "Concise" } Concise still keeps full detail for error reports, security warnings, and destructive-action confirmations — you lose narration, not safety rails.
documents.s: Pair it with Concise output style

documents.t: Use /design when Skip it when The visual decision is the hard part (new surface, unclear layout) You already know the layout; you just need the code You want to compare 3+ directions cheaply before committing You are iterating on an existing screen's logic, not shape The stakeholder needs a clickable-ish artifact to approve The screen must match an existing design system 1:1 The failure/empty/loading states matter You are prototyping throwaway internal tooling
documents.s: When /design wins vs. writing code directly

documents.t: The canvas URL is shareable. Because artboards live on artifacts, the link works for anyone with access to your Claude account view — you can send it to a designer or PM without exporting anything. Iteration is dual-channel. You can edit on the canvas and keep prompting in the Claude Code thread. Both feed the same context. Implementation still respects your repo. Once you say "implement", Claude Code goes back to normal repo-aware behavior — it will use your Tailwind config, your components, your file structure. The artboard is the target; your codebase is the terrain. Check yourself 0/4
