Notes OpenAI — GPT-Live ChatGPT Voice (consumer) Yes — speech-native Delegates hard tasks to a frontier model mid-conversation; no API yet OpenAI — Realtime API (gpt-realtime) Developer API, GA Speech-to-speech, single model Production voice agents: SIP phone calling, remote MCP servers, image input Google — Gemini Live API Developer API (AI Studio / Vertex, GA) Native-audio, streaming Barge-in, "proactive audio" (speaks only when relevant), affective dialog, tool use + Google Search ElevenLabs — Agents Agent platform (launched Mar 2026) Orchestrated stack with proprietary turn-taking model TTS/STT + turn-taking + tool calls; 70+ languages; sub-500 ms first-turn claims; phone/web/app channels Anthropic — Claude Voice mode in the Claude apps; push-to-talk /voice in Claude Code (Mar 2026, multilingual out of beta Jun 2026) No — turn-based Speak, get spoken replies with a saved transcript. No speech-native full-duplex model announced as of the verify date — don't let anyone tell you otherwise Kyutai — Moshi Open weights + code (GitHub, Hugging Face) Yes — the open-source proof ~160–200 ms latency, dual-stream audio, "Inner Monologue"; runs locally Two takeaways from that table most coverage misses: (1) "voice agent" today means two different architectures — genuinely speech-native full-duplex models (GPT-Live, Moshi, Gemini's native audio) versus very fast, well-orchestrated pipelines with a learned turn-taking model on top (ElevenLabs Agents). Both can feel good; only the first can overlap speech. (2) The open-source option is real: Moshi proves you can run full-duplex on your own hardware, which matters if your use case can't ship audio to a cloud (see Choosing a Model for that decision framework).

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Audio streams in continuously⌄ There is no record-then-send. Your microphone audio is encoded into tokens frame by frame (Moshi's codec uses 80 ms frames) and fed to the model as it arrives — even while the model is mid-sentence. ←PreviousNext→ 2The model makes micro-decisions constantly⌄ Many times per second it chooses: keep talking, stop, stay silent, drop a backchannel ('mhmm'), or start a reply. Turn-taking is a prediction the model learned from real conversation, not a silence timer. ←PreviousNext→ 3You interrupt; it yields instantly⌄ Barge-in is native: the model hears you the moment you start because it never stopped listening. It cuts its own sentence, absorbs what you said, and adjusts — no 'stop' keyword needed. ←PreviousNext→ 4Hard questions get delegated, softly⌄ Ask something needing web search or real reasoning and GPT-Live hands it to the frontier model in the background — while keeping the conversation alive ('let me check that... so anyway—'). The answer is woven back in when ready. ←PreviousNext→ 5Silence is a valid move⌄ A full-duplex model can deliberately say nothing — letting you think out loud without hijacking the turn. Pipeline bots literally could not do this; their VAD treated your pause as an invitation. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: How a full-duplex conversation actually flows

documents.t: Now genuinely viable: Customer support and phone workflows. Sub-second turn-taking plus barge-in removes the two biggest complaint drivers. The Realtime API's SIP support and ElevenLabs Agents both target exactly this. Hands-free and eyes-busy use. Driving, cooking, field work, accessibility — the interaction finally keeps up with speech (voice mode on the Claude apps already covers the capture-and-transcribe version of this). Live translation and language practice. Listen-while-speaking makes near-simultaneous interpretation and natural conversation drills possible for the first time. Voice as an agent front-end. The delegation pattern — chat with a fast voice model while a slow frontier model does the work — is OpenAI's stated bet for managing "long-running agentic work" by voice. Still breaks: Hallucinated audio. Speech-native models can hallucinate in sound, not just facts: wrong-language drift, mangled names and numbers, or off accents (GPT-Live's launch translation demo drew exactly this criticism). Never trust a spoken number you didn't confirm. Noisy environments and crosstalk. Always-open microphones hear everything — side conversations, TV, a second speaker. Full-duplex makes the model more exposed to ambient audio, not less. Safety of real-time actions. A model that acts at conversational speed can act on a misheard sentence at conversational speed. Any voice agent that touches money, messages, or deletions needs explicit spoken confirmation gates and a bias toward read-only defaults — the same rules as any agent (see Foundations), but with a lower-fidelity input channel. Emotional reliance. A system that backchannels, hesitates, and never tires of you is engineered to feel like a friend. OpenAI itself flags monitoring for this. Design (and use) accordingly. System-prompt skeleton for a voice agent (works on speech-native models and pipelines) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are a voice assistant for {company}. You are SPEAKING, not writing. Style: - Short sentences. One idea per sentence. No lists, no markdown, no URLs read aloud. - If the user interrupts, stop immediately and address what they said. - If the user pauses mid-thought, stay silent. Do not fill silence. Safety: - Before ANY action that sends, buys, deletes, or changes something: say back exactly what you will do and wait for a clear spoken "yes". - Repeat numbers, names, and addresses back for confirmation — always. - If audio is unclear or noisy, say what you think you heard and ask. - If asked for something outside {scope}, say so and offer a human handoff. Check yourself 0/4 Key takeaways The old stack wasn't badly built — it was structurally too slow: stacked STT/LLM/TTS latency plus a silence timer, versus the ~0–200 ms humans expect Full-duplex = one speech-native model that listens while speaking; barge-in, backchannels, and deliberate silence become learned behaviors, not hacks GPT-Live (July 8, 2026) mainstreams full-duplex in ChatGPT and pioneers delegation: fast voice model up front, frontier model reasoning in the background The landscape splits in two: speech-native full-duplex (GPT-Live, Gemini native audio, Moshi — open source since 2024) vs fast orchestrated pipelines with learned turn-taking (ElevenLabs Agents); Claude's voice remains turn-based Voice agents are now viable for support, hands-free, and translation — but audio hallucinations, noisy rooms, and real-time action safety still demand confirmation gates

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط Google was expected to ship Gemini 3.5 Pro in July 2026. Instead, on 21 July 2026 they shipped three Flash-tier models — Gemini 3.6 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, and Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber — and left the Pro tier in partner testing. If you build on Claude and use Gemini as a cross-check, the shape of that release matters more than any single benchmark: Google is telling the market that the workhorse tier, not the flagship, is where the real money is. This page walks a Claude user through what actually landed, at what price, and what breaks when you port an existing call. What you'll learn Understand what shipped on 21 July 2026 — three Flash models, and why Google skipped 3.5 Pro Read the price table honestly: 17% cheaper output plus 17% fewer output tokens compounds into a ~30% real cost drop Know when Flash-Lite ($0.30 in / $2.50 out, 350 tok/s, 1M context) is the right cross-check versus Claude Haiku See how Flash Cyber outscored Claude Opus 4.6 at V8 bug-hunting — and why you almost certainly cannot use it Migrate cleanly: which sampling knobs were removed, and what the new thinking_level enum accepts
documents.s: Gemini 3.6 Flash, Flash-Lite & Flash Cyber for Claude Users

documents.t: Google's 21 July 2026 release is a Flash-tier refresh with no Pro — a new workhorse (3.6 Flash, $1.50 in / $7.50 out, 1M context, Computer Use built in), a cheaper high-throughput sibling (3.5 Flash-Lite, $0.30 in / $2.50 out, 350 tokens/second), and a security-only fine-tune (3.5 Flash Cyber) that Google is gating to governments and trusted partners via its CodeMender program. The interesting story is not the model. It is the choice: Google pushed a workhorse and a cheap tier while explicitly holding Pro back, and Logan Kilpatrick said Pro is "currently testing with partners" after missing internal performance targets. That is a different bet than the OpenAI GPT-5.6 launch two weeks earlier, which led with a flagship (Sol) — see the GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna page for the mirror-image comparison.
Everyone is writing the "17% cheaper" headline. Here are the details a Claude user should not miss.
documents.s: Three things about this launch that surprise people

documents.t: This is not how Google usually ships. In previous refreshes the flagship led the launch and the smaller siblings followed. On 21 July 2026 Google shipped only Flash-class models and confirmed 3.5 Pro is still in partner testing after missing internal performance goals. Product lead Logan Kilpatrick said the team hopes to "land soon." Read that literally: at the highest tier of intelligence, Google does not yet have a step function it can ship. It does have a strong workhorse and a bug-hunter it can gate. If your workflow depends on "the smartest Gemini you can buy," today that is still 3.5 Pro-Preview or the older 3.5 Ultra tier — not a July-2026 model.

The launch chart shows Gemini 3.6 Flash output pricing at $7.50 per 1M tokens, down from $9 on 3.5 Flash — a 17% cut. Look one row down: Google also reports 17% fewer output tokens on the same workloads (measured on the Artificial Analysis Index). Those compound: 0.83 × 0.83 ≈ 0.69, so real-world output cost drops roughly 31% on comparable jobs, not 17%. On DeepSWE Google claims token reductions "up to 65%." When you cross-check a Claude Sonnet 5 pipeline against 3.6 Flash, do the multiplication before you decide whether to swap — the headline is understating the delta.
documents.s: 2. The 17% output-price cut is really ~30% because output tokens dropped 17% too

documents.t: Google reports that Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber discovered 55 unique confirmed vulnerabilities on internal V8 JavaScript engine benchmarks, versus 47 for standard 3.5 Flash and 36 for Claude Opus 4.6. Ten of those bugs were found by no other model. On the CyberGym benchmark it lands at 83.2%, close to Claude Mythos 5 (83.8%) and GPT-5.5-Cyber (85.6%). Impressive — and gated. Flash Cyber ships only through Google's CodeMender program to governments and trusted enterprise partners. There is no public API, no pricing, no self-serve access. If you saw a headline that said "Google's cyber AI beat Claude" and expected to try it: you cannot. The takeaway a defender should extract is not "swap models"; it is that fine-tuning a mid-tier model on a narrow domain now beats a bigger general-purpose model on that domain. That pattern will repeat.
documents.s: 3. Flash Cyber beat Claude Opus 4.6 at V8 bug-hunting — but you almost certainly cannot use it

documents.t: آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-22. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. المصادر: Google DeepMind launch post + TechCrunch/SiliconANGLE/MarkTechPost coverage of the 21 July 2026 release Model Input $/1M Output $/1M Cached input $/1M Context Max output Notes Gemini 3.6 Flash $1.50 $7.50 $0.15 1,048,576 65,536 Workhorse; Computer Use built in Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite $0.30 $2.50 (not stated) 1,048,576 65,536 350 tokens/second output; rolling out in Google Search Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber (not public) (not public) (not public) (not public) (not public) Governments & trusted partners via CodeMender only Benchmark deltas Google published for 3.6 Flash vs 3.5 Flash (higher is better): DeepSWE: 49% vs 37% (+12 points) MLE Bench: 63.9% vs 49.7% (+14.2 points) OSWorld-Verified: 83.0% vs 78.4% (+4.6 points) GDPval-AA v2: 1421 Elo vs 1349 (+72 Elo) GPQA Diamond: 92.8% MMMU-Pro: 83.2% Humanity's Last Exam: 38.3% Chatbot Arena Elo (Text Overall): 1485 Artificial Analysis Coding Index: 69.2% Two knobs are more useful than any single benchmark row. Knowledge cutoff jumped from January 2025 to March 2026 — a 14-month leap. For "answer from the model directly" tasks (no RAG, no browsing) this is often bigger than a benchmark score. Output speed is quoted at 304 tokens/second for 3.6 Flash and 350 tokens/second for Flash-Lite, which changes how much latency-hiding your UI has to do.

For high-volume, latency-sensitive Claude workflows — classification, extraction, moderation, autocomplete — Flash-Lite at $0.30/$2.50 with 1M-token context and 350 tok/s is now the obvious cross-check against Claude Haiku 4.5. It is not a Sonnet replacement, and you should not use it for planning-heavy agent loops. But if you have a "cheap model behind a queue" tier in your stack, budget a day to A/B it.
documents.s: Flash-Lite is the real story for high-volume Claude workflows

documents.t: The Gemini API surface changed with 3.6. If you carry a Claude-shaped call over, four things break. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Swap the model ID⌄ Use `gemini-3.6-flash` for the workhorse or `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` for the cheap tier. There is no public model ID for 3.5 Flash Cyber. 3.5 Pro is not shipping yet — do not pin to it. ←PreviousNext→ 2Delete temperature, top_p, and top_k⌄ These sampling knobs were removed from 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite. If your Claude-side code carries them over via a shim, Gemini will reject or ignore them depending on the SDK. Delete them; the model handles sampling internally now. ←PreviousNext→ 3Replace thinking_budget with thinking_level⌄ The integer-tokens `thinking_budget` field was replaced with a `thinking_level` enum. Flash defaults to medium; Flash-Lite defaults to minimal. Set it explicitly if you were tuning budgets — you cannot carry over the old integer. ←PreviousNext→ 4Do not end a conversation on a model turn⌄ 3.6 Flash rejects prefilled model turns (a conversation ending on a non-empty `model` role). If you were using Anthropic-style prefill to steer output, restructure — Gemini will 400 the request. ←PreviousNext→ 5Drop candidate_count⌄ `candidate_count` is unsupported on 3.6 Flash. If you were requesting multiple completions in one call, call the API N times or move that job to a different tier. ←PreviousNext→ 6Wire Computer Use as a built-in tool, not an integration⌄ In 3.6 Flash, computer use — operating a GUI — is now a *client-side built-in tool* in the Gemini API and Gemini Enterprise, not a separate integration. Enable it in the tools block rather than plumbing a separate SDK. Anthropic's equivalent lives in the [Claude computer-use section](/docs/models/computer-use-agents). ←PreviousNext→ Minimal 3.6 Flash call (Python SDK) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from google import genai client = genai.Client() # picks up GOOGLE_API_KEY resp = client.models.generate_content( model="gemini-3.6-flash", contents="Extract the 3 riskiest lines from this diff and cite line numbers.", config={ "thinking_level": "medium", # was thinking_budget=<int> # do NOT pass temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count "tools": [{"computer_use": {}}], # built-in, not a separate SDK }, ) print(resp.text)
documents.s: Migration: what a Claude user actually has to change

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for 3.6 Flash: high-volume tool loops where token efficiency dominates cost, and workflows that benefit from the March 2026 knowledge cutoff (14 months fresher than the older 3.5 Flash). Reach for Flash-Lite: latency-sensitive classification/extraction on 1M-token inputs where Haiku is your baseline. Stay on Claude: SWE-Bench-Pro-style real-repo bug fixes, long agent runs where extended thinking discipline matters, and anywhere you already trust Sonnet 5 planning quality. Do not chase Flash Cyber: unless you are a government or a CodeMender partner, treat its numbers as a research signal, not a purchasing decision. For a broader Gemini-vs-Claude framing that predates this release, see Gemini for Claude users and the coding-focused Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding. For the mirror-image OpenAI launch two weeks earlier, GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna. For the cross-model porting rules that make any of these swaps survive contact with production, porting prompts across models.

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash on 13 August 2026, exactly three weeks after 3.6 Flash. Same tier, same context window, same shape — but a 16.3-point jump on DeepSWE, ~3× the output throughput of the closest GPT-5.6 competitor, and an introductory price that halves 3.6 Flash's cost for four and a half months. This lesson walks a Claude user through what actually changed, which numbers are load-bearing, and the decisions that get worse if you take the launch headlines at face value. What you'll learn Recognise what shipped on 13 August 2026 — and why the three-week cadence after 3.6 Flash is the real signal Read the intro pricing correctly: $0.75 in / $3.75 out doubles to $1.50 / $7.50 on 1 January 2027 Understand the DeepSWE 49% → 65.3% jump — and why it matters more than a small GDPval move Use the ~3× token-throughput advantage where it pays off (agent loops) and ignore it where it doesn't (chat) Migrate from 3.6 Flash to 3.7 Flash with one model ID and no surprises — plus the parts of the 3.6 migration that still bite

documents.t: Gemini 3.7 Flash is the same-tier successor to 3.6 Flash — 1M-token context, 65,536-token output, three thinking_level values (low, medium, high, default medium) — with meaningful coding-agent gains and a 50%-off introductory sticker that expires 31 December 2026. Model ID: gemini-3.7-flash. Rolled out to Google AI Studio, Android Studio, the Gemini API, and Google Antigravity on day one. The interesting story is not any single benchmark row. It is that Google is now iterating the workhorse tier on a three-week cadence — 3.6 Flash on 21 July, 3.7 Flash on 13 August — while still holding 3.5 Pro back. Read that literally: at the workhorse tier Google has a fast feedback loop with developers; at the flagship tier it does not yet have a step function it wants to ship. For the mirror image on the OpenAI side, see GPT-5.6 August update. آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-20. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. المصادر: Google DeepMind launch post 13 Aug 2026, Google AI for Developers docs, Google Antigravity blog, VentureBeat and DataCamp coverage
Everyone is writing the "half price" headline. Here is what a Claude user should not miss.
documents.s: Three things about this launch that surprise people

documents.t: Google's launch post is explicit: $0.75 per 1M input tokens and $3.75 per 1M output tokens is an introductory rate available "through 31 December 2026." Standard pricing kicks in 1 January 2027: $1.50 / $7.50, matching the 3.6 Flash sticker. If you model 2027 cost on the intro number you will be off by 2×. Budgeting rule for a Claude shop cross-checking pipelines: run the A/B at the intro price, but pin the decision to the post-January number, because that is what your Q1 invoice will look like. See What AI costs across providers for the framework.
documents.s: 1. The intro price expires — and doubles — on 1 January 2027

documents.t: Google's launch benchmarks (3.7 Flash vs 3.6 Flash, higher is better): Benchmark 3.6 Flash 3.7 Flash Delta DeepSWE v1.1 (real bug fixes) 49.0% 65.3% +16.3 pts FrontierCode 1.1 Main (production code) 34.4% 43.6% +9.2 pts WebDev Arena (Elo) 1538 1588 +50 Elo AutomationBench (agent workflows) 17.0% 30.4% +13.4 pts GDPval AA v2 (knowledge work, Elo) 1421 ~1525 +~104 Elo The GDPval move is real but it still trails Claude Sonnet 5 at 1598 and GPT-5.6 Terra at 1578 for knowledge work. The DeepSWE and AutomationBench moves are where a workhorse model was previously embarrassed — real-repo bug fixes and multi-step agent runs. Read the shape, not the average: 3.7 Flash closed the coding-agent gap while barely moving on general knowledge work. That tells you what job Google is now willing to point Flash at.
documents.s: 2. The DeepSWE jump is bigger than the GDPval jump — and that asymmetry is the whole story

documents.t: Third-party measurements clock 3.7 Flash at roughly 340 output tokens/second, versus ~110 tok/s for GPT-5.6 Terra on comparable prompts — roughly 3×. For a user typing in a chat UI this is invisible: humans read at ~250 words/minute (~5 tok/s), so anything above ~50 tok/s just streams. For a serial agent loop — 20 calls, each with a couple hundred output tokens — 3× compounds across every step and turns a minute of cumulative generation into ~20 seconds. If you are shopping Flash for a customer-facing chat, throughput is a rounding error. If you are shopping it for a coding agent or a research agent, throughput is often the biggest single win. The physics behind this is on Fast inference and token speed.
documents.s: 3. The ~3× throughput advantage matters for agents, not chat

documents.t: Spec Gemini 3.7 Flash Model ID gemini-3.7-flash Context window 1,048,576 input tokens Max output 65,536 tokens Thinking levels low, medium (default), high Modalities in text, image, audio, video, PDF Modalities out text Tools function calling, structured output (JSON schema), code execution, grounding, computer use Intro price (through 31 Dec 2026) $0.75 in / $3.75 out per 1M tokens Standard price (from 1 Jan 2027) $1.50 in / $7.50 out per 1M tokens Availability Google AI Studio, Android Studio, Gemini API, Google Antigravity, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Note the thinking_level default is medium, not low or "auto." A blind port from 3.6 Flash will pay for medium reasoning by default; drop it to low for classification/extraction jobs where the extra planning is wasted. High is only worth it on the hardest coding and multi-step agent problems — Google's own migration guide warns "higher isn't automatically better."

The good news for anyone already on 3.6 Flash: the API surface is unchanged. You swap the model ID and re-run your evals. The bad news for anyone porting from Claude or from older Gemini: the 3.6-era API changes still bite. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Swap the model ID⌄ Use `gemini-3.7-flash`. Do not pin to `gemini-3.6-flash` if you want the new pricing and benchmark deltas. ←PreviousNext→ 2Re-benchmark thinking_level for your workload⌄ Default is medium. For low-variance classification, drop to `low` and measure quality delta. For long-horizon agent runs with tool calls, try `high` on a small sample — but only if your evals show the win. ←PreviousNext→ 3Delete temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count if carried over from Claude⌄ 3.7 Flash inherits the 3.6-era removal of these sampling knobs. A Claude-shaped call that carries them over will fail or be silently ignored depending on the SDK. See the 3.6 migration list on [Gemini 3.6 Flash for Claude users](/docs/models/gemini-3-6-flash-family) — the same list still applies. ←PreviousNext→ 4Stop prefilling the assistant turn⌄ Gemini 3.7 Flash still rejects prefilled model turns (conversations ending on a non-empty `model` role). If you use Anthropic-style prefill to steer output, restructure into a user turn before porting. ←PreviousNext→ 5Budget the 2027 cost, not the intro cost⌄ If your ROI analysis needs 3.7 Flash to be cheaper than Claude Haiku 4.5, do the math with $1.50 / $7.50 — the price that starts 1 January 2027 — not the four-and-a-half-month intro sticker. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal 3.7 Flash call (Python SDK) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from google import genai client = genai.Client() # picks up GOOGLE_API_KEY resp = client.models.generate_content( model="gemini-3.7-flash", contents="Given this diff, list the 3 riskiest lines with file:line and 1-sentence rationale each.", config={ "thinking_level": "medium", # default; drop to "low" for pure extraction, raise to "high" for hardest agent steps # do NOT pass temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count "tools": [{"function_declarations": [...]}], # or {"computer_use": {}} }, ) print(resp.text)

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for 3.7 Flash: serial coding-agent loops (DeepSWE-shaped work), web-development scaffolding, and any workflow where the ~3× throughput advantage compounds across many calls. Reach for 3.7 Flash: high-volume tool loops during the intro window — the 2× price gap versus Claude Haiku 4.5 (on Anthropic's current Haiku sticker) is genuine and closes on 1 January 2027. Stay on Claude Sonnet 5: knowledge-work tasks where 3.7 Flash still trails on GDPval AA v2 (1525 vs 1598), and long-horizon agent runs where extended-thinking discipline matters more than raw throughput. Stay on Claude for any workload where you rely on prefilled assistant turns, temperature control, or Anthropic's tool-use loop — you'll fight the Gemini API instead of using it. Cross-check both: for anything customer-facing, run a small eval on both at the tier you actually plan to ship. The DeepSWE headline is genuine but does not survive contact with every codebase. For the broader Claude-vs-Gemini framing predating this release, see Gemini for Claude users, the coding-focused Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding, and Choosing a model. For the OpenAI side of the same week, GPT-5.6 August update. For cross-model porting rules that keep any of these swaps stable, Porting prompts across models.

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways The intro price ($0.75/$3.75) is a four-and-a-half-month window, not the number to build a 2027 budget on — pin decisions to $1.50/$7.50. The DeepSWE +16.3-point jump is the load-bearing benchmark: 3.7 Flash closed the coding-agent gap Flash was previously embarrassed by. ~3× throughput vs GPT-5.6 Terra compounds in serial agent loops and disappears in chat — pick the workload where it pays. نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2, 2026, twenty days after 3.7 Flash and its third Flash release in six weeks. Same tier, same 1M window, same $0.75 / $3.75 introductory sticker, same model-ID pattern. What changed is the shape of the model's behavior: Google says 3.8 Flash "works harder," executing extra reasoning steps and calling tools iteratively on complex tasks, and the benchmark table shows what that buys. DeepSWE v1.1 moved from 65.3 to 73.7, within a third of a point of Claude Opus 5. Terminal-bench 2.1 reached 89.4, a hair above Opus 5's 89.1. And on Terminal-bench 4.0, the harder successor, 3.8 Flash posts 19.1 against Opus 5's 51.8. This lesson is for a Claude user deciding whether to route work to it. It covers the numbers that are load-bearing, the token-usage cost of "working harder," the migration checklist that has not changed since 3.7, the gated Cyber variant, and the workloads where Claude is still the right default. What you'll learn Recognize what shipped on September 2, 2026 and why a three-week Flash cadence (3.6 → 3.7 → 3.8) is the real signal Read the benchmark table with the right lens: near-parity with Opus 5 on DeepSWE and Terminal-bench 2.1, a 33-point gap on Terminal-bench 4.0, a lead on domain-agent benchmarks Price the 'works harder' behavior: ~30% more output tokens per task, so the same sticker costs more per task than 3.7 Flash Migrate a 3.7 Flash or Claude call to gemini-3.8-flash without surprises (the 3.6-era API removals still apply) Know what Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is, what the Fairwind Program gates, and why you almost certainly cannot call it آخر تحقّق: 2026-09-15. Launch date, pricing window, "works harder" language, Cyber benchmarks, and Fairwind details from Google's launch post. Model ID, thinking_level values and default, context and output limits, and the migration list from Google AI for Developers: latest model. Knowledge cutoff and the DeepSWE / Terminal-bench 2.1 / LVBench deltas from the DeepMind model card. The full comparison table (Opus 5, Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra columns) is Google's evaluation report as reproduced by Vellum; the "~30% more output tokens per task" figure is Emergent's analysis of that report. Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index and cost-per-task numbers are as reported by The Register on September 2. Note a discrepancy: Google's 3.8 report lists 3.7 Flash at 1482 on GDPval-AA v2, while third-party coverage at the 3.7 launch put it near 1525; we show Google's figure here. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

documents.t: Gemini 3.8 Flash is the same-tier successor to 3.7 Flash, model ID gemini-3.8-flash, 1M-token context, 64K max output, thinking_level of low / medium (default) / high, priced at $0.75 in / $3.75 out per 1M tokens through December 31, 2026 and $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027. It is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity, Android Studio, Stitch, Gemini Enterprise, the Gemini app (AI Pro and Ultra), AI Mode in Search, and Google Sheets. Alongside it, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber replaces 3.5 Flash Cyber for vetted defenders through the new Fairwind Program. The cadence is the story again. 3.6 Flash on July 21, 3.7 on August 13, 3.8 on September 2: Google is iterating its workhorse tier every three weeks while the flagship stays quiet (The Register notes 3.5 Pro missed its June date). Read that as a fast developer feedback loop at the tier most teams actually pay for. Anthropic's answer this month is Claude Fable 5.1 at the top of the stack, not a cheaper Sonnet; OpenAI's is GPT-6 Astra.

Google's evaluation report, the rows a Claude shop should care about (higher is better): Benchmark 3.8 Flash 3.7 Flash Claude Opus 5 Claude Sonnet 5 GPT-5.6 Sol DeepSWE v1.1 (real bug fixes) 73.7% 65.3% 74.0% 53.8% 72.7% Terminal-bench 2.1 89.4% — 89.1% — 88.8% Terminal-bench 4.0 19.1% 11.2% 51.8% 12.4% 37.3% OSWorld-2.0 (computer use) 59.0% 50.6% 75.4% 42.6% 62.6% HLE-Verified 54.9% 53.6% 54.4% 31.0% 54.5% GDPval-AA v2 (Elo) 1545 1482 1824 1584 1710 Vals Finance Agent v2 61.4% 59.0% 58.6% 53.9% 53.8% Harvey Legal Agent 10.0% 8.8% 6.7% 5.0% 2.5% BioMysteryBench (hard) 56.5% 43.5% 49.4% 34.1% 44.7% Three reads. First, the DeepSWE +8.4 is the load-bearing number, exactly as the +16.3 was for 3.7 Flash: Google keeps pouring the workhorse's gains into repository-scale coding. Second, Terminal-bench 2.1 vs 4.0 is the same split we flag on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash the following week: a cheap model can saturate the older suite while the harder one, with longer adaptive shell sessions, still separates Opus 5 by more than 30 points. Third, on the domain-agent benchmarks (finance, legal, biology) 3.8 Flash now leads every column, including Opus 5. If your work is a finance or legal agent, that row is worth an eval on its own. If your work is an interactive coding session, the 4.0 row is the one to budget around.
documents.s: 1. Parity with Opus 5 on two headline benchmarks, a 33-point gap on the third

documents.t: Google's own description of the change: on complex tasks the model "exhibits greater diligence — executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively." The launch post also says developers can "utilize lower effort levels to minimize token overhead," which is a polite way of saying the default now spends more. Emergent's read of the evaluation report puts it at roughly 30% more output tokens per task; Artificial Analysis measured $0.58 per Intelligence Index task, about 40% more than 3.7 Flash, at the same per-token sticker. For a Claude user this is the familiar effort trade-off wearing a different name: the model reaches for more tool calls and more thinking before it answers. The sticker did not move; the bill per task did. Budget on task cost, not token price. And re-run any latency SLO you had on 3.7 Flash: more iterations means more wall-clock, even at Flash speed. The physics is on Why agents burn tokens.
documents.s: 2. "Works harder" is a token-usage decision Google made for you

documents.t: Artificial Analysis puts 3.8 Flash at 59 on its Intelligence Index (at high reasoning), tied with GPT-5.6 Sol at extra-high and Grok 4.6 at medium, versus Claude Opus 5 at 63 and Claude Fable 5.1 at 66 (both at max). Its cost-per-task figure for Fable 5.1 is about $3.76, roughly 6× 3.8 Flash's $0.58. Against Opus 5 on list price, Vellum's arithmetic is about 6.7× cheaper on both input and output. Against Sonnet 5 the gap is far smaller, and Sonnet 5 still leads on GDPval-AA v2 (1584 vs 1545). So the honest comparison is: 3.8 Flash is a Sonnet-tier price with DeepSWE and domain-agent scores that now reach Opus territory, and Terminal-bench 4.0 / OSWorld scores that do not. Current Claude list prices are on Models and pricing.

documents.t: Spec Gemini 3.8 Flash Model ID gemini-3.8-flash Release September 2, 2026 Context window 1M input tokens Max output 64K tokens Thinking levels low, medium (default), high; minimal not supported Modalities in text, image, audio, video Modalities out text Knowledge cutoff March 2026 (some domains limited to January 2025) Removed parameters temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count (since the 3.6 line) Intro price (through Dec 31, 2026) $0.75 in / $3.75 out per 1M tokens Standard price (from Jan 1, 2027) $1.50 in / $7.50 out per 1M tokens Availability Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity, Android Studio, Stitch, Gemini Enterprise, Gemini app (AI Pro/Ultra), AI Mode, Google Sheets The knowledge cutoff line is new information versus the 3.7 page and worth a second look: March 2026 headline, but the model card says some domains are limited to January 2025. If you rely on the model knowing a 2026 library API, verify with a grounding tool or paste the docs. That is the same advice we give for any model in Freshness half-life.

The API surface is unchanged from 3.7 Flash. The list of things that break a Claude port is also unchanged, and it keeps catching people. Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Swap the model ID⌄ Use gemini-3.8-flash. The 3.7 endpoint keeps working, but the benchmark deltas and the 'works harder' behavior only arrive with the new ID. ←PreviousNext→ 2Re-benchmark thinking_level, and this time watch tokens, not just accuracy⌄ Default is medium. Because 3.8 Flash reaches for more reasoning and more tool calls on hard tasks, the same level costs more per task than on 3.7. For extraction and classification, try low first and measure both accuracy and output tokens. ←PreviousNext→ 3Replace thinking_budget with thinking_level if you still carry it⌄ thinking_budget is deprecated in favor of the string enum. A call that still passes a numeric budget is running on legacy behavior. ←PreviousNext→ 4Delete temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count from Claude-shaped calls⌄ These sampling knobs have been gone since the 3.6 line. Depending on the SDK they fail or are silently dropped — either way your carefully tuned temperature is doing nothing. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stop prefilling the assistant turn⌄ Conversations ending on a non-empty model turn are rejected. Anthropic-style prefill steering has to become a user-turn instruction or a structured-output schema. ←PreviousNext→ 6Include call_id and name in every FunctionResponse⌄ Required on the generateContent API. A Claude tool_result carries an id; map it explicitly rather than relying on ordering. ←PreviousNext→ 7Budget on the 2027 price and the new task cost⌄ $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027, times roughly 1.3× the tokens per task 3.7 Flash used. That is the number to put in the Q1 forecast. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal 3.8 Flash call (Python SDK) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from google import genai client = genai.Client() # reads GOOGLE_API_KEY resp = client.models.generate_content( model="gemini-3.8-flash", contents="Review this diff. List the 3 riskiest hunks as file:line with a one-sentence reason each.", config={ "thinking_level": "low", # start low on 3.8 Flash; it already 'works harder' at medium # no temperature / top_p / top_k / candidate_count "tools": [{"function_declarations": [...]}], }, ) print(resp.text)

Alongside the general model, Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, replacing 3.5 Flash Cyber. Google's numbers: CWE-Bench patching at 47.2% pass@1 against "a leading frontier model" at 47.8%; a vulnerability-discovery success rate above 70% across 20 programming languages; 2.6× more correct patches to Chrome vulnerabilities than the best commercial models per Chrome Security; and, per Wiz, 7.5–9.7 points higher recall at 2.3–5.2× lower cost. You almost certainly cannot call it. Access runs through the Fairwind Program, limited to "trusted government authorities, as well as critical infrastructure operators and software maintainers," by application. This is the same shape as OpenAI gating GPT-6 Astra's exploit capability behind a vetted program (see the Astra field guide) and Anthropic's treatment of Mythos-class models. For a Claude user the practical takeaway is that the frontier's cyber capability now ships as a separate, gated SKU on all three stacks, and the general models are deliberately not it. Our security section covers what that means for the agents you can call.
documents.s: Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and the Fairwind Program

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for 3.8 Flash: repository-scale coding that looks like DeepSWE, where 73.7 vs Opus 5's 74.0 at a sixth of the task cost is a real trade. Reach for 3.8 Flash: finance, legal, and life-science agent workflows — it now leads every column on Vals Finance Agent v2, Harvey Legal, and BioMysteryBench, including Opus 5. Reach for 3.8 Flash: long-video and chart understanding (LVBench 87.8, CharXiv 86.2) where Claude has no equivalent input path. Stay on Claude Opus 5: interactive terminal agents and computer use. Terminal-bench 4.0 (51.8 vs 19.1) and OSWorld-2.0 (75.4 vs 59.0) are the widest gaps on the table. Stay on Claude for knowledge work where GDPval-AA v2 matters: Opus 5 at 1824 and even Sonnet 5 at 1584 are ahead of 3.8 Flash's 1545. Stay on Claude for anything built on prefilled turns, temperature control, or Anthropic's tool-use loop — you will fight the Gemini API rather than use it. Cross-check both, at the effort you will ship: 3.8 Flash's table is at default or high thinking and costs ~30% more tokens per task than 3.7; Claude's is at max effort. Neither is your production setting. For the broader framing, Gemini for Claude users; for the coding-specific comparison, Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding; for the durable decision framework, Choosing a model.
documents.s: When to reach for 3.8 Flash, and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways DeepSWE +8.4 to 73.7 is the load-bearing number: a Sonnet-priced model now within 0.3 of Opus 5 on repository-scale bug fixing. Terminal-bench 4.0 (19.1 vs 51.8) and OSWorld-2.0 (59.0 vs 75.4) are where Opus 5 stays far ahead — interactive agents and computer use stay on Claude. 'Works harder' means ~30% more tokens per task at the same sticker. Budget per task, start thinking_level at low, and re-check latency SLOs. The 3.6-era API removals (temperature/top_p/top_k/candidate_count, no prefill, call_id + name on FunctionResponse) still break Claude ports; the migration list has not shrunk. 3.8 Flash Cyber is a separate, Fairwind-gated SKU — the third stack this month to ship frontier cyber capability as something you cannot simply call.

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط On September 15, 2026 Google released two speech-to-speech models: Gemini 3.8 Live (gemini-3.8-live) and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking). Both are generally available today in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Google's launch post is mostly benchmarks and demos. If you are building a voice agent, the details that matter are in the developer docs: tools now run asynchronously by default, one config field now returns an error, and one feature is always on and billed while the model listens. This page collects those details in one place. What you'll learn Pick between the two models using the real API differences, not the marketing names Migrate a gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview agent without hitting the thinkingLevel, affective-dialog, and blocking-tool traps Design around the session walls: 15 min audio-only, 2 min audio+video, ~10 min per WebSocket connection Estimate what a voice session really costs, and why cost grows faster than minutes Ship a browser client without leaking an API key آخر تحقّق: 2026-09-15. Launched today. Model IDs, GA status and feature list come from the Gemini API changelog (September 15, 2026). Prices come from the Gemini API pricing page. Token limits and the migration list come from the gemini-3.8-live model page. Thinking, tool-scheduling and VAD details come from the Live API capabilities and tools guides. Session limits come from the session-management guide. Billing gotchas come from the Live API best-practices guide. Benchmarks and consumer availability come from Google's launch post. One discrepancy: the launch post says the models detect and switch between 97 languages mid-conversation, while the Live API overview still says live translation covers "70+ languages." Before quoting either number, check which feature it refers to. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

documents.t: Use gemini-3.8-live as the default for low-latency voice agents. Use gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking when the caller asks hard, multi-step questions and a short delay is acceptable. Both cost $3.00 / 1M audio input tokens (~$0.005/min) and $12.00 / 1M audio output tokens (~$0.018/min), plus $0.75 / $4.50 for text. Both have a 131,072-token input window and 65,536-token output limit, and both have a free tier in the Gemini API.

gemini-3.8-live gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking Google's positioning "Default option for most low-latency voice agent experiences" "High-reasoning audio-to-audio model supporting background reasoning during live audio interactions" Thinking Interleaved reasoning; thinkingLevel is not accepted thinkingLevel = low / medium / high (no minimal); includeThoughts: true for summaries Function calling Async by default (NON_BLOCKING); BLOCKING still available; scheduling INTERRUPT / WHEN_IDLE / SILENT Async only, with no blocking mode and no scheduling control Consumer surfaces Search Live Gemini Live app; Docs, Gmail, Keep for subscribers Headline numbers (Google) 2nd on Artificial Analysis' Speech Agent Arena 82.6 Speech-to-Speech Quality Index (1st); 68.6% τ-Voice; 35.1% τ-Voice-banking; 97.7% Big Bench Audio Look at the 35.1% on τ-Voice-banking, the number Google chose to publish. Even the top-ranked voice model completes only about a third of realistic banking tasks by voice. Treat that as the ceiling for unattended voice agents that handle money, and put confirmation gates on anything consequential (the same rule as in Full-duplex voice AI). Every audio output is watermarked with SynthID. If your product records or re-publishes model speech, AI-audio detectors can identify it.
documents.s: What shipped, and what Google claims

documents.t: Extended Thinking does not go silent while it thinks. Google says it "reasons and speaks simultaneously." It gives early verbal cues ("let me check that") and narrates progress while reasoning continues in the background. That changes how your client decides when the model is finished. On this model turnComplete: true does not mean the session is idle. Background reasoning can still be running. Check interaction_status instead (IN_PROGRESS vs IDLE) before you end a call, hand off to a human, or start the next scripted step. This is the same "fast talker, slow thinker" split OpenAI introduced with GPT-Live. The difference is that Google puts both roles in one model, where GPT-Live delegates the reasoning to a separate frontier model.
documents.s: 1. The "thinking" model narrates while it reasons

documents.t: Google's migration notes for gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview → gemini-3.8-live include four changes that alter what your code does: Remove thinkingLevel. 3.1 Flash Live defaulted to minimal. 3.8 Live does not accept the field, so a config copied from 3.1 must drop it. Tool calls are now asynchronous by default. On 3.1 Flash Live, "the model will not start responding until you've sent the tool response." On 3.8 Live the model keeps talking while your function runs. That is good for latency, but a tool that must finish first (an identity check, a payment) now needs behavior: BLOCKING set explicitly. The Extended Thinking model has no blocking mode, so those flows need a gate in your own code. Proactive audio is always on. The model can decide not to respond when speech isn't addressed to it. You cannot turn this off, and the best-practices guide notes that you are billed input tokens while it listens. Affective dialog is gone. If your agent relied on enableAffectiveDialog to adapt to the caller's tone, remove it and test the new default behavior. Two changes help you. send_client_content now works for the whole session, so you can inject text context (CRM data, a transcript of a transfer) mid-call. Turn coverage now defaults to TURN_INCLUDES_AUDIO_ACTIVITY_AND_ALL_VIDEO.
documents.s: 2. Upgrading from 3.1 Flash Live changes behavior, not just the model string

documents.t: Audio accumulates at roughly 25 tokens per second (about 1,500 per minute). That is where the per-minute prices come from: 1,500 × $3/1M ≈ $0.0045 in, and 1,500 × $12/1M = $0.018 out. The trap is that each turn re-processes the entire accumulated context, not only the new audio. The best-practices guide says so directly. Two smaller costs stack on top: enabling transcription bills text output on top of audio output, and proactive audio bills input tokens while the model listens. A rough illustration (our arithmetic, not a Google figure): take a 10-minute call with 20 turns. The context grows from 0 to about 15,000 tokens, so the average turn re-reads about 7,500 tokens of input. That is about 150,000 input tokens (~$0.45), compared with ~$0.045 if only new audio were counted. Longer calls cost more per minute, not just more in total. Context window compression, which you need anyway to get past the 15-minute wall, also limits this cost growth.
documents.s: 3. A voice session's cost grows faster than its length

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Know the three limits⌄ Without compression, audio-only sessions stop at 15 minutes and audio+video sessions at 2 minutes. Separately, each WebSocket connection lasts around 10 minutes. The 2-minute video limit catches most screen-share demos. ←PreviousNext→ 2Enable context window compression⌄ Set ContextWindowCompressionConfig with a sliding window and a token trigger threshold. This removes the session-length limit and also stops per-turn input cost from growing without bound. Choose the trigger deliberately: compression discards the oldest turns, so pin anything the agent must remember (policy, caller identity) in the system instruction or re-send it with send_client_content. ←PreviousNext→ 3Enable session resumption⌄ Configure SessionResumptionConfig and store the latest handle from each SessionResumptionUpdate. A handle stays valid for 2 hours after the session ends, so a dropped connection can resume with its state instead of starting a new call. ←PreviousNext→ 4Handle GoAway before the connection drops⌄ The server sends GoAway with a timeLeft field before it disconnects. Use that time to finish the current sentence and reconnect with the resumption handle, so the caller never hears a gap. ←PreviousNext→ 5Discard buffered audio on interruption⌄ When the server flags an interruption (barge-in), clear your client-side playback buffer immediately. Otherwise the caller hears the model finish a sentence it has already abandoned. ←PreviousNext→ 6Send small, correctly formatted chunks⌄ Input is raw 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz little-endian; output is 16-bit PCM at 24 kHz. Resample microphone input (usually 44.1 or 48 kHz) down to 16 kHz and send 20–40 ms chunks. Large buffers add latency no model can remove. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The session walls, and how to design around them

documents.t: Live sessions work best when the client connects directly to Google, because proxying real-time audio through your backend adds latency. The safe way to do this is an ephemeral token. Your server mints it, and the client uses it once. Defaults: the token expires 30 minutes after creation, it must be used to start a new session within 1 minute, and it allows 1 use. You can lock it with liveConnectConstraints to a specific model, response modality and resumption settings, so a stolen token cannot be used for anything else. Ephemeral tokens work only with the Live API and only on v1beta. System-instruction skeleton for gemini-3.8-live (async tools, always-on proactive audio) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are Ava, a voice assistant for Northwind Travel. You are SPEAKING, not writing. RESPOND IN ENGLISH. YOU MUST RESPOND UNMISTAKABLY IN ENGLISH. Style: - Short sentences, one idea each. Never read lists, markdown, or URLs aloud. - If speech is clearly not addressed to you (TV, side conversation), stay silent. Tools: - lookup_booking: invoke ONLY after the caller has given BOTH booking reference AND last name. - While a lookup is running, tell the caller you are checking. Do not guess the result. - change_booking: before invoking, read back the exact change and wait for a clear spoken "yes". Safety: - Repeat back every number, date, and name before acting on it. - If audio is unclear, say what you think you heard and ask. - Anything involving refunds or payment details: offer a human agent instead. The skeleton follows Google's own guidance for Live agents: state the output language explicitly in capitals, and give each tool a precise condition for when to call it. That second rule matters more with async tools, because the model talks while the tool runs and will fill the silence with a guess unless you tell it not to.
documents.s: Browser and mobile clients: never ship the API key

documents.t: vs Claude. Claude's voice features remain turn-based: voice mode in the Claude apps, push-to-talk in Claude Code. A common hybrid uses a Live model as the conversational front end and calls Claude as a tool for heavy reasoning or coding. Async function calling suits this pattern well, since the call can keep going while the tool runs. vs OpenAI. GPT-Live is a speech-native, full-duplex ChatGPT product. For developers, OpenAI's offering is gpt-realtime on the Realtime API (see Full-duplex voice AI for the landscape). Early community reports (Hacker News launch thread, unverified). Commenters praised latency, voice quality, accent handling and live translation. Others said Extended Thinking reasoned inconsistently and that the model "invents additional requirements" in agentic flows. These are anecdotes, not measurements, but they match the 35.1% banking score: test your own task end to end before trusting it. Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways Two GA models, one price: gemini-3.8-live is the low-latency default; gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking reasons in the background while it keeps speaking. Migrating from 3.1 Flash Live changes behavior: remove thinkingLevel, mark must-finish tools BLOCKING, expect always-on proactive audio (billed while listening), and drop affective dialog. Plan for the limits up front: 15 min audio-only, 2 min audio+video, ~10 min per connection. Compression, resumption handles and GoAway handling are required for production. Cost grows faster than call length because every turn re-reads the whole context. Compression is both the session-length fix and the cost fix. Even Google's best score on voice banking tasks is 35.1%. Keep spoken confirmation gates on anything that moves money or data.

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط Google opened the Gemini 4 generation on September 30, 2026 with a single model, Argon, and a number nobody else has: a 1 million token output limit, up from the previous 64K. Not the context window — that stayed at 1M. The output ceiling went up 16x. It landed at the top of Hacker News and stayed there. It also landed in a strange place commercially: Google's own post says Argon "leads or ties for the highest score in more categories than GPT-6 Astra or Claude Opus 5.5," while the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index published the same week puts Argon at 53 against Claude Opus 5.5's 58. Both statements are accurate. They measure different things, and the gap between them is the most useful thing on this page. This lesson is for a Claude user deciding whether Argon changes anything about their routing. It covers what the 1M output limit actually buys, how to read two contradictory benchmark stories, the per-task economics that the "40% cheaper" headlines invert, and why your access request will probably be declined. What you'll learn Separate the 1M output limit from the 1M context window — they are different ceilings and only one of them moved Reconcile Google's '13 of 18 categories' claim with the independent index that places Argon 5 points below Claude Opus 5.5 Price a task properly: why 62K output tokens against Astra's 27K means Argon's advantage is its rate card, not its efficiency Read the 15% hallucination rate for what it is — an abstention behaviour, not a knowledge win Understand what the Fairwind Program gates, what it requires of your org, and why Argon is effectively uncallable for most readers آخر تحقّق: 2026-10-01. Launch date, the "1M tokens, up from the previous 64K" output figure, introductory and standard pricing, the internal use-case numbers (quantum 40%, 300+ TiB, Fuchsia Zircon 800K lines, libgav1 32K lines / 2.7x) and the Wiz partnership come from Google's launch post. Fairwind eligibility and the access terms come from the Fairwind Program page; the cyber-specific benchmarks from DeepMind's Gemini cyber page. The Intelligence Index scores, 62K-vs-27K output tokens per task, AA-Omniscience hallucination rates and per-task costs are Artificial Analysis' figures as reported by The Decoder and Trending Topics. The 18-benchmark comparison table is Google's own evaluation report as reproduced by VentureBeat. Two discrepancies, both unresolved and both load-bearing. (1) Artificial Analysis' index is quoted as 53 by The Decoder and as 52.6 by Trending Topics, and Opus 5.5 as 58 and 57.6 respectively — the same numbers rounded or not. We use the unrounded pair where precision matters. (2) Google's framing and the independent index disagree on whether Argon leads the frontier; we present both rather than pick. No API model ID has been published — Google's docs do not yet list an Argon identifier, so anyone showing you one is guessing. Pricing is introductory and explicitly scheduled to double; re-check before you budget. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
documents.s: Gemini 4 Argon: The Field Guide for Claude Users (Sep 30, 2026)

documents.t: Gemini 4 Argon is Google's new frontier model, 1M-token input context and a 1M-token output limit (up from 64K), priced at an introductory $2 in / $10 out per 1M tokens with cached input at 95% off, rising to $4 / $20 after the introductory period. It is not generally available: it is rolling out to vetted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, then to paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers. On Google's own 18-benchmark set it leads or ties in 13 categories; on the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 53, tying GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 and sitting five points below Claude Opus 5.5.

Almost every summary of this launch says "1 million tokens" and leaves the reader to assume a context window. The context window did not change. Gemini has been at 1M input tokens since the 3.x line — Gemini 3.8 Flash has the same 1M window and a 64K output cap. What moved is the output ceiling, from 64K to 1M. These are separate limits and they fail in separate ways: Limit What it governs Gemini 3.8 Flash Gemini 4 Argon Input context How much you can send — files, transcripts, repo 1M 1M Max output How much the model can emit in one response, including reasoning tokens 64K 1M The practical consequence is about where a long task breaks. With a 64K output cap, a genuinely long-horizon job — refactor this subsystem, draft this filing, triage this codebase — has to be chunked by you, and every chunk boundary is a place where the model loses its own working state. Google's pitch is that Argon can hold a single uninterrupted chain of reasoning and execution across the whole job instead. Three things to keep in mind before you treat that as free: Reasoning tokens come out of the same budget. On Gemini, thinking tokens are output tokens. A 1M output allowance is not 1M tokens of deliverable; it is 1M tokens of thinking plus deliverable. Output is the expensive side. At introductory pricing, output costs 5x input ($10 vs $2). A response that actually used the full million output tokens would cost $10 on its own, and $20 once standard pricing lands. Nothing obliges the model to use it. A raised ceiling changes what is possible, not what is typical. Argon averages 62K output tokens per Intelligence Index task — around 6% of its ceiling.
documents.s: The number that is not what it looks like

documents.t: This is the part worth slowing down for, because the same pattern will repeat at every launch for the rest of the year. Story one — Google's evaluation report. Across 18 disclosed benchmarks, Argon leads or ties in 13 (12 outright leads, 1 tie): Benchmark Argon GPT-6 Astra Claude Opus 5.5 Harvey Legal Agent 19.6% 5.4% 3.8% GraphWalks 84.2% 71.8% 66.8% Vals Finance Agent v2 65.4% 53.5% 58.6% AutomationBench 51.3% 41.4% 42.5% LVBench (long video) 91.7% 87.5% 83.7% DeepSWE v1.1 77.9% 74.1% 74.2% CWE-bench v1 68% 68% (tie) 67% Gray Swan IPI (attack success — lower is better) 0.7% 8.5% 1.0% FrontierSWE v2 55.0% 65.5% — Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 57.6% 68.1% — Terminal-bench 4.0 57.4% — 66.4% PostTrainBench 45.3% — 49.3% Story two — Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, an independent aggregate run the same week: Model Intelligence Index Claude Opus 5.5 58 (57.6) Claude Sonnet 5.5 56 Gemini 4 Argon (High) 53 (52.6) GPT-6 Astra (max) 53 Claude Fable 5.1 53 GPT-6.1 Sol (max) 52 Argon ranks #8 of 224 models on that index — excellent, and five points behind Anthropic's flagship. Neither source is lying. They diverge for reasons you can name: Benchmark selection is a choice. Google picked 18 benchmarks that include three domain-agent evals (legal, finance, automation) where Argon's margins are enormous. An aggregate index weights a different basket. Change the basket, change the winner. The losses cluster. Argon's four clear losses — FrontierSWE v2, Terminal-Bench Science, Terminal-bench 4.0, PostTrainBench — are all interactive, multi-turn, tool-driven agent work. Its wins cluster in single-shot domain reasoning and long-context retrieval. That is a shape, not noise, and it maps cleanly onto routing decisions. Absolute numbers matter more than ratios. Harvey Legal Agent is the launch's most quoted row: 19.6% against 5.4%, a 3.6x lead. It is also a score of 19.6% — Argon fails roughly four out of five tasks on that benchmark. "Best available" and "good enough to deploy unsupervised" are different claims. Vendor benchmarks are not production behaviour. Trending Topics cites Bloomberg reporting that, per Google employees, the model performs worse in practical coding use than its scores suggest. Treat that as a single unverified report — but it is the kind of gap the is the model nerfed? protocol exists to measure. Pro tip When a launch post says 'leads or ties in N of M categories,' the load-bearing question is who chose M. Go find an aggregate index you did not have to be invited into, and compare the two baskets before you re-route anything.

Several outlets led with Argon being around 40% cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. The rate card supports that. Per-task cost tells a more interesting story, because Argon is a heavy token spender. Artificial Analysis measured average output per Intelligence Index task: Gemini 4 Argon: ~62,000 output tokens GPT-6 Astra: ~27,000 output tokens Argon emits roughly 2.3x more tokens to reach the same index score. Its cheaper bill is a pricing artefact, not an efficiency win. The measured cost per task: Model Cost per Intelligence Index task Index score GPT-6.1 Sol (max) $0.74 52 Gemini 4 Argon (intro pricing) $1.99 53 GPT-6 Astra (max) $3.26 53 Gemini 4 Argon (standard pricing) $3.98 53 Claude Opus 5.5 (max) $5.98 58 Read that table twice. Three separate conclusions fall out of it: Argon's advantage over Astra is scheduled to expire. At $2/$10 it costs $1.99 per task against Astra's $3.26 — a 39% saving. When pricing doubles to $4/$20, it costs $3.98, which is more than Astra. The entire cost argument lives inside the introductory window, and Google has not said how long that window is. GPT-6.1 Sol is the actual value pick on this table. One index point below Argon at 37% of Argon's intro cost and 19% of Opus 5.5's. If your work is not in Argon's strong domains, the cheap tier is where the ratio lives — the same lesson as every other month. Opus 5.5 costs 3x Argon's intro price for 5 more points. Whether that is worth it is entirely workload-dependent, which is the honest answer and also the reason choosing a model is a framework rather than a leaderboard. Measure tokens-per-task yourself before trusting any per-task cost claim CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ For the same 20 representative tasks from my own workload, I want to compare two models on cost, not on benchmark score. For each model, log per task: - input tokens, output tokens (split reasoning vs final answer if the API reports it) - wall-clock latency - a 0-5 quality score I assign blind, without knowing which model produced it Then compute, per model: - mean output tokens per task - mean cost per task at CURRENT list price - mean cost per task at the post-introductory price, if one is announced - cost per quality point Flag any model whose cost advantage disappears at post-introductory pricing. Do not quote vendor benchmark scores back to me — I only want my own 20 tasks.
documents.s: The economics are the opposite of the headline

documents.t: On AA-Omniscience, the component of the index that measures whether a model asserts false things, Argon posts a 15% hallucination rate against 51% for GPT-6 Astra and 54% for GPT-6.1 Sol. That is not an incremental improvement; it is a different regime, and it is the most under-reported number in the launch. The mechanism matters. Artificial Analysis' characterisation is that Argon is far more likely to admit it does not know than to produce a confident wrong answer. So the win is in calibration and abstention, not in knowing more. Practical consequences: For retrieval, research and compliance work this is the headline feature, well ahead of any coding number. A model that says "not in the provided documents" is worth more than one that scores two points higher and invents a citation. It will read as less helpful in casual use. A model tuned to abstain refuses to guess, and users experience refusal-to-guess as hedging. Expect "it keeps saying it doesn't know" complaints from exactly the same capability that makes it trustworthy. It does not transfer to your prompts automatically. Abstention is a trained disposition interacting with your instructions. Tell a well-calibrated model "always give a definitive answer" and you have spent the advantage.

This is where most readers' interest ends in practice. Argon is not a public endpoint. It is gated behind the Fairwind Program, the same mechanism Google introduced for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber — but this time it gates the flagship, not a cyber-specific SKU. Fairwind prioritises governments and national cyber authorities, critical-infrastructure operators (healthcare, telecoms, energy, finance) and core technology platforms, and vets applicants for "a proven track record of ethical operations and research." Accepted organisations must agree to: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1User-level authentication with phishing-resistant MFA⌄ Not an org-level API key. Each human using Argon must be individually authenticated behind phishing-resistant MFA, plus applicable access controls. That rules out the usual pattern of one service credential shared by a team or embedded in a deployment. ←PreviousNext→ 2Restrict access to specific internal teams⌄ Only internal cybersecurity, incident response or penetration testing teams may be granted access. Not the platform team, not the product org, not a general-purpose internal assistant. ←PreviousNext→ 3Track employee access and use⌄ The org must maintain records of who accessed Argon and what for. Plan for an audit trail as a deliverable, not an afterthought. ←PreviousNext→ 4No sharing, redistribution or resale⌄ You cannot wrap Argon in a product and sell access, or pass it to a subsidiary or client. This is why no gateway or proxy legitimately offers it — see our note on gray-market AI proxies. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stay inside the dual-use boundary⌄ Authorized threat simulation, reverse engineering and malware analysis for defensive and academic research only. Malware creation and offensive use are prohibited. ←PreviousNext→ 6Then wait for the general rollout⌄ Google says paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers come first after Fairwind, then developers, enterprises and consumers 'as soon as possible.' No date has been given. ←PreviousNext→ For trusted defenders, Fairwind can pair Argon with CodeMender, Google's code-security agent that automates vulnerability fixes, and grants a build of Argon without the cyber guardrails that the eventual public model will carry. The cyber case is strong on its own numbers: real-world vulnerability discovery at 85.8% (against 71.0% for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber), the Wiz penetration-test benchmark at 70.9% (from 58.2%), CWE-bench v1 at 68%, and the best measured prompt-injection resistance of any frontier model — 0.7% attack success at k=15 on Gray Swan's indirect prompt-injection suite, against 1.0% for Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable, and 8.5% for GPT-6 Astra. That last number deserves its own sentence. An 8.5% success rate means roughly one in twelve indirect injection attempts lands; 0.7% means about one in 143. If you build agents that read untrusted web content, that is a twelve-fold difference in exposure — and it is measured at k=15, meaning fifteen attempts per target, not one. Worth reading alongside prompt injection and coding agents under attack. Watch out Because Fairwind forbids sharing, redistribution and resale, any gateway, proxy or 'unlocked Argon' reseller claiming to offer it is either misrepresenting a different model or violating the program terms. Treat an Argon endpoint you did not get from Google as untrustworthy by default.

The launch post's internal case studies are more informative than its benchmark table, because they describe long-horizon work with verifiable outcomes: Quantum algorithm optimisation — beat the published baseline for spacetime resource cost by 40%. Fleet memory profiling — found optimisations freeing over 300 TiB, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB total once applied. C/C++ to Rust migration — including 800K+ lines of the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. libgav1 video decoder — replaced 32K lines of hand-written SIMD, producing code 2.7x faster than the Rust port while emitting bit-identical output. The libgav1 result is the most instructive one on the list. "Bit-identical output" is the detail that makes it credible: there was a mechanical oracle for correctness, so the model's work could be verified rather than reviewed. That is the shape of task where a 1M output budget genuinely pays — large, mechanical, and checkable by a machine. It is also the shape of task most teams do not have, which is worth being honest about before extrapolating from these numbers to your own backlog.
documents.s: What Google says it did with it internally

documents.t: Short answer for most readers: no, because you cannot call it. When it opens up, here is the honest split based on where the benchmarks cluster. Work Where it should go Why Interactive coding agents, terminal work, computer use Claude (Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5) Argon's four clear losses are all in this family — Terminal-bench 4.0 57.4 vs 66.4, FrontierSWE v2 55.0 vs Astra's 65.5 Legal and financial document reasoning Argon, with review Harvey 19.6% vs 3.8–5.4%, Vals Finance 65.4% — but 19.6% absolute means supervision, not automation Long-video and long-context retrieval Argon LVBench 91.7%, GraphWalks 84.2% Research where a wrong citation is worse than no answer Argon 15% hallucination rate against 51–54% Defensive security, autonomous patching Argon via Fairwind, if you qualify 85.8% vuln discovery, CWE-bench 68%, lowest injection susceptibility High-volume everyday work GPT-6.1 Sol or a Flash/Sonnet tier $0.74 per task for one index point less than Argon Anything you are budgeting past the intro window Re-price it first $2/$10 becomes $4/$20; cost per task goes $1.99 to $3.98 Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways The 1M is the OUTPUT limit (up from 64K), not the context window, which stayed at 1M. Reasoning tokens spend that budget, and output costs 5x input. Google's '13 of 18 categories' and Artificial Analysis' 53-vs-58 are both true about different baskets. Argon's losses cluster in interactive multi-turn agent work; its wins cluster in single-shot domain reasoning and long-context retrieval. Argon burns ~62K output tokens per task against Astra's ~27K. The cheaper bill is the rate card, not efficiency — and at standard pricing cost per task goes $1.99 to $3.98, above Astra's $3.26. The 15% hallucination rate against 51–54% is the most under-reported number here, and it comes from abstention. It is the strongest argument for routing research and compliance work to Argon, and the first thing a 'always answer definitively' instruction destroys. You almost certainly cannot call it: Fairwind gates it to internal cyber/IR/pentest teams with per-user phishing-resistant MFA and no redistribution. No API model ID has been published. Any third-party 'Argon' endpoint is suspect.
