نسخ بصيغة Markdown متقدّم What you'll learn Do the arithmetic the headlines skipped: the redaction cost 9.5 points, and the generation it shipped in had added 47.7 — so roughly four-fifths of the model's exploitation ability came from being a better general coding model Understand the mechanism that makes targeted data removal weak: Moonshot's own explanation is that long-horizon debugging skill generalises to exploitation, which means the capability was never localised in the data they removed See that the redaction moved Kimi down exactly one rung — past an open-weight competitor that nobody redacted at all Know the three thresholds in China's Announcement No. 48 that put a model under export control, and that a parameter count alone is one of them Spot the clock the exemptions create: already-public weights are exempt, so the rule rewards publishing sooner rather than later Recognise the verification asymmetry — xdev-bench-hard is internal and unpublished, so neither the 90.5% nor the 81.0% can be reproduced by anyone outside the lab Ask the one question nobody has answered, and the only one that decides whether a redaction is durable: does fine-tuning put it back? Apply an eight-point checklist to the next open-weight release that claims a safety reduction, before you build a threat model on the claim On October 23–24, 2026 Moonshot AI shipped Kimi K3.1 Pro and did something no frontier open-weight lab had done before: it published the price, in benchmark points, of deliberately making its own model worse at one thing. Before the open-weight release, Moonshot identified and removed cyber-related data from two training stages — the mid-training corpus and the reinforcement-learning environments — while keeping the general coding tasks the model needs to be useful. Then it reported what that cost on xdev-bench-hard, its in-house set of expert-curated vulnerability-discovery and exploitation tasks built from real source code: Model / checkpoint xdev-bench-hard (pass@3) K3.1 Pro checkpoint without the risk-reduction measures 90.5% Kimi K3.1 Pro as released 81.0% DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 85.7% GLM-5.3 57.1% Kimi K3 (the previous generation) 33.3% Read that table twice, because almost every write-up of it stopped at the first two rows. Three things in it are worth a page. The redaction bought 9.5 points. The generation it shipped in had bought 47.7. K3 solved 33.3% of these tasks; the unrestricted K3.1 Pro checkpoint solved 90.5%. Removing the cyber data undid about 17% of that gain and left the other 83% in place. Whatever makes K3.1 Pro good at finding and exploiting bugs, it mostly is not the data Moonshot took out. It did not change the ranking in the way the framing implies. At 81.0% the released model sits above GLM-5.3 and below DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 85.7% — an open-weight model whose publisher did no such filtering. If your threat model is "what can an adversary download", the redaction moved Kimi down exactly one rung, past a model nobody redacted. The number exists because of a rule, not a leaderboard. On 16 October 2026 — a week before the launch — China's commerce and science ministries put a revised export-control catalogue into effect, and it reaches models of exactly this size. The 81.0% is a disclosure produced for a compliance conversation. Moonshot's stated goal is the honest version of this: they aim not to release open weights that extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability, on the reasoning that diffusing capability gradually across open systems makes software more secure overall. That is a defensible position. It is also a relative goal, and the table is what a relative goal looks like when someone publishes the measurement. آخر تحقّق: 2026-10-26. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. المصادر: Primary: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro tech blog (kimi.ai/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro) for the two-stage data removal, the xdev-bench-hard pass@3 figures for K3.1 Pro (81.0%), the unrestricted checkpoint (90.5%), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (85.7%), GLM-5.3 (57.1%) and K3 (33.3%), the 'absolute frontier of cyber capability' rationale, the 1M context window, the Kimi Hallu Bench Hard figures (8.3% vs 23.4%) and the 4 November 2026 open-weight date. Architecture (2.8T total / 104B active, 16 of 896 experts) and API pricing are from secondary technical coverage, not the blog section fetched here — treat them as reported. China's Announcement No. 48: effective 16 October 2026, 23 AI technology areas, the 10^26 FLOPs / 2T-parameter / global-top-ten thresholds, the autonomous-malware total ban, the vulnerability-tooling restriction, and the API / public-domain / open-source exemptions are from reporting on the draft catalogue (the-decoder, TechTimes, Sheppard Mullin); the comment period closing 15 November 2026 and the naming of Kimi K3 (2.8T) and Qwen3.8-Max (2.4T) as above-threshold examples are from that reporting, not from a translation of the text itself. The 'GPT-5.6 Sol at 100%' comparison circulating in coverage is from implicator.ai and did not appear in the blog section retrieved here — do not cite it as Moonshot's figure. Everything about whether fine-tuning restores the removed capability is unresolved: no source consulted makes a claim either way. Benchmark positions and weight availability will move; the arithmetic in the first table is the durable part.
documents.s: Capability Redaction: What Kimi K3.1 Pro's Cyber Cut Actually Bought

documents.t: The most useful sentence Moonshot published is not about the data. It is the observation that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalise to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. That is a statement about where the capability lives, and it explains the 9.5 points. Finding an exploitable bug in unfamiliar source and chaining a working exploit is, mechanically, the same loop as debugging: read code you did not write, build a model of its invariants, hypothesise a violation, test it, keep state across many steps, try again. A lab can delete a corpus of exploit write-ups. It cannot delete "is good at reasoning about unfamiliar code over long horizons" without deleting the product. This is why the independent criticism lands. The sharpest version, from the analyst outlet Extrapolator, is that the cyber mitigation is the release's most uncertain claim, because the boundary of what counts as "cyber-related" is fuzzy by definition — the mitigation works as a filtering heuristic, not a principled capability boundary. What you'll learn Data filtering removes examples. It does not remove the general ability those examples happened to exercise. Expect redaction to be most effective against capabilities that need specific knowledge (a protocol, a toolchain, a named technique) and weakest against capabilities that are a general skill pointed at a target. Offensive security is mostly the second kind.
documents.s: Why targeted removal is weak, in the lab's own words

documents.t: xdev-bench-hard is Moonshot's own benchmark, and it has not been published. Neither has the methodology in full, nor any evidence about whether the removed capability can be restored. That produces an unusual situation. The claim "we reduced cyber capability by 9.5 points" is: falsifiable in principle — once the weights are public, anyone can measure exploit success on their benchmark; unfalsifiable as stated — nobody outside the lab can run xdev-bench-hard, so the specific comparison between the released model and the withheld checkpoint cannot be checked by anyone, ever, because the unrestricted checkpoint is not being shipped. Both halves matter. The second means the headline number is a vendor claim in the strict sense — the only one of the five rows in that table that nobody else can reproduce is the one the whole story rests on. The first means the direction of the claim is checkable from 4 November onward, and will be, by people with their own harnesses. If you are tempted to treat a published safety delta as a measurement, apply the same discipline you would to any vendor benchmark — how to read an AI benchmark without getting fooled is the general version of this, and the specific trap here is the withheld-comparison arm.

China's revised export catalogue took effect 16 October 2026 (circulated as Announcement No. 48), proposed by the commerce and science ministries, covering 23 artificial-intelligence technology areas across large models, agents, compute clusters and data processing. Reporting on it describes a comment period open until 15 November 2026. What triggers control, and what the treatment is: Element Detail Thresholds (any one) 10^26 FLOPs of training compute · ≥ 2 trillion parameters · global top ten by public evaluations, task performance, safety or usage What is controlled at threshold Core model technology: weights, checkpoints, source code, architecture, training and inference methods Total ban AI tools that can autonomously write or modify malware to attack critical infrastructure, military targets or government agencies Restricted, not banned Tools for finding software vulnerabilities — new export limits, no outright prohibition Also restricted Models trained on China's "important data" and serving on it, with narrow carve-outs Exempt API calls, apps, websites and SaaS · lightweight on-device versions · already-public open-source releases · academic research and papers Fast-track Open-source publication gets automatic licensing on filing What you'll learn Sources disagree on the catalogue's legal status and this page does not resolve it. TechTimes describes Announcement No. 48 as having taken effect on 16 October 2026 with a comment period to 15 November, and analyses obligations as already applying to transactions entered into after that date. The Decoder describes the same 16 October publication as a draft revision that China 'plans' to make, open for comment. Both readings are consistent with a published measure that is simultaneously operative and open to revision, which is common in this process — but if the distinction matters to a decision you are making, read the measure itself or ask counsel rather than trusting either framing here. Now put Kimi next to it. Secondary technical coverage puts K3.1 Pro at 2.8 trillion total parameters with 104 billion active (16 of 896 experts per token) and a 1,048,576-token context window, built on K3. Reporting on the catalogue names Kimi K3 (2.8T) and Qwen3.8-Max (2.4T) as examples that clear the parameter threshold outright. So a 2.8T model is above the line on parameter count alone, before anyone argues about rankings — and the strictest clause in the catalogue is a total export ban keyed to autonomous malware authorship. Against that backdrop, publishing a measured reduction in exploitation success, with the general coding ability intact, is exactly the artefact a fast-track filing wants. What you'll learn This page does not claim Moonshot said the redaction was done for Announcement No. 48; the blog frames it as a safety choice about the open-weight frontier, and the timing is a week apart. Both can be true. What is not in dispute is that a model of this size is within the catalogue's scope, that the strictest clause concerns autonomous malware, and that vulnerability tooling is named as restricted rather than banned.

Two carve-outs, read together, point one way: Already-public weights are exempt. Once something is in the public domain it is, as one legal analysis put it, beyond the reach of a national export rule. Open-source publication gets automatic licensing on filing. The consequence for anyone planning a release is immediate: the cheapest moment to publish open weights is before the rule hardens, not after. Kimi K3.1 Pro's weights were due by 4 November 2026 — eleven days before the comment period on the catalogue closes. The same asymmetry runs the other way for anyone consuming these models. Weights you already have are not retroactively controlled, and API access is exempt entirely. Reporting on existing deployments is consistent: organisations that had already licensed or deployed covered Chinese models are largely unaffected, while new licensing agreements, overseas server deployments or changes of control entered into after 16 October can trigger registration or licensing. Watch out Once weights are downloaded they cannot be recalled. That is the whole design of an open-weight release and it is also why a redaction is a one-shot decision: there is no patch channel, no revocation, and no telemetry. Whatever capability ships on 4 November is the capability that exists forever, in whatever form the first fine-tuner leaves it in.

None of the material published about K3.1 Pro says whether fine-tuning restores the removed capability. That omission is the single most important thing about the release, for a simple reason: a filtering heuristic applied before release has no defence against a filtering-shaped hole being refilled after release. It is also the question the open-weight ecosystem already knows how to answer, and has answered unfavourably before. The abliteration pipeline — a small, cheap post-hoc modification that removes refusal behaviour from an open model — is a working, widely distributed demonstration that post-release edits can undo pre-release safety work. See backdoored open weights for how that supply chain operates and what it means for anything you pull off a model hub. The distinction worth holding onto: removing a refusal and restoring a capability are not the same engineering problem. Abliteration works on a behaviour the model still has; capability restoration requires the model to relearn something. Whether 9.5 points of exploit success is cheap to relearn with a modest fine-tune is an empirical question with, as of this writing, no published answer. What you'll learn A redaction is durable only if it is expensive to reverse. A published redaction with no published reversal cost is an unfinished claim. If you are evaluating one, treat 'can a cheap LoRA put this back?' as the load-bearing question — and note that the lab is the party best placed to answer it and the party with the least incentive to.

If you do defensive security research. This is the group with a real grievance, and the community reaction on r/LocalLLaMA was mostly this: a redacted open-weight model is a worse local tool for vulnerability research, and nothing about the carve-outs helps you. But look at what is still available before concluding you have lost the capability: API access is exempt from the catalogue, unredacted open-weight alternatives exist at comparable or higher scores (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 85.7% is the example in Moonshot's own table), and on closed models there are now sanctioned routes — Anthropic runs an expanded Cyber Verification Program that makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. What you have lost is the default local option from one vendor, not the capability class. If you deploy Chinese open weights. Your exposure is about transactions, not usage. Weights already in hand are exempt as public-domain material; API and SaaS consumption is exempt; new licensing deals, new overseas deployments and control changes after 16 October are where obligations attach. If you have any of the second kind in flight, that is a question for counsel, not for a docs page — and note there is a symmetric set of US-side restrictions on the same models, so "which side's rules apply" is rarely one question. If you write threat models. Update one number and leave the structure alone. The structure was already "a capable open-weight model is downloadable, and therefore the capability is in the world"; the update is that the best-documented open-weight exploit score just moved from 90.5% to 81.0% while a competitor sits at 85.7%. If your threat model's conclusion changes when the leading open model's exploit success moves 9.5 points, it was keyed too finely to begin with.
documents.s: What this actually changes, by role

documents.t: The release drew an unusually direct endorsement from Ethereum's co-founder, and his argument is worth separating from the crypto-press framing of it. Buterin supported leaving advanced offensive cyber capabilities out of training on the grounds that defenders need more time to harden software against increasingly capable attacks, and offered the general principle that discriminating against use cases is much less bad than discriminating against users. He paired it with a warning: if the first wave of AI cyber risk is mishandled, the likely response is models locked down tightly with access gated behind KYC review, pervasive surveillance, and stratification by identity credentials and nationality. Asked whether other labs will build the capability anyway, he answered that of course they will. That last concession is the honest shape of the whole debate. The case for capability redaction is not that it prevents anything; Moonshot's own table shows it does not, and the person endorsing it says plainly that someone else will build it. The case is that it buys time, and that a use-case restriction is a cheaper price than a user restriction. Whether you find that persuasive is a judgement call. What you should not do is read 81.0% as a safety guarantee — including, and especially, if you are the person writing the policy that cites it.
documents.s: Vitalik Buterin's framing, and why it is the useful one

documents.t: There will be more of these. Here is the checklist to run before a published safety reduction changes anything you do. Guided walkthrough1 of 8 1Find the baseline, not the delta⌄ A reduction is meaningless without the number it reduced from and the number the previous generation scored. Moonshot published all three, which is why the 9.5-versus-47.7 arithmetic is possible at all. If a release gives you only 'reduced by X%', you cannot tell a real mitigation from a rounding error on a capability jump. ←PreviousNext→ 2Check whether the benchmark is published⌄ An internal benchmark makes the comparison unreproducible in principle, because the withheld checkpoint is never shipped. Note it as a vendor claim and look for an independent harness measuring the same capability class. ←PreviousNext→ 3Rank the redacted model against unredacted peers⌄ The question a threat model asks is 'what is downloadable', not 'what did this vendor withhold'. If a competitor at the same tier scores higher with no filtering, the redaction changed one vendor's posture and not the frontier. ←PreviousNext→ 4Ask where the capability lives⌄ If the lab itself says general ability generalises to the restricted task — as Moonshot does — the redaction is a heuristic. Capabilities that need specific knowledge are redactable; capabilities that are a general skill aimed at a target are not. ←PreviousNext→ 5Look for a stated reversal cost⌄ Has anyone measured what a fine-tune costs to restore it? If nobody has, the durability of the mitigation is unknown, and the honest summary is 'reduced at release, unknown thereafter'. ←PreviousNext→ 6Separate the regulatory artefact from the safety argument⌄ A number published in the same month as a rule that covers the model is doing two jobs. Both can be sincere. Read the thresholds yourself — parameter count, training FLOPs, ranking — and check which one the model crosses. ←PreviousNext→ 7Read the licence and the model card when the weights land, not the blog⌄ Pre-release blog posts describe intentions. The licence describes what you may do, and the card describes what shipped. For K3.1 Pro the licence terms, hardware requirements and quantisation formats were all still unpublished at announcement. ←PreviousNext→ 8Record the claim with its date⌄ Published safety deltas age badly: a new checkpoint, a community fine-tune or an independent eval can invalidate one within weeks. Whatever you write down, write down when it was true. ←PreviousNext→ Record a redaction claim in a form that survives contact with the next release CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Summarise this open-weight release as a capability-redaction record. Use only what the sources support and mark anything missing as UNPUBLISHED — do not estimate it. Fields: model, publisher, announce_date, weights_date, params_total, params_active redaction: what data, which training stages, stated rationale benchmark: name, is_public (yes/no), metric (e.g. pass@3) score_redacted, score_unredacted_checkpoint, score_previous_generation peer_scores: same benchmark, same tier, no redaction derived: points_removed_by_redaction derived: points_added_by_the_generation (previous_gen -> unredacted) derived: share_of_gain_undone = points_removed / points_added reversal_cost: any published evidence that fine-tuning restores it licence, model_card_url, independent_eval_urls verified_on: <date> Then answer one question in two sentences: does the redaction change what an adversary can download today, or only what this publisher ships? Check what a model hub actually hands you, before the weights matter CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Resolve the repo and read its metadata — no download, public API. REPO="moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro" # confirm the real id from the announcement curl -sf "https://huggingface.co/api/models/$REPO" \ | python3 -m json.tool \ || echo "404 — that id does not exist; find the canonical one first" # The file list arrives in the same response, under "siblings". # Three files answer 'what may I do, and what actually shipped': # LICENSE — terms were unpublished at announcement # README.md — the model card # config.json — architecture as shipped, not as blogged curl -sf "https://huggingface.co/api/models/$REPO" \ | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d.get('license')); [print(s['rfilename']) for s in d.get('siblings',[])]" # Fetch one small file without cloning the weights: curl -sfL "https://huggingface.co/$REPO/raw/main/config.json" # Then check the thing this page is actually about: derivatives. # A redacted base with a popular 'uncensored' or 'restored' fine-tune # listed against it is the signal that the redaction did not hold. curl -sf "https://huggingface.co/api/models?search=k3.1&sort=downloads&limit=30" \ | python3 -c "import json,sys; [print(m['id']) for m in json.load(sys.stdin)]" Watch out Repository ids on model hubs are not predictable from a product name, and this one did not resolve at the time of writing. Take the canonical id from the publisher's own announcement before scripting against it, and do not read a 404 as evidence that the weights were not released.

The cyber figure got the coverage. The one that will affect more readers is on the other side of the ledger: on Kimi Hallu Bench Hard — again Moonshot's own internal stress test, with tools enabled — the claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% on K3 to 8.3% on K3.1 Pro, a 65% relative reduction, with Moonshot noting that stress-test rates do not reflect typical use. Both numbers come from the same lab, on the same day, on two unpublished internal benchmarks. One is a reduction the lab chose and wants credit for; the other is an improvement the lab wants credit for. Hold them to the same standard: the hallucination figure is exactly as reproducible by you as the exploit figure, which is to say not at all until someone runs an open harness on the released weights. Key takeaways Removing cyber data from two training stages cost 9.5 points of exploit success (90.5% to 81.0%) — against a 47.7-point gain the same generation had delivered over K3's 33.3%. Roughly four-fifths of the capability survived the redaction. The lab's own explanation is why: general coding and long-horizon debugging skill generalises to exploitation. You cannot delete that without deleting the product, so targeted filtering is a heuristic rather than a capability boundary. At 81.0% the released model still scores above GLM-5.3 (57.1%) and below DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (85.7%), an open-weight model with no such filtering. The redaction moved one vendor's posture, not the downloadable frontier. xdev-bench-hard is internal and unpublished, and the unrestricted checkpoint is never shipped — so the headline comparison is the one row in the table nobody outside Moonshot can ever reproduce. China's Announcement No. 48 (effective 16 October 2026, comment to 15 November) controls weights, checkpoints, source code and training methods at any one of three thresholds: 10^26 training FLOPs, 2T parameters, or a global top-ten ranking. A parameter count alone is enough, and Kimi K3 at 2.8T is cited as an example. The catalogue bans autonomous-malware tooling outright but merely restricts vulnerability-finding tools — and exempts API access, SaaS, on-device builds and anything already public, with automatic licensing on filing for open-source releases. Those exemptions create a publication race in one direction and a transaction-shaped exposure in the other: weights you already hold and API calls are exempt, while new licences and deployments after 16 October are not. Nobody has published whether fine-tuning restores the removed capability. Until someone does, the honest summary of any redaction is 'reduced at release, unknown thereafter' — and the abliteration supply chain is the existing proof that post-release edits beat pre-release safety work. Buterin's defence of the cut concedes the point that matters: other labs will build the capability anyway. The claim is that redaction buys defenders time and that restricting use cases beats restricting users — not that it prevents anything. Check yourself 0/6
documents.s: One more number from the same release, for calibration

documents.t: Moonshot AI — Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence: https://www.kimi.ai/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro — the primary source. The two-stage data removal, the xdev-bench-hard pass@3 table (81.0% / 90.5% / 85.7% / 57.1% / 33.3%), the "absolute frontier of cyber capability" rationale, the Kimi Hallu Bench Hard figures and the 4 November 2026 weight date all come from here. Implicator.ai — Kimi K3.1 Pro Hacking Cut Rests on Unpublished Moonshot Test: https://www.implicator.ai/kimi-k3-1-pro-hacking-cut-unpublished-test/ — the clearest account of what Moonshot did and did not publish, including that the benchmark is internal and that no claim is made about fine-tuning restoration. Also the source of the Extrapolator criticism quoted here and of a "GPT-5.6 Sol at 100%" comparison that this page attributes to them rather than to Moonshot. The Next Web — Moonshot releases Kimi K3.1 Pro and says it cut its hacking skills: https://thenextweb.com/news/moonshot-kimi-k3-1-pro-open-weight-cyber — independent reporting, including the explicit caveat that the benchmark figures are Moonshot's own and unverified, and the Terminal-Bench 4.0 context (65.7% against Claude Opus 5.5's 66.4%). DataStudios — Moonshot AI Kimi K3.1 Pro: open-weight, 1M context, cyber safeguards: https://www.datastudios.org/post/moonshot-ai-kimi-k3-1-pro-open-weight-1m-context-cyber-safeguards — the specification and pricing detail, and the note that licence terms, hardware requirements and quantisation formats were unpublished at announcement. The Decoder — China plans to tighten export controls on open-weight models and 23 key AI technologies: https://the-decoder.com/china-plans-to-tighten-export-controls-on-open-weight-models-and-23-key-ai-technologies/ — the catalogue's scope, the three thresholds, the autonomous-malware ban, the vulnerability-tooling restriction and the exemption list. TechTimes — China's New AI Export Controls Apply Now if You Licensed or Deployed Covered Chinese Models: https://www.techtimes.com/articles/329196/20261019/chinas-new-ai-export-controls-apply-now-if-you-licensed-deployed-covered-chinese-models.htm — the Announcement No. 48 label, the 15 November comment deadline, the naming of Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8-Max as above-threshold examples, and the transaction-shaped analysis of existing deployments. Sheppard Mullin — Choosing Between U.S. and Chinese AI Models: The Export Control Risks on Both Sides: https://www.sheppard.com/insights/blogs/us-vs-chinese-ai-models-export-control-risks — the reminder that the two regimes are symmetric, so "which rules apply" is rarely a single question. crypto.news — Vitalik Buterin backs Kimi AI hacking limits, warns of KYC risks: https://crypto.news/vitalik-buterin-kimi-ai-hacking-limits-kyc-risks/ — the "use cases rather than users" principle, the KYC-and-surveillance warning, and the concession that other labs will build the capability anyway. Anthropic — Cyber Verification Program: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-cyber-verification-program — the sanctioned route for verified security professionals, expanded on 6 October 2026 into three tiers (Defense Access, Red Team Access, Specialized Access) with reduced blocking classifiers and access to Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1. Check the program page for current eligibility; the terms are the part most likely to have moved. Hugging Face — Moonshot AI's organisation page: https://huggingface.co/moonshotai — where the weights land, and where to check the licence and model card rather than the blog.

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط What you'll learn Separate the three cookies in OpenAI's ad stack — two on the advertiser's domain, one on .openai.com — and understand why only the third one links you Follow the sync flow: a 60-second RS256 JWT minted by ChatGPT and POSTed cross-site to a collector that sets the join key Learn why a cookie banner's "reject marketing" can leave this running, and why the advertiser's own consent call cannot switch it off See what Automatic Advanced Matching scrapes from a page nobody configured it to read — and which fields OpenAI's own docs say travel unhashed Know exactly where the mechanism does not work (and why an iPhone is a different threat model from an Android) Check your own browser in five minutes, and harden your own pixel in two settings Most people's mental model of ChatGPT ads is a box: ads appear inside ChatGPT, personalized by what you said inside ChatGPT, and the box has a wall around it. Advertisers buy placements; they never see your conversations. That part is true, and OpenAI says it plainly. The part outside the box is the interesting part. OpenAI also ships a measurement pixel that advertisers install on their own websites, the way they install Meta's or Google's. Measurement pixels need a join key: some identifier that says the browser that saw the ad is the browser that reached checkout. In September 2026 an independent researcher traced how that join key gets created, and it turns out to be minted by ChatGPT itself, handed to an OpenAI ad collector, and then carried by your browser to every advertiser site running the pixel. The flow is not a leak or a bug. It's a designed ad-measurement pipeline — the same shape Meta and Google have run for a decade. What makes it worth a page is one specific design choice about consent classification, plus a default that flipped on in August 2026 and quietly turned a lot of advertiser websites into identity scrapers.
documents.s: ChatGPT's Ad Pixel and the __obi Cookie

documents.t: Read any of the coverage and you will see __obi, __obref and __oppref used almost interchangeably. They are three different things with three different privacy profiles, and conflating them is how people end up either overreacting or reassuring themselves with the wrong control. Cookie Set on Set by Lifetime What it is __oppref the advertiser's own domain the pixel SDK 30 days from each write Attribution ID captured from the landing-page URL. Ordinary click-tracking. __obref the advertiser's own domain the pixel SDK 365 days A random browser reference, scoped to that one advertiser. __obi .openai.com bzr.openai.com 365 days (Max-Age=31536000) The cross-site join key. HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=None. The first two are documented by OpenAI in its public advertiser docs. They are first-party to the advertiser and, on their own, do not link you across sites — the researcher's capture bears this out: 2,828 of 2,860 observed __obref values appeared under exactly one advertiser, which is what a per-site cookie should look like. __obi is the one that isn't per-site. It lives on .openai.com with SameSite=None, which is precisely the configuration that lets a browser attach it to requests made from someone else's page. Of 30 distinct __obi values the researcher observed, 12 appeared under more than one advertiser — one of them under ten. That is the cross-site graph, measured. ★ __obi is HttpOnly. No JavaScript on any page can read it, including the pixel's. That sounds protective and mostly isn't: the browser attaches it automatically to requests aimed at bzr.openai.com, so the pixel never needs to read it. HttpOnly stops page scripts from stealing the identifier; it does nothing to stop the identifier from being used.

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1ChatGPT mints a token⌄ The ChatGPT web client generates 16 random bytes and POSTs to /backend-api/bazaar/obi/sync-token on chatgpt.com — or /backend-anon/… when you are logged out. The response is an RS256 JWT with a 60-second expiry. ←PreviousNext→ 2The token names you⌄ Decoded claims include iss: "chatgpt-wadi", aud: "bzr.openai.com", purpose: "obi_sync", a 22-character obi identifier, a sub holding a 64-hex account identifier, a subject_type of either account_user or anonymous, and — the claim this whole page turns on — consent_decision: "analytics_allowed". ←PreviousNext→ 3The collector plants the cookie⌄ The JWT is POSTed cross-site to bzr.openai.com/v1/obi/sync ("bzr" is believed to be an internal name, Bazaar). The response carries Set-Cookie: __obi=…; Domain=.openai.com; HttpOnly; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; SameSite=none; Secure. ←PreviousNext→ 4Advertiser pages carry it back⌄ Any page running the pixel loads bzrcdn.openai.com/sdk/oaiq.min.js and POSTs conversion events to bzr.openai.com/v1/sdk/events. Because those requests target openai.com, the browser attaches __obi to them. The advertiser's page never touches the cookie; it just triggers the request. ←PreviousNext→ Of 932 sync tokens the researcher decoded, 736 carried subject_type: account_user and 196 were anonymous. So in roughly four out of five observed syncs, the identifier being planted was minted in the context of a logged-in ChatGPT account. The author is careful about what that does and does not prove, and you should be too: the join from __obi back to an account was inferred from the token design, not directly observed. What is observed is that ChatGPT mints an account-scoped token, a collector converts it into a long-lived cross-site cookie, and that cookie then shows up under multiple unrelated advertisers.

Here is the part that makes this different from "Meta has a pixel too." OpenAI's cookie policy lists __obi under analytics. The campaign-measurement cookies of Google, Meta, LinkedIn, TikTok, Reddit and Microsoft sit under marketing in the same interface. The JWT that triggers the sync carries consent_decision: "analytics_allowed" — not a marketing consent. Follow the consequence through a normal European cookie banner: You click "Reject marketing, allow analytics" — a choice a large fraction of privacy-conscious users make, and one many consent platforms present as the sensible middle. Analytics consent is granted, so the sync token issues. __obi gets planted on .openai.com for a year. Every advertiser pixel you subsequently hit receives it. You declined the category the behaviour belongs to, and the behaviour happened anyway, because it was filed under a different category. The researcher asked OpenAI about exactly this — why __obi is classified as analytics, and whether users refusing marketing consent still receive it — by mail to press@openai.com and privacy@openai.com on 2026-09-14. OpenAI Support acknowledged the inquiry and answered neither question. ★ The advertiser's consent switch cannot help you. OpenAI's docs give advertisers oaiq("consent", false), which "removes both cookies" — meaning __obref and __oppref, the two on the advertiser's own domain. It has no reach into .openai.com. A site that gates the pixel perfectly behind its CMP is gating the two cookies that were never the linkability problem. There is a separate, real control in ChatGPT itself: Settings → Data Controls → Marketing Privacy, reported as on by default for free accounts and off for paid ones. Treat its relationship to __obi as unresolved: the investigation did not test whether flipping it stops the sync, OpenAI did not answer when asked, and a setting labelled marketing governing a cookie filed as analytics is exactly the mismatch at issue. Turn it off — it is the right switch to reach for — but do not assume it is the one that stops the wire behaviour until someone captures traffic with it off. آخر تحقّق: 2026-09-21. Primary report at buchodi.com, cross-checked against OpenAI's own Developers documentation for the ads pixel. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
documents.s: The consent classification is the whole story

documents.t: A conversion pixel's problem is that click identifiers go missing — blocked, stripped, or lost across a redirect. The industry answer is advanced matching: send hashed identity alongside the event so the ad platform can join on that instead. Meta has shipped it for years. OpenAI's version has one twist worth knowing about. Automatic Advanced Matching (AAM) does not wait for the advertiser to pass anything. OpenAI's docs say the pixel "automatically detects supported customer information from your website." The researcher's capture shows four labelled collection sources: Label Source How it gets the value in Advertiser-supplied The site deliberately passes it fm Form fields Scraped from recognizable inputs on the page ht Page text Parsed out of rendered content js Tag manager Read from window.dataLayer, the Adobe data layer, or renamed GTM layers In the observed events, scraped identity outnumbered advertiser-supplied identity 685 to 255. The pixel was, most of the time, collecting things nobody asked it to collect. Hashed vs clear — straight from OpenAI's own docs. Email, phone, external ID, first name and last name are normalized and SHA-256'd in the browser. Country (ISO code), region, city and postal code are listed as clear fields. OpenAI's line "raw customer information is not sent to OpenAI through automatic advanced matching" is scoped to the identity set; geography is not in that set. The capture agrees: postal code was the most-harvested form field, 100 events across 28 sites, unhashed. There is a denylist — OpenAI excludes passwords, one-time codes, card numbers, SSNs, dates of birth, medical history, diagnosis and court-related fields. That is a real mitigation and worth crediting. It is also a denylist, which means it protects the categories someone thought of. Identity is not the only payload. The events also carry the URL path of the page that fired them — product pages, article URLs, checkout steps — with query-string search terms reported as stripped. For a retailer that means the specific items you looked at; for a publisher it means the specific articles you read. ★ The default flipped on 2026-08-17. AAM was already the default for newly created Web pixels; on that date OpenAI turned it on for existing pixels too, opt-out rather than opt-in. The researcher found AAM enabled on 638 of 881 pixels whose settings were visible. If you installed an OpenAI pixel in early 2026 and never touched it since, your site started scraping form fields in August without a deploy on your side.
documents.s: Automatic Advanced Matching: the pixel reads the page

documents.t: This is not a universal tracker, and the exceptions matter more than they usually do: Chrome for Android — the platform the researcher reproduced it on. Affected. Safari, and Chrome on iOS — not affected. Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention blocks the third-party cookie, and every iOS browser runs on WebKit, so "Chrome on iPhone" inherits the same block. An iPhone user and an Android user are genuinely in different threat models here. Desktop Chrome — untested in the published work. Unknown, not safe. Coverage is partial anyway. Only about 20% of observed ChatGPT sessions produced a sync token at all; the mobile web client serves ads without syncing. Whatever graph exists is sparse, not total. That last number cuts both ways. It means the identifier is far from universal — and it means "I checked once and saw nothing" is not evidence of absence.

Five minutes, no tooling beyond DevTools. Do this on Android Chrome if you want to see the mechanism at all. Look for the sync, then the cookie CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # 1. Open ChatGPT with DevTools → Network, filter: obi # Look for a POST to: # /backend-api/bazaar/obi/sync-token (logged in) # /backend-anon/bazaar/obi/sync-token (logged out) # then a cross-site POST to: # https://bzr.openai.com/v1/obi/sync # 2. Paste the JWT from the sync-token response into a local decoder. # You are looking for these claims: # iss: "chatgpt-wadi" aud: "bzr.openai.com" # purpose: "obi_sync" consent_decision: "analytics_allowed" # subject_type: "account_user" | "anonymous" # 3. Application → Cookies → https://chatgpt.com # Look for __obi on domain .openai.com, Max-Age 31536000, # HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=None. # 4. Now visit a retailer that runs the pixel and filter for: # bzrcdn.openai.com/sdk/oaiq.min.js # bzr.openai.com/v1/sdk/events # Check the Cookies tab of that events request: __obi riding along # is the cross-site join, observed on your own machine. Decode the JWT locally. Pasting a token that contains an account-scoped sub into a web-based decoder hands that identifier to a third party — a slightly absurd way to end a privacy investigation.

You are a data controller here in a way the pixel's install snippet did not make obvious. Two settings and one habit: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Decide about AAM deliberately⌄ Ads Manager → Tools → Conversions → Data Source → Edit pixel, then turn Automatic Advanced Matching off (or confirm you want it on). The setting is per-pixel — if you run several, you change several. Since 2026-08-17 the default is on, so inaction is a decision. ←PreviousNext→ 2Gate the pixel before it initializes, not after⌄ Verify your consent platform actually blocks the script from loading pre-consent rather than calling oaiq("consent", false) afterwards. And know the limit: that call removes __obref and __oppref, both on your domain. It cannot remove __obi from .openai.com. ←PreviousNext→ 3Audit what your own forms expose⌄ Load a checkout or signup page with DevTools open, submit test data, and read the event payload going to bzr.openai.com. Confirm which of your fields the fm and ht collectors picked up. Fields you never intended as ad signal — a postal code, a support-form free-text box — are the ones to look for. ←PreviousNext→ 4Update your privacy notice and records⌄ If AAM is on, your site transmits hashed customer identity and clear geography to OpenAI. That belongs in your privacy policy and your processing records whether or not your CMP is configured correctly. ←PreviousNext→ ★ Hashed is not anonymous. SHA-256 of an email address is a deterministic identifier: anyone holding the same email computes the same digest. That is the entire point — it is how the join works. Treat hashed identity as pseudonymous personal data in your compliance analysis, not as de-identified.

Turn off Settings → Data Controls → Marketing Privacy. Right switch to reach for; effect on __obi unconfirmed, as above. Use the cookie manager, not only the account setting — for logged-out browsing, the "Manage Cookies" / "Your Privacy Choices" footer link is the only surface you have. Send Global Privacy Control. OpenAI states it honours GPC as a legally valid opt-out signal. Firefox and Brave send it natively; there are extensions for Chrome. It is a machine-readable signal with regulatory weight behind it in California and several other jurisdictions. Browser choice is a real control here. Safari blocks the mechanism today. That is not an argument to switch browsers over one cookie — it is a reminder that third-party cookie policy is doing more work in your privacy posture than any toggle you will find in a settings screen.

Worth keeping straight, because the coverage blurs it: Established by capture: the endpoints, the cookie attributes, the JWT claims including consent_decision, the four collection sources, the field-level hashed/clear split (which OpenAI's own docs confirm), the counts — 936 pixels across 1,029 hostnames, 12 of 30 __obi values under multiple advertisers, 638 of 881 pixels with AAM on. Inferred, and labelled as such by the author: that __obi is joined back to a ChatGPT account server-side. The token design points that way; the join was not observed. Unanswered by OpenAI: why __obi is classified as analytics, and whether declining marketing consent still results in the sync. Untested: desktop Chrome, and whether the Marketing Privacy toggle stops the wire behaviour. Check yourself 0/5
documents.s: What is actually established, and what is not

documents.t: Buchodi — "ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector" — the primary investigation: endpoints, JWT claims, cookie attributes, collection-source labels, and the counts quoted throughout this page. Includes the author's own stated limitations. daily.dev — "ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector" — the aggregator entry for the story that reached the Hacker News front page on 2026-09-21. OpenAI Developers — Ads: Measurement Pixel — official docs for __obref / __oppref, the SHA-256 hashed field list, the clear geographic fields, and oaiq("consent", false). OpenAI Developers — Ads — the advertiser-facing product surface the pixel belongs to. OpenAI Help Center — Conversion Measurement — OpenAI's description of Automatic Advanced Matching and the per-pixel setting path. OpenAI Help Center — Ads in ChatGPT — the user-facing controls, including Settings → Data Controls → Marketing Privacy. Cybersecurity News — "ChatGPT Ad Tracking Cookie Follows Users Across Third-Party Advertiser Websites" — independent write-up with the cookie-attribute detail. What Your Coding Agent Actually Uploads — the same question one layer down: measuring egress instead of trusting a privacy toggle. Sign in with ChatGPT — the other place your OpenAI account identity leaves openai.com. نسخ بصيغة Markdown متقدّم What you'll learn Understand the two bypasses in Claude for Chrome — a missing event.isTrusted check and a URL-parameter that self-elevates the side panel See why Anthropic marking the tracker "Resolved" before June 9, then shipping eight more releases (v1.0.73 → v1.0.80) unchanged, is the real story here Learn the general defensive pattern: client-only allowlists are not a security boundary when another extension shares your origin Take three concrete mitigations you can apply in under two minutes right now On 7 July 2026, Anthropic released Claude for Chrome v1.0.80. Manifold Security tested it the same day and found their two May bug reports still reproducible byte-for-byte from v1.0.72. Any other extension on your browser with script access to claude.ai — a permission thousands of Chrome extensions request — can silently instruct Claude to open Gmail, read a message, and act on it. No approval dialog. No user gesture. آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-22. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. The story is not "an extension had a bug." Chrome extensions ship bugs constantly. The story is that a shipped agentic-browser product, given nine months of scrutiny and a public "ClaudeBleed" incident behind it, still enforces its permission model in a place an attacker fully controls — the client — and marks the tracking issue Resolved without the code changing.
Two independent bugs. Either one alone is enough to trigger every hardcoded task. Together, one gives you the trigger (fake click) and the other gives you silent execution (auto-elevate).
documents.s: The two flaws in one picture

documents.t: Every event a browser dispatches has an isTrusted boolean. Real user actions — a physical click, a keypress, a touch — arrive with isTrusted: true. Anything JavaScript synthesises via dispatchEvent(new MouseEvent(...)) arrives with isTrusted: false. It is the browser's only reliable user-vs-code signal, and it exists precisely so security-sensitive handlers can tell them apart. The Claude for Chrome content script listens for clicks on the element with id #claude-onboarding-button and, if the click matches one of nine allowlisted task IDs (usecase-gmail, usecase-gdocs, usecase-calendar, usecase-salesforce, plus DoorDash, Zillow and three onboarding challenges), forwards the matching prompt to Claude's side panel to execute. The handler never checks event.isTrusted. In the researchers' words: from the extension's point of view, a fake click and a real one are indistinguishable. That matters because of an easy-to-miss architectural point: any other Chrome extension you have installed with content_scripts matching https://claude.ai/* shares Claude's origin from Chrome's perspective, and can inject a script into the page. That permission is not exotic — password managers, note-clippers, translation tools, ad blockers, and countless "productivity" extensions request it as a matter of course. Once a script runs in that page, dispatching a synthetic click on #claude-onboarding-button is roughly six lines of code. Manifold's report calls out that exact size to make a point: the fix is one if statement, and the exploit is one dispatch call. The nine-prompt allowlist was Anthropic's earlier mitigation for ClaudeBleed — the idea being "even if a click is faked, only a fixed list of safe tasks can run." That model breaks the moment "run Gmail integration" is on the list. Reading and acting on Gmail is not a safe task. Pro tip The lesson isn't "add isTrusted" — it's the lesson underneath: an allowlist of "safe" agent tasks is only as safe as the least-safe task on it. Fine-grained per-integration user consent belongs on every one of those triggers, not just the untrusted freeform ones.

Chrome extension side panels have their own URL, and that URL's query string is readable inside the panel via window.location.search. Claude's side panel reads a skipPermissions parameter. If it equals "true", the panel initialises with permissionMode = "skip_all_permission_checks" — the same internal mode as when a user manually enables Act without asking. That is client-side, self-served privilege escalation. The panel is asking itself for permission and answering yes based on a value the panel itself received in its URL — which anything that can chrome.sidePanel.open({...}) or navigate the panel can supply. Manifold rates that scenario CVSS 9.6 Critical, because in that mode there is no approval box at all: the nine allowlisted prompts execute silently. The synthetic-click flaw alone (with the normal approval box still showing) rates 7.7 High, because a user could in principle notice the dialog before pressing enter. The right shape of the fix is not "sanitise the URL parameter." It is that transitions between permission modes should require an explicit, isTrusted user gesture on a real UI control after the panel has loaded — never a value the panel reads out of its own URL, its own storage, or a message channel any other extension can post on. That is the same architectural constraint browsers already apply to fullscreen, camera and clipboard permissions, and for the same reason.

The timeline is what makes this a governance story, not just a code story: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 121 May 2026 — Manifold reports both issues⌄ Two separate bug reports filed with Anthropic against v1.0.72. ←PreviousNext→ 222 May — acknowledged and closed⌄ Anthropic acknowledged both. Report #1 was closed as a duplicate of an existing tracker; report #2 dismissed as "informational" on the argument that the URL parameter is "only used by the extension itself" — which is exactly the assumption the bug violates. ←PreviousNext→ 3Before 9 June — internal tracker marked "Resolved"⌄ The umbrella "ClaudeBleed" issue was flipped to Resolved in Anthropic's internal tracking — apparently on the strength of the nine-prompt allowlist mitigation, not a fix for the two underlying bugs. ←PreviousNext→ 47 July — v1.0.80 ships, code byte-identical⌄ Eight releases (v1.0.73 → v1.0.80) went out between report and now. Researchers re-verified: the click handler and the panel init are unchanged from the version they originally tested. ←PreviousNext→ 514 July — public disclosure⌄ No CVE. No Anthropic advisory. Public blog post + Hacker News + industry press coverage. As of this page: still unpatched. ←PreviousNext→ Two failure modes worth internalising, because they are common outside this story: Mitigation collapse. A mitigation that changes an exploit's shape ("you now have to click one of nine buttons") gets treated as a fix. When the trigger for those buttons is itself forgeable, the mitigation adds no security — it only changes the attack recipe. "Resolved by design" drift. Bug #2 was closed on the theory that only the extension itself sets skipPermissions. That is a description of intent, not of the browser's actual enforcement. Anything with sidePanel access or a redirect through the panel URL can also set it. Both patterns show up in security-review anti-patterns lists for a reason. Watch for them in your own code.

The nine hardcoded task IDs, from Manifold's report: Category Task IDs Roughly what the prompt tells Claude to do Google usecase-gmail, usecase-gdocs, usecase-calendar Read Gmail (incl. an "unsubscribe from promo emails" flow that iterates inbox), read Google Docs comments, read Calendar availability and create meetings CRM / commerce usecase-salesforce, usecase-doordash, usecase-zillow Read Salesforce leads and convert them to opportunities; run through DoorDash / Zillow flows Onboarding three onboarding challenges Guided tour prompts Reach depends on which connectors the victim has enabled. If Gmail is connected, usecase-gmail reads Gmail. If Salesforce is connected, usecase-salesforce touches the CRM. The panel is doing what a user asked it to do — just not this user, and not now. Watch out "Act without asking" is not a special developer mode. It's a checkbox in Claude for Chrome settings. If it is on, flaw #1 alone triggers real Gmail / Docs / Calendar / Salesforce reads. If it is off, flaw #2 (?skipPermissions=true) can re-enable it silently for the panel's lifetime.
documents.s: What runs, and what data it can reach

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Turn off Act without asking⌄ Claude for Chrome settings → disable "Act without asking". Approval prompts are annoying, but they are the only user-visible signal that flaw #1 alone leaves you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Audit which extensions can touch claude.ai⌄ chrome://extensions → Details on each → Site access. Anything set to All sites or that lists claude.ai can inject a content script into the Claude page. Downgrade or remove ones you do not actively trust. Password managers and note-clippers are the two categories worth double-checking. ←PreviousNext→ 3Prune connectors you don't use⌄ In Claude → Settings → Connectors, disconnect Gmail / Docs / Calendar / Salesforce integrations you don't rely on. The nine hardcoded tasks are only dangerous against connectors that are actually connected. ←PreviousNext→ If you run agentic extensions for a whole team, add a fourth: runtime observation of what agents actually execute — not just what permissions they hold. Both flaws pass a permission audit and fail behaviour observation, because they cause the agent to do things the user never asked for. That gap is where Manifold's own recommendation lands, and it generalises well beyond this one product. Chrome extension audit prompt for Claude CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Here is my current chrome://extensions export (or a list I'll paste): {LIST}. For each extension: 1. Is its "site access" set to "All sites" or does it match claude.ai? Flag those. 2. From its Chrome Web Store description, what content_scripts permissions does it plausibly require? Is claude.ai a required domain for its stated function? 3. Rate each on a "trust to run a script inside my Claude tab" scale from 1 (dedicated password manager from a known vendor) to 5 (random productivity extension with <10k installs). 4. Give me a two-column recommendation: KEEP AS-IS / RESTRICT TO SPECIFIC SITES / REMOVE — with a one-line reason per row. Do not soften. If something looks sketchy, say sketchy.
documents.s: Three things to do now (two minutes)

documents.t: Zoom out from Claude for Chrome. The same shape shows up in a growing number of agentic products: A trusted UI (extension, desktop app, IDE plugin) exposes an agent that can take real actions on user data. To constrain risk, the vendor adds an allowlist of tasks/prompts/tools the agent may execute without approval. The trigger for entries on the allowlist stays inside the client — a click, a URL, a stored setting, a message on a channel other components share. Any other code in the same trust zone (same extension host, same origin, same IPC bus) can forge the trigger. The lesson each round teaches is the same. Cf. also docs/security/agentic-browsers-same-origin.mdx (agent reads-above-SOP), docs/security/coding-agents-under-attack.mdx (auto-approve is the new attack surface) and docs/security/prompt-injection.mdx (untrusted content becomes untrusted instructions). Every one of those is a case of the boundary is drawn where the attacker already stands. Two invariants worth writing on a sticky note: A permission check the attacker can call is not a permission check. If any of "any script on this page", "any URL parameter", "any storage value", or "any postMessage from unknown origin" can flip your agent from ask to act, that flip belongs behind an isTrusted gesture on a real DOM element you rendered. Allowlists are not a substitute for consent. If any single task on the list would surprise the user when executed unprompted (read my Gmail qualifies), the allowlist reduces attacker choice but not attacker impact.
documents.s: The wider pattern — client-only allowlists, agentic scope

documents.t: Check yourself 0/4 Key takeaways v1.0.80 of Claude for Chrome (7 Jul 2026) is still vulnerable to the two Manifold bugs first reported on v1.0.72 in May — synthetic-click bypass of the nine-prompt allowlist, and self-elevation via ?skipPermissions=true in the panel URL. Both bugs are client-only permission checks. "Resolved" in the tracker referred to a mitigation (the allowlist), not to the underlying enforcement gaps. Right now: turn off Act without asking, audit which other Chrome extensions can inject scripts into claude.ai, and disconnect connectors you don't use. General rule: a permission check any script on the page can call is not a permission check. Mode transitions must ride an isTrusted gesture on a real UI element, not a URL / storage / message value.

Manifold Security — ClaudeBleed Reopened: browser extensions can still push Claude for Chrome to read your Gmail (primary technical write-up; timeline, CVSS ratings, the byte-identical-code observation) The Hacker News — Researchers Say Claude for Chrome Flaw Lets Rogue Extensions Trigger Gmail Reads (industry coverage; Anthropic's public response) BleepingComputer — Claude Chrome extension flaw lets malicious extensions trigger AI actions (attack surface, permission requirements) TechRadar — The bypass is still six lines of JavaScript (context on why the fix is a single conditional) Related on AILmanac: Agentic Browsers Break the Same-Origin Policy, When Coding Agents Get Weaponized, Prompt Injection: the safety model you can't ignore OWASP — Top 10 for LLM Applications (LLM01 Prompt Injection & LLM06 Excessive Agency are the two categories these bugs map to)

نسخ بصيغة Markdown متوسط آخر تحقّق: 2026-09-21. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. المصادر: github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill (README; skills/security-audit/SKILL.md, RECONNAISSANCE.md, HUNTING.md, VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md, AI-AND-LLM.md, report-schema.json; 18.5k stars and +2,428 on GitHub Trending on Sep 21, 2026; MIT); Cloudflare blog 'Build your own vulnerability harness' (June 18, 2026, Grant Bourzikas); Hacker News item 49736466 (Sep 17, 2026, 211 points); github.com/vercel-labs/skills. Token figures are individual HN reports, not a benchmark. The skill is actively edited (14 commits on main at the time of writing): re-check phase names and file names against SKILL.md. What you'll learn Explain why 'ask Claude to find vulnerabilities' produces confident garbage, and what separation of powers between hunters and verifiers fixes Walk the six phases and name the artefact each one produces, from architecture.md to NEEDS-VALIDATION.md Read a findings.json correctly: what confirmed, needs_validation and rejected each require, and why only confirmed records get a severity Run the skill in Claude Code inside a sandbox that meets its rules, validate the outputs mechanically, and re-run for coverage Budget it: what the token bill looks like, the rule that makes the skill refuse to launch hunters, and the three ways to keep a run affordable Cloudflare open-sourced a single skill in mid-September 2026 and it became the fastest-growing repo on GitHub: cloudflare/security-audit-skill sat at 18.5k stars on September 21 after adding 2.4k in one day, and had already drawn a 211-point Hacker News thread on September 17. The reason it matters is not the star count. It is that this skill is the seed of the fleet-wide vulnerability harness Cloudflare described in June, the one that ran across 128 repositories and produced 7,245 actionable findings. The public skill is the single-repo version you can run today with Claude Code. It is worth being precise about what it is. There is no binary, no rules engine, no model of its own. It is a SKILL.md plus fourteen hunting guides and two zero-dependency Node validators. Everything it does, it does by making your agent spawn isolated sub-agents with narrow briefs and refusing to accept their output until a different agent has tried to break it.
documents.s: Cloudflare's security-audit Skill: Adversarial AI Security Audits with Claude Code (2026)

documents.t: Cloudflare's June write-up contains the sentence that explains the whole design: an unconstrained agent "will edit the source code so its own exploit works, then triumphantly report the bug it just created." And the companion rule: "If a Hunter is allowed to grade its own homework, it will confidently validate everything it outputs." That is the failure mode of every one-shot "audit my repo" prompt. The model that spent 80k tokens forming a theory is the last model you want judging that theory. The skill's answer is structural: Hunters cannot file findings. They return candidates and are forbidden from editing the target source, the architecture notes, the ledger, or the findings file. Verifiers cannot hunt. A fresh verifier receives one candidate, the architecture facts and the schema, and nothing else, not even another verifier's conclusion. Its job is to disprove. Nothing is retained unless deterministic code accepts it. The parent agent writes the shared files; validate-findings.cjs and validate-coverage-ledger.cjs reject anything that breaks the schema. Cloudflare's internal version goes further and uses a different model for validation than for discovery, on the theory that separate weights give an unbiased second opinion. The public skill does not enforce that, but nothing stops you from routing the verifier sub-agents to a different model.
documents.s: Why "find the vulnerabilities" fails on its own

documents.t: Phase Who runs Output 1. Reconnaissance 4 parallel research agents (stack and build; principals and auth; entry surfaces and sinks; what is offline-testable) that return facts only architecture.md (about 1,000 words) and a seeded coverage-ledger.json 2. Coverage-led hunting Waves of isolated hunters, one or more ledger units each; a coverage critic after every wave Candidates with proposed_verdict, unit dispositions, hardening notes, newly discovered gaps 3. Candidate validation One fresh verifier per unique candidate fingerprint A decision per candidate: confirmed, needs_validation or rejected 4. Structured output The parent only findings.json, sorted by fingerprint, schema-validated 5. Independent record verification One fresh verifier per confirmed or needs_validation record verified or replace; any material replacement gets a second fresh verifier 6. Target-neutral reporting The parent, after phase 5 passes REPORT.md, FINDINGS-DETAIL.md (medium and up only), NEEDS-VALIDATION.md Everything lands under ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>/, with per-agent agents/<id>/scratch/ and agents/<id>/artifacts/ directories. Only the parent writes the shared files. The coverage ledger is the mechanism most people miss. A unit is one material combination of entry surface, trust boundary, subsystem and attack class, with starting paths in the repo. Units move through planned, in_progress, blocked, covered or candidate, and each state has rules about which evidence fields must be filled. A coverage critic reads the whole ledger after a wave and looks for unmapped entry points, unchecked parallel paths and unjustified exclusions; it can reopen a unit (archiving the prior attempt) but can never propose a finding. That is what makes re-runs additive: a second run picks up the units the first left blocked or reopened, instead of re-auditing everything.
documents.s: The six phases and what each leaves behind

documents.t: The schema is strict about which fields each verdict may use, and the validator enforces it. Verdict Means Must have Must not have confirmed Independently reproduced in the sandbox from source, minimum observed effect only root_cause, intended_behavior, trace (entrypoint to sink), evidence, conditions, execution, remediation, severity, confidence claimed_root_cause, blockers, validation_plan, reason needs_validation Source-grounded, but blocked by one exact fact that cannot be resolved locally (a deployment setting, an owner-only config) claimed_root_cause, trace, evidence, blockers, validation_plan severity, execution, remediation rejected The verifier disproved it claimed_root_cause, trace, evidence, reason severity, execution, remediation, blockers Three consequences follow: A needs_validation finding has no severity by design. It is not a "medium"; it is a question for the code owner with an exact plan to answer it. NEEDS-VALIDATION.md exists so that list is not mistaken for a vulnerability list. Severity requires demonstrated impact, not a checklist miss. The calibration in SKILL.md: critical is unauthenticated code execution, full data access or account takeover; high is a complete defeat of an explicit control (auth bypass, cross-tenant access); medium is limited blast radius or uncommon preconditions; low is non-secret disclosure; informational is a confirmed observation with minimal impact. "Missing best practice" is explicitly not a finding. A clean run reports zero. The reporting guide says a proportional report may have no confirmed findings and must say so plainly. If your run "finds" twenty criticals in a small service, suspect the sandbox setup before you suspect the service. For readers of this section, the AI/LLM hunting guide is the sharpest part. Its opening rule: "Prompt injection alone is not a finding. Require a code-level boundary failure." A hunter must show the attacker, the affected principal, the execution identity, and an unauthorised action or disclosure, with a source trace from attacker-controlled input to the side effect. The patterns it sends hunters after are the ones in our prompt injection and MCP tool poisoning pages, but framed as code defects: tool arguments reaching SQL or a shell without handler-side validation, sub-agents inheriting full credentials instead of least authority, tool descriptions treated as authorisation, model output rendered into HTML or a command without encoding, cross-tenant context bleed from over-broad cache keys. Persuading the model to say something rude does not count.
documents.s: The three verdicts, and why only one carries a severity

documents.t: SKILL.md requires that any target-controlled code (tests, fixtures, the project's own build) run inside an OS-enforced sandbox with no external network, an isolated loopback namespace at most, read-only target source, writes confined to scratch/, and strict CPU, memory, process and file-size limits. Verifiers are told that if the sandbox is unavailable, the candidate simply stays unvalidated. Promotion from scratch/ to retained artifacts/ refuses symlinks, multiply-linked files, archives and recursive copies, and reopens nothing by path. This is the same threat model as our coding agents under attack page, turned inward: the repository you are auditing may be hostile, and its test suite is code you are about to execute. In Claude Code, that means running the audit with the sandbox and credential masking controls on, not in your daily shell with your real environment variables. One gotcha from Cloudflare's own harness applies if you nest Docker inside a container: it needs seccomp=unconfined and apparmor=unconfined "or it will silently fail." Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Install the skill where your agent can see it⌄ npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill --skill security-audit. The skills CLI (vercel-labs/skills) drops it into .claude/skills/ for Claude Code or .agents/skills/ for Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI; add -g for a global install, -a claude-code to target one agent. Read SKILL.md before you run it: it is the contract you are about to execute. ←PreviousNext→ 2Open the repo in a sandboxed session⌄ Start Claude Code in the target repo with sandboxing and credential masking on, no production credentials in the environment, and network egress limited to your model provider. The skill needs an agent that can spawn parallel sub-agents; Claude Code's Agent tool qualifies. ←PreviousNext→ 3Trigger full-audit mode deliberately⌄ Say 'security audit this codebase' or 'find security vulnerabilities in ./src'. A narrower question ('is this JWT check safe?') triggers guidance mode instead, which answers without creating a run directory. For a first run, point it at one bounded directory, not the monorepo root. ←PreviousNext→ 4Watch the run directory, not the chat⌄ Everything appears under ~/security-audit-skill/<repo>/run-1/. architecture.md should exist within minutes; coverage-ledger.json grows unit by unit; findings.json appears only after phase 4. If nothing has landed after recon, check the agent has a sandbox it can execute in. ←PreviousNext→ 5Validate mechanically before you read prose⌄ node <skill-dir>/validate-findings.cjs run-1/findings.json and node <skill-dir>/validate-coverage-ledger.cjs run-1/coverage-ledger.json. The skill runs these itself, but running them yourself is the cheapest way to catch a run that was cut short by a session limit. ←PreviousNext→ 6Read NEEDS-VALIDATION.md first, then re-run for coverage⌄ Answer each blocker (it is phrased as a question about your deployment) and either promote or drop the record. Then run again: the ledger's prior_status fields make the second run target blocked and reopened units rather than starting over. Cloudflare's own data says one run finds roughly half of what repeated runs find. ←PreviousNext→ Trigger phrases and the validator commands CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Full audit (creates ~/security-audit-skill/<repo>/run-N/) security audit this codebase find security vulnerabilities in ./src # Guidance mode (no run directory, no sub-agent fleet) is the session cookie handling in auth/session.ts safe against fixation? # After a run: mechanical checks, zero dependencies beyond Node node .claude/skills/security-audit/validate-findings.cjs ~/security-audit-skill/<repo>/run-1/findings.json node .claude/skills/security-audit/validate-coverage-ledger.cjs ~/security-audit-skill/<repo>/run-1/coverage-ledger.json # What the schema hard-limits (validator rejects beyond these) # findings.json: 5 MiB, 1,000 findings, 64 nesting levels # coverage-ledger.json: 5 MiB, 10,000 units, 1,000 entries per collection
documents.s: The sandbox rule is not advice

documents.t: The HN thread is mostly about the bill. One user reported "I threw 1M tokens for nothing in a medium codebase"; another put the practical ceiling at 150k tokens, "where you start hitting the dumb zone" of degraded attention. Those are anecdotes, not measurements, but they match the shape of the design: four recon agents, a wave of hunters, a verifier per candidate, a critic per wave, then a second verifier per surviving record. Cloudflare's fleet numbers give the honest scale: a standard 30k-line repository took 3 to 4 hours for about 100 raw findings, and across the fleet 58% of raw candidates survived validation (12,057 of 20,799). Three things in the skill itself keep it from running away: The budget-reserve rule. Before each wave the parent must reserve budget for the hunters, the validation pass, the post-wave critic and a final clean critic. HUNTING.md says: if those mandatory reserves do not fit, launch no hunter from that wave, and mark the units deferred with the budget reason. A run that ends with deferred units is a run that respected your budget, not a broken run. Narrow briefs. Every sub-agent gets one unit or one candidate. Cloudflare's harness kept each agent under 25% of its context window and credits that, more than any prompt wording, for the quality of findings. Guidance mode. Most security questions do not need the pipeline. Ask them directly and the skill answers without spawning anything. On your side: scope the first run to one directory; use a model with a large context and cheap cache reads for the hunters and a stronger one for verifiers; put a task budget on the session; and treat a run cut short by a session limit as partial, not failed, because the ledger records exactly where it stopped.
documents.s: What it costs, and how to keep it affordable

documents.t: It is not a replacement for static analysis and does not try to be. Cloudflare's post has a telling detail: they wired Semgrep into the harness and the agents "ignored it completely," preferring to read and run the code. Static tools give you deterministic, cheap, repeatable coverage of known patterns; this skill gives you expensive, probabilistic, reasoning-heavy coverage of boundary failures that pattern matchers cannot express, with a validation step that static tools do not have. Run both. And do not confuse it with PR-time review: Alibaba's open-code-review is a diff reviewer that runs in seconds per pull request; this is a multi-hour audit of a codebase at rest. Check yourself 0/6
